Overview

SBTK: Small Body Toolkit#

SBTK is a MATLAB toolkit for the interior density distribution of asteroids and other small bodies. It computes the gravity coefficients, center of mass and moments of inertia of a density model inside a polyhedral shape model, and it estimates the densities of such a model from measured gravity coefficients and moments of inertia. This site documents version 1.0.0.

Capabilities#

The following are implemented and covered by the test suite (Validation).

Density models
A background density, uniform components (spheres, triaxial ellipsoids, tori with any axis, layers below the surface, latitude–longitude–radius sectors) and an optional Gaussian random density field, clipped to a closed polyhedral shape model that is star-shaped about the expansion origin (Density distributions).
Gravity and moment calculations
Fully normalized spherical-harmonic coefficients to any degree, the center of mass and the inertia tensor of such a model, from exact polyhedral integrals over the cones between the expansion origin and each surface facet (Gravity and moment calculations).
Frames
Coefficients about the center of mass in the shape-model axes, the spin axes or the principal axes of inertia, and bodies, measurements and models carried into another frame (Frames of a gravity field).
Measurement sets
Gravity coefficients with a full covariance, moment-of-inertia elements, linear combinations of them, the libration ratio (B−A)/C and the center of mass, simulated (exact values, or with uncertainties and Gaussian noise) or read from files (Measurement sets).
Density estimation
Weighted least squares for the background density and the relative density of each component, with the total mass as an equality constraint, bounds on the densities, optional Tikhonov regularization, optional estimation of the position of spheres, ellipsoids and tori and of the axis of ellipsoids and tori, linearized 1σ uncertainties, and a χ2 test of the fit (Density estimation).
Comparison with a true model
For synthetic tests: the fraction of the variance of the true density explained by the estimate (R2), the largest value the chosen components allow, and a cell-by-cell comparison of density grids (Goodness of fit and model comparison).
Exchange packages
Plain-text packages of measurements, interior models and solutions with their units, frame and normalization, for comparisons between teams (Exchange packages).

The assumptions behind these calculations and what SBTK does not do are listed in Assumptions and limitations.

Status and requirements#

SBTK 1.0.0 has not been publicly released; its source repository is private. It requires MATLAB R2024b or newer with the Optimization Toolbox. The polyhedral gravity kernel is a compiled C function, provided for macOS and buildable on other platforms (Installation).

Overview

Assumptions and limitations#

This page lists the physical and numerical assumptions of SBTK 1.0.0 and the calculations it does not perform. Each item links to the page where the behavior is described.

Physical model#

  • The body is rigid and its density does not change with time. The gravity field is described by spherical-harmonic coefficients only; SBTK does not evaluate the potential or the gravitational acceleration at field points.
  • The density is a background density plus uniform components plus an optional Gaussian random field (Density distributions). Gradients within a component, other than through the random field, are not modeled.
  • The shape model is fixed and exact: its uncertainty is not propagated into the coefficients or the estimates.
  • The total mass is treated as exact. A measured GM enters only as the mass of the model; its uncertainty is not used (sbtk.exchange.read_shadr reads it and states that it is not used).

Geometry#

  • The shape model must be closed, ordered outward and star-shaped about the expansion origin: every facet must face away from it, except small overhangs holding less than 10⁻⁶ of the volume (Shape models). Bodies with larger overhangs cannot be integrated.
  • Layers and sectors are defined along rays from the expansion origin (the center of mass), not along the local surface normal (Coordinate systems).
  • The z-axis of the shape-model frame is taken as the spin axis and as a principal axis in the definition of the libration ratio (Moments of inertia). For a homogeneous body the axis of the largest moment is 3.8° from the shape-model z-axis for Didymos and 0.7° for Dimorphos.
  • Measurements, models and estimates of one body are in one frame, that of its shape model. sbtk.data.to_frame turns the axes of a measurement set only when its inertia rows are exact (the values of sbtk.data.simulate): rows with uncertainties would mix with correlations that the rows cannot hold. An inversion result cannot be transformed; invert in the frame wanted (Frames of a gravity field).
  • The spin axes are those of a body in principal-axis rotation (z along the axis of the largest moment); the rotation state itself is not modeled, and a spin pole known with an error is represented only by the noise of C¯21, S¯21.
  • When a field with uncertainties is moved to its center of mass or rotated into its principal axes, the covariance is propagated through the translation and rotation as linear maps; the uncertainty of the center of mass and of the principal axes themselves is not added.

Numerical integration#

  • Facet-cone integrals of the whole body are exact up to rounding (Gravity and moment calculations).
  • A sphere entirely inside the body is integrated as a point mass, which is exact.
  • Other components are integrated by sampling their radial extent along 9 sub-rays per facet and averaging the exact cone integrals over them. The result is exact when the radial interval is the same along every sub-ray of a cone and otherwise converges with the mesh resolution. Sector boundaries in latitude and longitude are resolved at the sub-ray spacing. The validation tests bound the errors for particular cases (Validation).
  • The crossings of a ray with a sphere, ellipsoid or torus are exact (roots of a quadratic or quartic). The integrals of these components are continuous in their position and orientation, but smooth only on scales larger than the ray spacing: where a ray grazes a component, its piece inside changes like a square root. The derivatives used to estimate geometry are therefore taken over steps of 0.1 m and 0.01° (Estimated geometry).
  • The random density field is integrated with one value per radial shell (24 shells per facet cone).

Estimation#

  • The measurements are linear in the densities. Positions and axes of components, when estimated, are found by Gauss–Newton iteration with a trust region and optional a priori constraints and limits; the geometry of layers and sectors, and of every component not marked for estimation, is fixed. An estimated geometry can absorb signal from structure the model lacks (Estimated geometry).
  • The uncertainties are the linearized covariance with the mass constraint and fixed parameters eliminated. The inequality bounds on the densities are not reflected in the covariance; fit.at_bound flags densities at a bound.
  • The χ2 test assumes Gaussian measurement errors with the stated covariance.
  • Simulated noise is Gaussian, drawn from the stated covariance of the coefficients and from the σ of each inertia row independently (sbtk.data.add_noise).
  • The libration ratio obtained from a libration amplitude (sbtk.data.libration_ratio_from_amplitude) uses planar forced libration to first order in the eccentricity, about a point-mass primary; free libration, the primary's oblateness and the mutual dynamics of a binary are not included.

Data formats#

  • Coefficients must be fully normalized without the Condon–Shortley phase (Gravity coefficients). sbtk.exchange.read_shadr rejects files whose header does not state full normalization; other conversions are the user's responsibility.
  • The exchange format gives the center of mass separately from the gravity coefficients, so a covariance between the center of mass and the other coefficients cannot be written (sbtk:exchange:correlatedCenterOfMass).
  • The SBTK measurement text format stores only the diagonal of the coefficient covariance; the .mat file keeps the full matrix (Results folders and figures).

Software#

  • MATLAB R2024b or newer with the Optimization Toolbox (lsqlin). The compiled kernel is provided for macOS (Apple silicon and Intel) and must be compiled once on other platforms (Installation).
  • Version 1.0.0 is not publicly released.

Getting started

Installation#

Requirements#

  • MATLAB R2024b or newer. SBTK 1.0.0 is tested with R2025a.
  • Optimization Toolbox, for lsqlin in the inversion.
  • A compiled copy of the polyhedral gravity kernel ComputePolyhedralCSBar_mex for the platform. Binaries for macOS on Apple silicon (.mexmaca64) and Intel (.mexmaci64) are included; on other platforms it must be compiled once (below).

No other toolboxes or external libraries are used.

Repository layout#

Folder Contents
toolbox/+sbtk/ The toolkit: one function per file, one folder per package (+units, +shape, …).
sbtk_setup.m Adds toolbox/ to the MATLAB path for the current session.
data/shapes/ Shape models in OBJ format, lengths in km.
data/gravity/ The OSIRIS-REx gravity field of Bennu (JPL, 2019).
examples/ Eight tutorial scripts, ex01_quick_start.m … ex08_moments_of_inertia.m (Tutorial scripts).
projects/ Runner scripts for the project template, Bennu and the Hera blind test (Projects).
results/ Output of every run, created on demand (Results folders).
tests/ Unit and integration tests, longer studies and test reports (Validation).
tools/ Maintenance scripts (reduced shape models, benchmark, README figures).
docs/ Notes in Markdown and earlier documents.

Setting the path#

Scripts in examples/ and projects/ add toolbox/ to the path themselves, so they can be run directly, also section by section. For the Command Window or other scripts, run sbtk_setup.m once per MATLAB session:

MATLAB
run("/path/to/SBTK/sbtk_setup.m")     % replace /path/to/SBTK with the location of the repository

It prints the version and the repository folder. sbtk.version and sbtk.root return them.

Runner scripts locate themselves with fileparts(which('<script name>')) rather than mfilename, because under Run Section MATLAB executes a temporary copy of the script. A copied runner must have the name inside which changed to its own file name.

Compiling the gravity kernel#

On platforms without a compiled kernel, with a C compiler configured for MATLAB (mex -setup C):

MATLAB
cd(fullfile(sbtk.root, "toolbox", "+sbtk", "+internal"))
mex -O ComputePolyhedralCSBar_mex.c

Then run the tests; the regression test compares the kernel output with stored values.

Files that are not in the repository#

File Needed by Source
data/shapes/g_01165mm_spc_obj_didy_0000n00000_v003.obj (Didymos, 1.165 m sampling, about 160 MB) sbtk.shape.bundled("didymos_highres"), tools/make_reduced_shapes.m, examples/ex01_quick_start.m DART shape models on ESA's SPICE server, spiftp.esac.esa.int/data/SPICE/HERA/kernels/dsk/
data/shapes/g_00243mm_spc_obj_dimo_0000n00000_v004.obj (Dimorphos, 0.243 m, about 160 MB) sbtk.shape.bundled("dimorphos_highres"), tools/make_reduced_shapes.m same
Uncertainty files of the Hera end-to-end test the simulation runners of projects/hera_hlp6 Hera working group; not distributed (Hera blind test)

All other shape models used in the examples and tests are in data/shapes/.

Checking the installation#

MATLAB
run(fullfile(sbtk.root, "tests", "run_tests.m"))

This runs 129 unit and integration tests in about three minutes and writes tests/reports/test_report.txt. Every test should pass (Validation).

Getting started

First script#

The script below runs the complete SBTK sequence on the shape model of the asteroid Didymos: it defines a body and a known interior (the true model), computes the exact gravity coefficients and moments of inertia of that interior, turns them into measurements by giving them uncertainties and adding noise, estimates the densities of the interior from those measurements, and compares the estimate with the true model. It takes about 15 s.

Script#

Replace /path/to/SBTK with the location of the repository and run the script.

MATLAB script: first_script.m
run("/path/to/SBTK/sbtk_setup.m")

% 1. Body: shape model, total mass [kg], reference radius of the gravity field [km]
body = sbtk.body.from_mass("Didymos", sbtk.shape.bundled("didymos"), 5.273e11, 0.43);
sbtk.body.summary(body)

% 2. A known interior: a dense core and a low-density surface layer
components = [sbtk.interior.sphere("core", body.centroid_km, 0.170, +450), ...   % center [km]: the center of figure
              sbtk.interior.layer("regolith", 0, 0.012, -900)];        % from 0 to 12 m below the surface
interior = sbtk.interior.create(components);

% 3. The true model and its exact gravity coefficients (degrees 1-4) and moments of inertia
[exact, truth] = sbtk.data.simulate(body, interior, 4, "first_script");

% 4. Measurements: 1-sigma uncertainties, then one realization of noise drawn from them
unc = sbtk.data.uncertainties([sbtk.units.offset_to_degree1(0.002, 0.43), ...   % degree 1: 2 m in the center of mass
                               1e-4, 2e-4, 4e-4], ...                           % degrees 2, 3, 4
                              2e-3, ...                                         % each inertia element / (M R_ref^2)
                              0.02);                                            % libration ratio
obs = sbtk.data.add_noise(sbtk.data.set_uncertainties(exact, unc), 1);
sbtk.data.summary(obs)

% 5. Estimate the relative densities of the same components (the values given above are not used)
fit = sbtk.invert.solve(body, components, obs);
sbtk.invert.summary(fit)

% 6. Compare the estimate with the true model
cmp = sbtk.compare.with_truth(body, truth, fit);
sbtk.compare.summary(cmp)
sbtk.plot.truth_vs_estimate(body, truth, fit);

What each step does#

  1. Body. sbtk.shape.bundled reads the DART shape model of Didymos (version 3, 9.3 m sampling, 49,152 facets) in km. sbtk.body.from_mass attaches the total mass M=5.273×1011 kg and the reference radius Rref=0.43 km of the coefficients; the bulk density M/V follows from the shape volume. The center of figure is 57 m from the origin of the shape-model file, which is not the body's center (Coordinate systems and origins).
  2. Interior. The core is a sphere of radius 170 m centered at the center of figure, body.centroid_km, 450 kg/m³ denser than the background; positions of spheres, ellipsoids and tori are shape-model coordinates, and the origin of this file is 57 m from the center of figure (Where to place components). The regolith is everything within 12 m of the surface, measured along rays from the center of mass, 900 kg/m³ lighter than the background. The background density is not given: it is set so that the total mass equals M (Density distributions).
  3. True model. sbtk.data.simulate computes the fully normalized gravity coefficients of degree 1 to 4, the six inertia elements and the libration ratio of this interior, about its center of mass (Gravity and moment calculations). It returns the true model (truth) and its exact values (exact), with no uncertainties: none are involved in the forward model. Degree-1 coefficients give the center of mass (Gravity coefficients).
  4. Measurements. sbtk.data.set_uncertainties gives every coefficient the 1σ of its degree and every inertia quantity its 1σ; sbtk.data.add_noise adds one Gaussian realization drawn from them with seed 1 (Measurement sets).
  5. Estimation. sbtk.invert.solve fits the background density and the relative density of each component to the 24 coefficients and, with the standard settings of sbtk.invert.options, to Ixx, Iyy and Izz, with the total mass as a constraint (Density estimation). The reduced χ2 of 1.11 with p=0.32 means that the model fits the data within their uncertainties (Goodness of fit).
  6. Comparison. sbtk.compare.with_truth evaluates both densities throughout the body. R2=0.37 is the fraction of the variance of the true density that the estimate explains; Rmax2=1 because the estimate uses the true geometry. Each component's estimate is within 2.1σ of its true density. The core is not resolved (its relative density is smaller than its 1σ): a core concentric with the body changes the field much as the background and the regolith layer do, so at these uncertainties the three are hard to tell apart. An off-center core, or more precise inertia measurements, separate them better (Tutorial ex08).

Conventions

Units#

SBTK uses one set of units in every function, structure and file. Every stored quantity that has a unit carries it at the end of its name; a name without a unit suffix is dimensionless.

Quantity Unit Name suffix Example
Lengths, positions, radii, depths km _km center_km = [0.02 0 0] (20 m along x)
Densities and relative densities kg/m³ _kgm3 drho_kgm3 = -900
Mass kg _kg mass_kg = 5.273e11
Volume km³ _km3 volume_km3 = 0.20336
Gravitational parameter GM km³/s² _km3_s2 GM_km3_s2 = 3.519e-8
Angles: latitude, longitude, rotations degrees _deg lat_deg = [40 90]
Gravity coefficients C¯lm, S¯lm dimensionless fully normalized (Gravity coefficients)
Moments of inertia in measurement sets I/(MRref2), dimensionless _norm Izz≈0.38 for Didymos with Rref=0.43 km
Moments of inertia in reports and text files kg m² _kgm2, _kg_m2 inertia_tensor_kg_m2
Gravitational constant G km³ kg⁻¹ s⁻² 6.67430 × 10⁻²⁰ (CODATA 2018), sbtk.units.G

sbtk.units.table prints this table in MATLAB.

Where units are given at input#

Two inputs carry a unit chosen by the caller:

  • Shape files. sbtk.shape.load and sbtk.shape.from_arrays require the length unit of the vertices, "km", "m" or "cm"; there is no default. sbtk.units.length_scale gives the conversion factor to km.
  • Moments of inertia in kg m². sbtk.units.moi_to_norm converts them to I/(MRref2) before sbtk.data.add_moi; sbtk.units.norm_to_moi converts back.

All other arguments take the units of the table; their names say which (sbtk.interior.sphere(name, center_km, radius_km, drho_kgm3)).

Conversions inside the toolkit#

Volumes are in km³ and densities in kg/m³, so the mass of a region of density ρ and volume V is ρV×109 kg. Moments of inertia are normalized with Rref in km, so I/(MRref2) needs no further factor; converting to kg m² multiplies by M(103Rref)2.

A center-of-mass offset d (km) along one axis corresponds to the fully normalized degree-1 coefficient d/(3Rref) (sbtk.units.offset_to_degree1); this is how a center-of-mass uncertainty enters sbtk.data.uncertainties.

Conventions

Coordinate systems and origins#

Shape-model frame#

Every position in SBTK is given in the shape-model frame: the origin and axes of the shape model in use, lengths in km. The z-axis is taken as the spin axis. Measurements, models and estimates of one body are in the same frame. sbtk.body.to_frame, sbtk.data.to_frame and sbtk.interior.to_frame carry a body, its measurements and its interior into another frame, for example the spin or principal axes of a true model, which then becomes the shape-model frame of everything that follows; sbtk.gravity.center_of_mass_frame expresses a gravity field in the shape-model, spin or principal axes (Frames of a gravity field).

Three points of the shape-model frame are distinct in general:

Point Definition Where SBTK stores it
Shape-model origin The point (0, 0, 0) of the shape file, chosen by its makers. For the DART Didymos model v003 it is 57 m from the center of figure; for the OSIRIS-REx Bennu model it is the center of mass found from the tracking data, 1.4 m from the center of figure; the HLP6 makers keep the origin of the DART files, and a package moved to the center of mass has its origin there (The shape model of a package). the origin of every coordinate
Center of figure Centroid of the volume enclosed by the shape model: the center of mass of a homogeneous body. body.centroid_km, props.centroid_km
Center of mass Center of mass of the density model. It differs from the center of figure when the density is not uniform. truth.com_km, obs.com_minus_cof_km, center_of_mass.txt of a measurement package

Expansion origin#

Gravity coefficients, first moments and the inertia tensor are computed about a point, the expansion origin. It is stored as origin_km in measurement sets (obs.origin_km), true models (truth.origin_km), inversion results (fit.origin_km) and geometries (geo.origin_km).

  • sbtk.data.simulate expands about the true center of mass of the simulated interior. Because layers and sectors are measured from the expansion origin, the center of mass depends on the origin; the simulation repeats the calculation about the new center of mass until it moves by less than 1 mm.
  • sbtk.data.expand_about expands a simulated field and its inertia about another point, for example [0 0 0], the origin of the shape model file, about which the HLP6 makers give their data.
  • Measurement packages read with sbtk.exchange.read_data are about the origin of their shape model file, as given, or about the measured center of mass; in the second case the inversion moves its predictions to the model's own center of mass (Density estimation).
  • sbtk.gravity.geometry takes any expansion origin about which the shape is star-shaped.

Positions of components#

Components are positioned in two different ways:

  • Spheres, ellipsoids and tori are placed in shape-model coordinates. center_km = [0 0 0] is the shape-model origin, not the center of figure. A torus lies about its axis, the third of component.axes, through component.center_km, in the plane at height_km along that axis; as constructed this is the z-axis through the origin. To place components from the center of figure, as recommended, use body.centroid_km: a sphere at body.centroid_km + offset, a torus with center_km = body.centroid_km (Where to place components).
  • Layers and sectors are measured along rays from the expansion origin: a layer's depth is the distance below the surface along the ray through the point; a sector's radial fraction is the distance from the origin divided by the distance from the origin to the surface along the same ray, and its latitude and longitude are measured about the origin.

Latitude and longitude#

For a vector 𝐱=(x,y,z) from the point of reference, latitude ϕ is measured from the xy-plane toward +z and longitude λ from +x toward +y:

𝐱=d(cosϕcosλ, cosϕsinλ, sinϕ).

sbtk.interior.latlon returns 𝐱 from ϕ, λ (degrees) and d (km). Sector longitudes are compared in [−180°,180°) with ranges that may extend beyond ±180°; for example [150°,240°] includes −170°.

Ellipsoid orientation#

An ellipsoid's semi-axes (a,b,c) lie along x, y, z before rotation. The rotation is R=Rz(ψ)Ry(θ)Rx(φ) with ψ the yaw (about z), θ the pitch (about y) and φ the roll (about x), given in degrees as [yaw pitch roll]. The columns of R (component.axes) are the ellipsoid's axes in the shape-model frame, and a point 𝐱 is inside when ∑i([R𝖳(𝐱−𝐜)]i/ai)2<1.

Axes of the inertia tensor and the coefficients#

Coefficients and inertia elements are given about the center of mass but in the axes of the shape-model frame, not in principal axes of inertia, so C¯21, S¯21 and S¯22 are in general not zero. For a homogeneous body, the axis of the largest moment of inertia is 3.8° from the shape-model z-axis for Didymos (DART v003, 1.165 m model) and 0.7° for Dimorphos (v004, 0.243 m model), and the axis of the smallest moment is turned 32.2° and 7.8° from x toward −y; in the shape-model axes the homogeneous Didymos has, about its center of mass with Rref = 410 m, C¯21=4.4×10−3, S¯21=9.4×10−4 and S¯22=−7.6×10−3. In the spin axes of a field (z along its axis of the largest moment) C¯21=S¯21=0, and in its principal axes also S¯22=0; the interior-model package states the principal axes of the true model (Frames of a gravity field). A field and its shape model must be in the same frame: when they are not, carry the shape model into the frame of the field with sbtk.body.to_frame. The libration ratio uses the principal moments in the xy-plane computed from the tensor (Moments of inertia), and takes z as a principal axis, which holds exactly in the spin and principal axes.

Conventions

Gravity coefficients#

Expansion of the potential#

Outside the smallest sphere about the expansion origin that encloses the body (the Brillouin sphere), the gravitational potential is

U(r,ϕ,λ)=GMr∑l=0L(Rrefr)l∑m=0lP¯lm(sinϕ)[C¯lmcos(mλ)+S¯lmsin(mλ)]

with r, latitude ϕ and longitude λ measured from the expansion origin in the axes of the shape-model frame (Coordinate systems). U>0 and the acceleration is +∇U. C¯00=1. Rref is a chosen reference radius; SBTK computes the coefficients and does not evaluate the series.

For a density ρ(𝐱) of total mass M the fully normalized coefficients are

C¯lm=1(2l+1)M∫ρ(rRref)lP¯lm(sinϕ)cos(mλ)dV, S¯lm=1(2l+1)M∫ρ(rRref)lP¯lm(sinϕ)sin(mλ)dV.

Normalization#

The coefficients are fully normalized (the 4π normalization of geodesy) and the associated Legendre functions have no Condon–Shortley phase (−1)m:

P¯lm=NlmPlm,Nlm=(2−δm0)(2l+1)(l−m)!(l+m)!,Plm(x)=(1−x2)m/2dmdxmPl(x),

so that the mean of [P¯lm(sinϕ)cos(mλ)]2 over the sphere is 1. Unnormalized coefficients are Clm=NlmC¯lm. Examples: N20=5, N21=5/3, N22=5/12, N30=7. The zonal coefficients are Jl=−Cl0=−2l+1C¯l0.

Coefficients in another convention must be converted before use: multiply by (−1)m to remove a Condon–Shortley phase, and by 1/Nlm to normalize. sbtk.exchange.read_shadr checks the normalization state in the file header and rejects unnormalized files; sbtk.io.read_jpl_gravity converts Jl to C¯l0.

Reference radius#

Changing the reference radius from R to R′ multiplies a coefficient of degree l by (R/R′)l; its variance by (R/R′)2l. sbtk.data.use_uncertainties applies this when it takes uncertainties from a data set with another reference radius. The examples on this site use Rref=0.43 km for Didymos and 0.10 km for Dimorphos.

Order of coefficients#

Vectors of coefficients are ordered by degree, and within a degree as Cl0, then Clm,Slm for m=1…l:

C00, C10, C11, S11, C20, C21, S21, C22, S22, C30, C31, S31, …

sbtk.gravity.labels returns the names to a given degree and pk describes the order. Measurement sets (obs) leave out C00 and store the names in obs.coef_labels. Where coefficients are given as matrices (sbtk.data.from_coefficients), C(l+1, m+1) holds C¯lm and S(l+1, m+1) holds S¯lm.

Degree 1 and the center of mass#

About an expansion origin O, with (xc,yc,zc) the center of mass minus O,

C¯10=zc3Rref,C¯11=xc3Rref,S¯11=yc3Rref.

About the center of mass these vanish. A measured center of mass enters a measurement set as these three coefficients with their uncertainties (sbtk.data.add_center_of_mass, sbtk.units.offset_to_degree1).

Frame of the coefficients: coef_about#

Each measurement set states what its coefficients are about (obs.coef_about):

  • 'origin': every coefficient, degree 1 included, and the inertia are about obs.origin_km. Simulated measurements are of this kind, with the origin at the true center of mass; sbtk.data.expand_about expands them about another point, for example [0 0 0], the origin of the shape model file. Packages about the origin of their shape model file, as the HLP6 makers send, are read as this kind.
  • 'center_of_mass': the coefficients of degree 2 and higher are about the body's center of mass, as a radio-science solution is; the degree-1 coefficients give the measured position of the center of mass relative to obs.origin_km. Packages about the center of mass and fields given to sbtk.data.add_center_of_mass are of this kind.

The inversion treats both as described in Density estimation. sbtk.data.move_origin changes the origin of 'center_of_mass' data; only the degree-1 values change.

Conventions

Frames of a gravity field#

A set of gravity coefficients means nothing without the point it is expanded about and the axes its latitude and longitude are measured in. Changing the point or the axes changes every coefficient but not the potential outside the body. This page covers:

  • the two changes used for small bodies: moving the expansion point to the center of mass, and turning the axes into the spin axes or the principal axes of inertia;
  • what each change makes zero;
  • the frames used for past measured and modeled fields;
  • how the frame affects a comparison with a homogeneous body;
  • which frame a team that makes data sets (maker) or estimates interiors from them (finder) should use, including for a body that may be tumbling, such as Dimorphos.
Frame Expansion point Axes Coefficients that vanish
Shape-model origin origin of the shape-model file shape-model axes none
Center of mass, shape-model axes center of mass shape-model axes C¯10, C¯11, S¯11
Center of mass, spin axes center of mass z along the axis of the largest moment, x toward the shape-model x-axis degree 1, and C¯21, S¯21
Center of mass, principal axes center of mass principal axes of inertia degree 1, and C¯21, S¯21, S¯22

In SBTK, coefficients are always expanded about the center of mass, in the axes of the shape model in use. The functions that work with frames are:

  • sbtk.gravity.center_of_mass_frame gives any field in the shape-model, spin or principal axes, with its principal axes and moments.
  • sbtk.plot.difference_from_homogeneous compares fields with the homogeneous body in any of the three.
  • sbtk.body.to_frame, sbtk.data.to_frame and sbtk.interior.to_frame carry a body, its measurements and its interior or true model into another frame. Every later step (simulation, packages, density grids, plots and comparisons) then works in that frame.

Summary#

  • The information is the same in every frame. The terms a frame makes zero become its definition: three coordinates of the center of mass and up to three angles. Both must be known relative to the shape model.
  • Spin axes reproduce fields measured by radio science from a body that rotates about its axis of the largest moment (OSIRIS-REx at Bennu): C¯21=S¯21=0, but S¯22≠0 because the x-axis is set by a surface feature, not by the mass distribution.
  • Principal axes suit rotational dynamics and bodies without a fixed spin axis (tumbling), and also a synchronous satellite.
  • Makers should send the measurements, the shape-model file, the true model and the density grid in one frame: spin axes for a body like Didymos, principal axes for Dimorphos (Which frame to use).
  • Finders should work in the frame of the package they receive and report in it.
  • Against a homogeneous body, the frame-independent results are the angles between the principal axes of the field and of the homogeneous body (axes_deg) and the power of each degree.

Moving the expansion point to the center of mass#

Degree 1#

About an expansion point O, with d=(xc,yc,zc) the center of mass minus O, the degree-1 coefficients are (Gravity coefficients)

C¯10=zc3Rref,C¯11=xc3Rref,S¯11=yc3Rref,

so they vanish about the center of mass and only there. A radio-science field is expanded about the center of mass because the spacecraft orbit is integrated about it. The position of the center of mass relative to the shape model is then a separate result, not part of the coefficients.

Higher degrees#

Moving the expansion point changes the coefficients of every degree. The coefficients of degree l about the new point are a linear combination of those of degree ≤l about the old point, weighted by powers of the displacement: lower degrees enter higher ones, never the reverse. For degree 2 this is the parallel-axis theorem. With IO=Icm+M(|d|21−dd𝖳) and the relations between the inertia tensor and the degree-2 coefficients (Moments of inertia), the unnormalized coefficients about O are

C20O=C20+2zc2−xc2−yc22R2,C21O=C21+xczcR2,S21O=S21+yczcR2, C22O=C22+xc2−yc24R2,S22O=S22+xcyc2R2,

where C2m, S2m are about the center of mass. The change is of second order in |d|/R. For the Didymos model below, the shape-model origin is 57 m from the center of mass (|d|/Rref = 0.13). As a result, C¯21 is 3.67×10−3 about the center of mass but 1.49×10−3 about the origin.

SBTK applies the translation to all degrees at once with a matrix built from the solid harmonics of point masses (sbtk.internal.sh_translation). The map is linear and finite, so the result is exact to rounding. The covariance of a measurement set is propagated through the same matrix.

Rotating the axes#

Principal axes from the degree-2 coefficients#

About the center of mass, the degree-2 coefficients fix the inertia tensor up to a multiple of the identity (MacCullagh's formula). With unnormalized coefficients,

I−Izz1MRref2=(C20−2C22−2S22−C21−2S22C20+2C22−S21−C21−S210).

Its eigenvectors are the principal axes of inertia. Its eigenvalues are the principal moments A≤B≤C minus Izz, divided by MRref2. SBTK orders the principal axes so that:

  • x′ is the axis of the smallest moment, y′ of the middle one and z′ of the largest;
  • each axis points to the positive side of the shape-model axis nearest to it;
  • the frame is right-handed (sbtk.internal.principal_axes).

An eigenvector has no sign, so a field in principal axes must state these choices. Reversing x′, for example, changes the sign of every coefficient that is odd in x, such as C¯31. When two moments are equal (a body symmetric about an axis), the axes in their plane are not defined.

What a rotation changes#

A rotation mixes the 2l+1 coefficients of each degree among themselves and with no others. For fully normalized coefficients, the mixing matrix of each degree is orthogonal, so the power of each degree,

σl2=∑m=0l(C¯lm2+S¯lm2),

is unchanged. SBTK builds the rotation matrix of each degree from the solid harmonics of points and their rotated images (sbtk.internal.sh_rotation). It is exact to rounding and also rotates a covariance.

Rotating the coefficients gives the same result as computing the field of the rotated body. The homogeneous field of the shape model with its vertices rotated into the principal axes equals the rotated homogeneous coefficients to 10−12 (testDifferenceInPrincipalAxes). Simulating a model whose body, components and random field are all carried into another frame also gives the rotated field, density and inertia (testChangeOfFrameEqualsSimulationInIt, Validation).

Principal axes#

In the principal axes the products of inertia vanish, so

C¯21=S¯21=S¯22=0,C20=A+B−2C2MR2,C22=B−A4MR2  (unnormalized),

and the whole degree-2 power is in C¯20 and C¯22. Degree 1 stays zero. No rotation makes the coefficients of degree 3 and higher zero: their values change but their power does not.

Spin axes#

The spin axes remove only the tilt of the axis of the largest moment:

  • z′ is the axis of the largest moment (the third principal axis);
  • x′ is the shape-model x-axis projected onto the plane normal to z′;
  • y′=z′×x′.

Of all frames with z′ along that axis, this one turns the shape-model axes the least.

The products of inertia that involve z vanish, so C¯21=S¯21=0. S¯22 is in general not zero, and the axis of the smallest moment lies at longitude

λ22=12atan2(S¯22,C¯22).

These are the conditions of a body-fixed frame of a body in principal-axis rotation, whose spin axis is the axis of its largest moment. The prime meridian here is the direction of the shape-model x-axis.

One field in four frames#

Below is the true model of the documentation example (core, torus, regolith, boulder and a random density field in the 9.3 m Didymos model, Results folders and figures) in the four frames, made by documentation/tools/make_samples.m:

Output
Example true model of Didymos (shape model didymos_g_9309mm_spc_obj_0000n00000_v003), R_ref = 0.43 km

Coefficients of the true model
coef  shape-model origin    center of mass    center of mass    center of mass
       shape-model axes  shape-model axes         spin axes    principal axes
C10       -4.572228e-02      0.000000e+00     -1.289007e-18     -3.710172e-20
C11        2.051808e-02      0.000000e+00      4.758569e-17      1.083458e-17
S11        5.758028e-02      0.000000e+00     -7.278009e-19      1.071706e-18
C20       -3.226924e-02     -3.256747e-02     -3.279488e-02     -3.279488e-02
C21        1.485208e-03      3.665234e-03      4.219222e-18     -1.689108e-17
S21       -5.134086e-03      9.837596e-04      1.553676e-17     -2.088580e-17
C22       -6.163254e-04      2.746776e-03      2.863367e-03      7.152014e-03
S22       -3.893035e-03     -6.638447e-03     -6.553811e-03     -5.354679e-17
  • About the shape-model origin, degree 1 is the largest part of the field: the origin is 57 m from the center of mass.
  • About the center of mass, degree 1 is zero. The parallel-axis terms above change the degree-2 coefficients; S¯21 even changes sign. Degrees 3 and 4 change too.
  • In the spin axes, C¯21 and S¯21 are zero to rounding. C¯22 and S¯22 barely change, because the tilt is only 4.0°.
  • In the principal axes, S¯22 is zero as well. C¯22 grows from 2.9×10−3 to 7.2×10−3: the axes turn by 33° about z, and the degree-2 power is the same in all three axes.
MATLAB script: A field in four frames
run("/path/to/SBTK/sbtk_setup.m")
body = sbtk.body.from_mass("Didymos", sbtk.shape.bundled("didymos"), 5.273e11, 0.43);
cof = body.centroid_km;                                             % positions from the center of figure
interior = sbtk.interior.create([sbtk.interior.sphere("core", cof, 0.170, +450), ...
                                 sbtk.interior.sphere("boulder", cof + sbtk.interior.latlon(25, 60, 0.250), 0.040, +900)]);
[exact, truth] = sbtk.data.simulate(body, interior, 4, "frames");

pk = sbtk.internal.sh_packing(4);
about_origin = truth.coef*sbtk.internal.sh_translation(-truth.origin_km, pk, body.R_ref_km)';
cs = sbtk.gravity.center_of_mass_frame(truth, body, "shape");        % degree 1 = 0
cz = sbtk.gravity.center_of_mass_frame(truth, body, "spin");         % and C21 = S21 = 0
cp = sbtk.gravity.center_of_mass_frame(truth, body, "principal");    % and C21 = S21 = S22 = 0
disp(table(cs.labels(1:8)', about_origin(2:9)', cs.coef(1:8)', cz.coef(1:8)', cp.coef(1:8)', 'VariableNames', ...
           ["coefficient" "about the origin" "shape axes" "spin axes" "principal axes"]))
power = @(c, l) sum(c(pk.deg(2:end) == l).^2);
fprintf("degree-2 power: %.6e (shape), %.6e (spin), %.6e (principal)\n", power(cs.coef, 2), power(cz.coef, 2), ...
        power(cp.coef, 2))
fprintf("axis of the largest moment %.2f deg from the shape-model z-axis; smallest at longitude %.1f deg\n", ...
        acosd(cp.principal(3, 3)), 0.5*atan2d(cz.coef(cz.labels == "S22"), cz.coef(cz.labels == "C22")))
fprintf("principal moments minus their mean, I/(M R^2): %.5f %.5f %.5f\n", cp.moments)

Comparison with the homogeneous body#

sbtk.plot.difference_from_homogeneous subtracts the field of the homogeneous body (density M/V) from a field. Both are taken about their own center of mass and expressed in the same axes, which belong to the field (frame argument). Degree 1 shows the center of mass minus the center of figure in those axes.

Output
True model minus the homogeneous body (both about their own center of mass)
coef   shape-model axes         spin axes    principal axes
J2        -3.231612e-03     -3.202163e-03     -3.202163e-03
C21        1.721657e-05      3.803159e-04      1.995238e-04
S21        1.005986e-04      2.168021e-04      3.896582e-04
C22       -2.103466e-04     -2.023064e-04     -4.383788e-04
S22        3.748967e-04      3.900043e-04     -2.924388e-05

axis of the largest moment from the shape-model z-axis:   true model 3.99 deg, homogeneous body 3.56 deg
axis of the smallest moment from the x-axis, in longitude: true model -33.3 deg, homogeneous body -33.2 deg
principal axes of the homogeneous body from those of the true model: tilt 0.44 deg, turn 0.11 deg
in the spin axes, axis of the smallest moment at (1/2) atan2(S22, C22) = -33.2 deg
principal moments minus their mean, I/(M R_ref^2): true model -0.03368 -0.01521 0.04889
                                               homogeneous body -0.03663 -0.01703 0.05367
center of mass - center of figure: -0.6 0.6 -0.1 m

What each frame shows:

  • Shape-model axes. Both fields keep their own C¯21, S¯21, S¯22. The differences mix two things: how far the interior turns the principal axes, and how much it changes the moments.
  • Spin axes. The field has C¯21=S¯21=0. The differences in these two terms are therefore minus the homogeneous body's own terms, and measure the tilt between the two axes of the largest moment (0.44° here). The differences in C¯22 and S¯22 contain the turn of the equatorial axes and the change in B−A.
  • Principal axes. The field has C¯21=S¯21=S¯22=0, so all of the misalignment is in the homogeneous body's terms: C¯21, S¯21 for the tilt and S¯22 for the turn (0.11° here). The difference in C¯22 is then the change in B−A.

For small angles, a rotation ε about one principal axis gives the homogeneous body a product of inertia proportional to ε times the difference of the other two moments:

|C¯21|≈C−A5/3MR2|εy|,|S¯21|≈C−B5/3MR2|εx|,|S¯22|≈B−A25/12MR2|εz|.

A mass excess m at (x,y,z) adds the products of inertia −mxz, −myz and −mxy. An excess at mid-latitude, away from the z-axis, tilts the axis of the largest moment. An excess in a direction between the x′- and y′-axes turns the axes in the equatorial plane.

In the example, (C−A)/(MR2)=0.083 and the tilt is 0.44°, which gives about 5×10−4, shared between C¯21 and S¯21 according to the direction of the tilt (2.0×10−4 and 3.9×10−4 in the principal axes): several times the 1σ of 10−4 assumed for degree 2. The plot returns the tilt and the turn as axes_deg. They, and the power of each degree, do not depend on the frame. Which frame to plot in depends on what the plot is for: the spin axes show the tilt directly in C¯21, S¯21, as a mission field would; the principal axes isolate all orientation differences in the homogeneous body's terms.

Frames used for measured and modeled fields#

Body-fixed frames of measured fields#

Gravity fields from radio science, and the shape models made with them, are given in a body-fixed (cartographic) frame:

  • z is the spin pole;
  • x points to the prime meridian, which is defined by a surface feature;
  • the origin is the center of mass found from the tracking data.

NEAR at Eros, Dawn at Vesta and Ceres, and OSIRIS-REx at Bennu all used frames of this kind. For a body in principal-axis rotation, the spin pole is the axis of the largest moment, so C¯21=S¯21=0. The prime meridian, however, has nothing to do with the mass distribution, so S¯22 is not zero.

Example: Bennu#

The OSIRIS-REx field of Bennu (JPL, 2019) and the Bennu shape model of the Bennu project, with the homogeneous Bennu in the same frame (documentation/tools/make_samples.m):

Output
Bennu: OSIRIS-REx gravity field (JPL 2019), shape model bennu_higher_qual, R_ref = 0.290 km
Body-fixed frame of the shape model and the field: z the spin pole, x the prime meridian, origin the center of mass
center of figure (centroid of the shape model): 1.34 -0.44 0.24 m from the origin (1.43 m)

coef           measured      1-sigma       homogeneous
C20       -1.926101e-02     5.20e-05     -1.875290e-02
C21       -2.178217e-14     7.75e-10      4.653539e-04
S21        3.000970e-15     7.75e-10     -9.420563e-05
C22        3.064995e-03     5.27e-05      3.538331e-03

axis of the largest moment from z:      measured 0.000 deg, homogeneous 0.754 deg
axis of the smallest moment, longitude: measured -9.83 deg, homogeneous -7.08 deg
between the axes of the largest moment of the field and of the homogeneous body: 0.754 deg
  • The origin is the center of mass. The field has no degree-1 terms. The centroid of the shape model (the center of figure) is 1.4 m from the origin, which itself is a sign of a non-uniform interior.
  • C¯21 and S¯21 are zero. Their values are ~10−14 with a 1σ of 8×10−10, so they were constrained to zero by taking the spin pole as the axis of the largest moment.
  • The frame is not the principal frame of the shape. The homogeneous Bennu has C¯21=4.7×10−4: its axis of the largest moment is 0.75° from the spin pole.
  • S¯22 is not zero. The measured field's axis of the smallest moment is at longitude −9.8°; the homogeneous body's is at −7.1°.

An interior model of Bennu must therefore tilt the axis of the largest moment by 0.75° and turn the equatorial axes by 2.7°. In Cavale et al. (Icarus) this is what the boulders that target C¯21/S¯21 and C¯22/S¯22 do. Rotating the field 9.8° about z would make S¯22 zero. It would also separate the field from the frame of the shape model, the maps and the navigation, and gain nothing, since the angle is already given by S¯22/C¯22.

Principal-axis frames#

Principal axes are used for:

  • rotational dynamics: the equations of rotation (Euler's equations) are diagonal in them;
  • model fields made for dynamics studies before a body is visited;
  • tumbling asteroids, whose rotation state is solved in the principal axes of the body (for example 4179 Toutatis and 99942 Apophis).

Which frame to use#

Makers#

The HLP6 makers agreed (20 October 2026) on the first of these two choices.

  1. The frame and origin of the shape model file, as distributed (the HLP6 choice). The package names the shape model file, which every team has. The gravity field is expanded about its origin, so degree 1 gives the center of mass and is not zero, and C¯21, S¯21 are those of the whole body in the shape-model axes (the homogeneous Didymos v003 alone has C¯21=3.7×10−3). The moments of inertia are about the same origin. Make the exact values with sbtk.data.simulate and expand them about [0 0 0] with sbtk.data.expand_about. Nothing is moved or rotated, so every team can compare with its own computation on the file as it is; a package of the homogeneous body lets the makers check that they compute the same field (Hera blind test).
  2. Moved to the center of mass and rotated (kept in SBTK; tutorial ex09). The origin is the center of mass of the true model, and the axes are - the spin axes for a body observed to rotate about one axis (Didymos): C¯21=S¯21=0 and S¯22≠0, as a mission field would look. The homogeneous Didymos v003 is already 3.8° off the shape-model z-axis, and the example true model 4.0°; - the principal axes for a body that may be tumbling, or a synchronous satellite (Dimorphos; Tumbling bodies).

The body, the exact values and the true model are carried into that frame (code below), and the package contains the moved and rotated shape model.

In either case, use one frame for everything you send: the measurements, the shape model file, the interior-model package and the density grid, so that the receiving teams' density grids coincide with yours. Define the interior in the frame of the shape model file.

Points to check:

The next three points concern the moved and rotated frame.

  • The frame of the true model is exact. A real spin pole has an error ε, which leaves |C¯21|,|S¯21|≈(C−A)ε/(5/3MR2), about 1.1×10−4 for Didymos at ε=0.1°. A package of exact values has C¯21=S¯21=0 exactly; the 1σ a receiving team gives them stands for the pole error. If that 1σ is much smaller, the data define the pole more precisely than a mission would.
  • The rotation carries information about the interior. It is the same information the field gives in the shape-model axes (C¯21, S¯21), and the same a mission's pole and field give together, no more. conventions.txt records the change of frame from the original shape-model file.
  • The origin is the center of mass. Mission body-fixed frames put the origin at the estimated center of mass (Bennu: the centroid is 1.4 m from the origin). The shape model, the gravity field and the moments of inertia then share one origin, and a receiving team has nothing to move. The origin of the original file has no physical meaning (Didymos v003: 57 m from the center of figure). Moving the origin adds no information: a package of exact values gives the exact center of mass in center_of_mass.txt anyway, together with the center of figure, and their offset, which the interior sets, is the same in every frame. For a package with noise, a mission's origin is the measured center of mass; translate to it after sbtk.data.add_noise (a translation applies to any set).
  • Uncertainties belong to a frame. A table of one σ per coefficient describes the solution it comes from, in that solution's axes. In other axes the same covariance has correlations, and two coefficients of one degree can have very different σ (in a principal-axis solution, for example, σ(C¯22)≪σ(S¯22)). Applying such a table coefficient by coefficient in other axes is an approximation. sbtk.data.to_frame rotates a full covariance exactly.
  • Components tied to the rotation. A component defined in the shape-model frame, such as a torus about its z-axis, is tilted relative to the spin axes by the angle between them. If it should lie about the spin axis, as an equatorial torus does, set its axis with sbtk.interior.align_with_spin_axis before simulating (Axes of components). interior_model.txt gives the geometry in the frame of the package.

Finders#

  1. Work in the frame of the package. Its shape model and its measurements are in the same frame. Define the components of the inversion model in that frame.
  2. A package in the frame and about the origin of the shape model file (the HLP6 choice): fit the coefficients, degree 1 included, and the moments of inertia as they are, about the origin of the file, with no change of frame. sbtk.exchange.read_data returns them about [0 0 0] (coef_about = 'origin'), and the inversion predicts the model's coefficients and inertia about the same point. The homogeneous body already has a degree 1 (its center of figure, 57 m from the origin of the Didymos v003 file) and a C¯21, S¯21; the interior has to account for the difference, in particular the offset of the center of mass from the center of figure.
  3. If a field and its shape model are in different frames (for example a field in principal axes and a shape model in its own frame, with the rotation given), rotate the shape model with sbtk.body.to_frame, not the measurements.
  4. Report the solution and its density grid in the frame of the package, so that the cells coincide with those of the interior-model package.
  5. To interpret the orientation of the field, compare it with the homogeneous body in the spin or principal axes, and quote the angles axes_deg.

Packages moved to the center of mass and rotated#

MATLAB script: Measurement and interior-model packages in the spin axes
run("/path/to/SBTK/sbtk_setup.m")
body = sbtk.body.from_mass("Didymos", sbtk.shape.bundled("didymos"), 5.273e11, 0.43);
cof = body.centroid_km;                                                      % place from the center of figure
torus = sbtk.interior.torus("torus", 0.370, 0.055, 0, -500);
torus.center_km = cof;
interior = sbtk.interior.create([sbtk.interior.sphere("core", cof, 0.170, +450), torus]);
interior = sbtk.interior.align_with_spin_axis(body, interior, "torus", 0.01, 20);   % torus about the spin axis
[exact, truth] = sbtk.data.simulate(body, interior, 4, "spin example");      % in the frame of the shape-model file

spin  = sbtk.gravity.center_of_mass_frame(truth, body, "spin");             % or "principal"
body  = sbtk.body.to_frame(body, spin.com_km, spin.axes, "didymos_v003_com_spin_axes");   % origin: center of mass
truth = sbtk.interior.to_frame(truth, spin.com_km, spin.axes);
exact = sbtk.data.to_frame(exact, spin.com_km, spin.axes);                   % C21 = S21 = 0

folder = tempname;                                                           % exact values: no uncertainties, no noise
data  = sbtk.exchange.write_data(folder, "DOC-DATA9-Didymos", body, exact, "Example team");
model = sbtk.exchange.write_model(folder, "DOC-MOD9-Didymos", "DOC-DATA9-Didymos", body, truth, exact, 0.040, ...
                                  "Example team");
[received, rbody] = sbtk.exchange.read_data(data);                           % what a receiving team reads
fprintf("%s: C21 %+.1e, S21 %+.1e\n", rbody.shape.name, received.coef(5:6))
unc = sbtk.data.uncertainties([sbtk.units.offset_to_degree1(0.002, 0.43), 1e-4, 2e-4, 4e-4], 2e-3, 0.02);
received = sbtk.data.set_uncertainties(received, unc);                       % the receiving team's uncertainties

The package contains DOC-DATA9-Didymos_didymos_v003_com_spin_axes.obj, named after the package because no other package has this shape model: the DART shape model with every vertex moved to the center of mass of the true model and rotated into its spin axes, x′=(x−c)A with c the center of mass and the columns of A the spin axes, both in the frame of the original file. The center of mass is at the origin of that file, and the gravity field, the moments of inertia and every position of both packages are in its frame, so a receiving team uses it as it is. Its conventions.txt states what the origin and the axes are (read from the values: the center of mass at the origin, C¯21=S¯21=0) and the change of frame from the original file. interior_model.txt describes the torus with its axis in the new frame: along z, because it was aligned with the spin axis. The package has exact values without uncertainties (Packages of exact values). The HLP6 runners have a FRAME setting that does this (Hera blind test).

Tumbling bodies and Dimorphos#

The gravity field does not depend on the rotation. The coefficients and the principal axes describe the mass distribution in a body-fixed frame and do not change with the rotation state.

What changes for a tumbling body is the meaning of "spin axis". In principal-axis rotation the body spins about its axis of the largest moment. A tumbling body (non-principal-axis rotation) has angular momentum fixed in space, but its angular velocity moves through the body, so no body-fixed axis is the spin axis. The rotation is described in the principal axes, in which Euler's equations are diagonal.

Dimorphos. Before the DART impact, Dimorphos was taken to rotate synchronously with its orbit about Didymos. In that state the body-fixed frame (z the orbit normal, x toward Didymos on average) is close to its principal axes. The impact changed its orbit, and simulations (Agrusa et al., 2021, Icarus) showed that it could have excited non-principal-axis rotation. Its present rotation state is not known; Hera will measure it. The DART shape model v004 is from before the impact, and the impact may have changed the shape.

For making and finding data sets this means:

  • Frame. Use the principal axes. They suit a tumbling body and, within a few degrees, a synchronous one. The spin axes remain a valid body-fixed frame for a tumbler, but their z-axis is no longer a spin axis.
  • What the rotation measures.
  • A librating synchronous body gives the libration ratio (B−A)/C (Moments of inertia).
  • A tumbling body gives two ratios of principal moments, for example A/C and B/C, because Euler's equations depend only on ratios. Together with the degree-2 field, which fixes B−A and C−(A+B)/2 in units of MR2, two ratios fix all three moments, including the trace that the gravity field cannot give.

A tumbling Dimorphos would therefore constrain the radial density structure better than a librating one. - Moment-ratio measurements in SBTK. In principal axes the ratios are the linear rows Ixx−rAIzz=0 and Iyy−rBIzz=0, with σ = σrIzz, added with sbtk.data.add_moi_row. In other axes the weights follow from the principal axes of the degree-2 field. The exchange format gives inertia elements and the libration ratio but not moment ratios. A group can give Ixx, Iyy, Izz in principal axes, which are A, B, C, or agree on an extension of the format. - The interior model is made as before. The true interior is defined in the shape-model frame and carried into the principal axes; the rotation state affects only the rotation measurements. Finders invert as usual in the frame of the package.

MATLAB script: Ratios of principal moments of a tumbling Dimorphos
run("/path/to/SBTK/sbtk_setup.m")
body = sbtk.body.from_mass("Dimorphos", sbtk.shape.bundled("dimorphos"), 2.700e9, 0.10);
interior = sbtk.interior.create(sbtk.interior.ellipsoid("core", body.centroid_km + [0.004 0 0], [0.045 0.040 0.028], ...
                                                        [15 0 0], +400));
[exact, truth] = sbtk.data.simulate(body, interior, 3, "tumbling example");
cp = sbtk.gravity.center_of_mass_frame(truth, body, "principal");
exact = sbtk.data.to_frame(exact, [0 0 0], cp.axes);           % Ixx = A, Iyy = B, Izz = C
I = exact.moi_tensor_norm;
rA = I(1, 1)/I(3, 3);  rB = I(2, 2)/I(3, 3);  sigma_r = 0.005;
obs = sbtk.data.select_moi(exact, strings(1, 0));
obs = sbtk.data.add_moi_row(obs, "A_over_C", [1 0 -rA 0 0 0], 0, sigma_r*I(3, 3));
obs = sbtk.data.add_moi_row(obs, "B_over_C", [0 1 -rB 0 0 0], 0, sigma_r*I(3, 3));
fprintf("A/C = %.4f, B/C = %.4f; off-diagonal elements in principal axes: %.1e\n", rA, rB, max(abs(I(~eye(3)))))

Conventions

Moments of inertia#

Inertia tensor#

The inertia tensor about the expansion origin, in the axes of the shape-model frame, is

Iij=∫ρ(r2δij−xixj)dV,

so the products of inertia carry the minus sign: Ixy=−∫ρxydV. SBTK stores the six independent elements in the order [Ixx,Iyy,Izz,Ixy,Ixz,Iyz], normalized by MRref2 in measurement sets and models (truth.inertia_norm, fm.inertia_norm) and in kg m² in reports (Units).

Relation to the degree-2 coefficients#

About the center of mass, in the same axes and with the same Rref, the unnormalized degree-2 coefficients are

C20=Ixx+Iyy−2Izz2MR2,C21=−IxzMR2,S21=−IyzMR2,C22=Iyy−Ixx4MR2,S22=−Ixy2MR2,

and C¯lm=Clm/Nlm (Gravity coefficients). These relations are verified by testDegreeTwoAndInertia (Validation).

The degree-2 field fixes five combinations of the six elements. The sixth, the trace (for example through the polar moment Izz), is the information that a moment-of-inertia measurement adds to the gravity field: it measures how strongly the mass is concentrated toward the center, which the gravity coefficients alone cannot distinguish from other radial distributions of the same field. Tutorial ex08 compares inversions with different inertia measurements.

Measurement rows#

A moment-of-inertia measurement is one linear combination of the elements:

𝐰·[Ixx,Iyy,Izz,Ixy,Ixz,Iyz]MRref2=v±σ,

stored as a moi row with weights 𝐰, value v and sigma σ. A single element has one weight equal to 1 (sbtk.data.add_moi); any other combination is added with sbtk.data.add_moi_row. sbtk.data.select_moi chooses the rows a data set contains and opts.moi_labels (opts.moi_labels) the rows an inversion fits.

Libration ratio#

The libration ratio is

k=B−AC,

with A≤B the principal moments of inertia about the axes in the xy-plane and C=Izz; the spin axis z is taken as a principal axis, which holds exactly in the spin or principal axes of the field (Frames of a gravity field). For a tumbling body the rotation gives ratios of principal moments instead (Tumbling bodies). With a the angle of those principal axes from the x-axis,

B−A=cos(2a)(Iyy−Ixx)+sin(2a)·2Ixy,

which is linear in the tensor once a is fixed. sbtk.data.add_libration takes a from the measured C¯22 and S¯22, since (cos(2a),sin(2a)) is proportional to (C22,−S22) about the center of mass, and adds the linear row

cos(2a)(Iyy−Ixx)+sin(2a)·2Ixy−kIzz=0±σkIzz,

labeled libration, with weights [−cos(2a),cos(2a),−k,2sin(2a),0,0] (sbtk.internal.libration_weights). Together with C22 and S22, which give B−A, the ratio measures C with a relative precision of about σk/k. If C22=S22=0 the principal axes in the xy-plane are undefined and the function stops with sbtk:data:axisymmetric.

Libration ratio from a libration amplitude#

For a synchronously rotating satellite in a Keplerian orbit of eccentricity e about a point-mass primary, the forced libration angle γ of the long axis from the direction to the primary obeys, to first order in e,

γ¨+3n2kγ=2en2sinM,

with mean motion n and mean anomaly M, so γ=GsinM with

G=2e3k−1,k=13(1+2eG).

sbtk.data.libration_ratio_from_amplitude returns k and its 1σ from G, e and their uncertainties by first-order error propagation. G<0 for k<1/3 (elongations up to about 1.4 : 1). The sensitivity of G to k grows near k=1/3, where the free libration period equals the orbital period. Free libration, the primary's oblateness and the mutual dynamics of a binary are not included.

Models and calculations

Shape models#

A shape model is a closed triangular mesh, stored in SBTK as a shape structure with vertices in km.

Reading and creating shape models#

Function Input
sbtk.shape.load Wavefront OBJ file: v x y z and f i j k records; normals, texture coordinates and faces written as f i/t/n are accepted, other records ignored. The length unit of the file ("km", "m" or "cm") is a required argument.
sbtk.shape.bundled A model shipped with SBTK, by name (table below).
sbtk.shape.from_arrays Face and vertex arrays with their length unit.
sbtk.shape.ellipsoid A triaxial ellipsoid: an icosahedron subdivided level times (20·4^level facets) with vertices projected onto the ellipsoid.
sbtk.shape.write_obj Writes a shape model as OBJ with vertices in km.

Requirements#

The forward model integrates over the cones from the expansion origin to every facet (Gravity and moment calculations). The mesh must therefore be

  • closed: every edge is shared by exactly two facets that traverse it in opposite directions;
  • ordered outward: the enclosed volume computed from the facets is positive;
  • star-shaped about the expansion origin: every facet faces away from it, so that each ray from the origin crosses the surface once.

sbtk.shape.properties reports all three, the last about the centroid (props). sbtk.gravity.geometry stops with sbtk:gravity:notStarShaped when facets face the expansion origin, unless their cones hold less than 10−6 of the volume. Such small overhangs occur in high-resolution models: seen from a point 4.6 m from the center of figure of the 0.243 m Dimorphos model, two facets of 0.025 m² face it, with 2.5×10−9 of the volume. Their cones count with their sign, which is exact for the body (the signed cones of any closed mesh add up to its volume integrals) and leaves an error of the order of their volume in layers and sectors.

MATLAB script: Checking a shape model
run("/path/to/SBTK/sbtk_setup.m")
shape = sbtk.shape.bundled("didymos");
p = sbtk.shape.properties(shape)
fprintf("volume %.5f km^3, centroid [%.1f %.1f %.1f] m\n", p.volume_km3, 1e3*p.centroid_km)

Shape models in the repository#

Files in data/shapes/, lengths in km, in the body-fixed frame of each model (z along the spin axis).

bundled name File Sampling Facets Volume (km³) Description
"didymos" didymos_g_9309mm_spc_obj_0000n00000_v003.obj 9.3 m 49,152 0.20336 DART stereophotoclinometry (SPC) model of Didymos, version 3
"didymos_highres" g_01165mm_spc_obj_didy_0000n00000_v003.obj 1.165 m 3,145,728 0.20381 The same model at full resolution (not in the repository, Installation)
"didymos_every8" g_01165mm_spc_obj_didy_0000n00000_v003_every8.obj 9.3 m 49,152 0.20375 Every 8th grid point of the 1.165 m model
"dimorphos" g_00243mm_spc_obj_dimo_0000n00000_v004_every8.obj 1.94 m 49,152 0.0017597 Every 8th grid point of the DART SPC model of Dimorphos, version 4 (before the DART impact)
"dimorphos_highres" g_00243mm_spc_obj_dimo_0000n00000_v004.obj 0.243 m 3,145,728 0.0017602 The Dimorphos model at full resolution (not in the repository)
"bennu" bennu_higher_qual.obj 196,608 OSIRIS-REx shape model of Bennu
"example_asteroid" example_asteroid.obj A synthetic body of about 1.2 km, used by the project template
"dimorphos_placeholder" dimorphos_placeholder.obj 20,480 A synthetic stand-in used by tests; not a mission model

The 9.3 m Didymos file is distributed separately by the DART team and is not a subsample of the 1.165 m model. For a homogeneous body with Rref=0.43 km, tools/make_reduced_shapes.m gives these differences from the full-resolution models:

Model compared with the full resolution Volume Center of figure Largest coefficient difference, degree 2 / 3 / 4
didymos_every8 −0.030% 0.01 m 1.2e-5 / 5.0e-6 / 2.8e-6
didymos (9.3 m file) −0.224% 0.35 m 3.1e-4 / 1.7e-4 / 4.2e-5
dimorphos (every 8th point, Rref=0.10 km) −0.031% 0.00 m 1.5e-5 / 1.3e-6 / 5.1e-6

Differences of this size between the shape used to simulate data and the shape used to invert them act as a systematic error in the coefficients. Measurement packages therefore name the shape model they were made with, and include it unless it is one of SBTK's files as distributed (Exchange packages). The HLP6 makers agreed on didymos_highres, the 1.165 m model (Didymos and Dimorphos values).

Reducing high-resolution models#

High-resolution shape models have more facets than coefficients to degree 4 or 5 require. Two functions reduce them:

  • sbtk.shape.reduce_spc keeps every step-th grid point of an SPC model stored in its grid order (6 cube faces of (q+1)2 vertices, 12q2 facets), triangulated as the original. The grid is radial, so the result stays star-shaped about the body's center; a cell whose triangles would face the center is split along its other diagonal.
  • sbtk.shape.reduce applies MATLAB's reducepatch to any mesh and checks that the result is closed, outward and star-shaped about its centroid; a general reduction can fold facets, in which case it stops with sbtk:shape:reduce.
MATLAB
big   = sbtk.shape.load("g_00243mm_spc_obj_dimo_0000n00000_v004.obj", "km");   % q = 512, 3,145,728 facets
small = sbtk.shape.reduce_spc(big, 8);                                         % q = 64, 49,152 facets
sbtk.shape.write_obj(small, "g_00243mm_spc_obj_dimo_0000n00000_v004_every8.obj");

Bodies#

A body (body) is a shape model with its total mass and the reference radius of its gravity coefficients. sbtk.body.from_mass takes the mass; sbtk.body.create takes the bulk density and computes the mass from the volume. The bulk density is M/V; the background density of a model with components differs from it (Density distributions).

MATLAB fragment. Requires the variables defined in Checking a shape model.
body = sbtk.body.from_mass("Didymos", shape, 5.273e11, 0.43);    % mass [kg], reference radius [km]
sbtk.body.summary(body)
sbtk.plot.shape(body);

Models and calculations

Density distributions#

Density model#

The density at a point 𝐱 inside the body is

ρ(𝐱)=ρbg+∑c:𝐱∈cΔρc+δρ(𝐱),

where

  • ρbg is the background density, the density outside every component;
  • Δρc is the relative density of component c: its density minus the background density (component.drho_kgm3). Where components overlap their relative densities add. Everything outside the shape model is excluded;
  • δρ is an optional Gaussian random density field.

The background density is not an input of a simulation: sbtk.gravity.forward sets it so that the total mass equals the mass of the body,

ρbg=M−∑cΔρcVc−∫δρdVV,

with Vc the volume of component c inside the body. In an inversion it is estimated or held at the bulk density (Density estimation). sbtk.data.simulate stops with sbtk:data:negativeDensity if the density is negative anywhere.

An interior model (interior) holds the components and the random field; sbtk.interior.create builds it. sbtk.interior.density_at evaluates the density of any model at given points.

Component types#

Each constructor returns one component. A point 𝐱 (shape-model frame) belongs to the component when the condition in the table holds. 𝐨 is the expansion origin, ts the distance from 𝐨 to the surface along the ray through 𝐱, r=|𝐱−𝐨|.

Type Constructor Membership condition Measured from
Sphere sbtk.interior.sphere(name, center_km, radius_km, drho_kgm3) |𝐱−𝐜|<rs shape-model origin
Ellipsoid sbtk.interior.ellipsoid(name, center_km, semi_axes_km, angles_deg, drho_kgm3) ∑i([R𝖳(𝐱−𝐜)]i/ai)2<1 shape-model origin
Torus sbtk.interior.torus(name, ring_radius_km, tube_radius_km, height_km, drho_kgm3) (q12+q22−Rr)2+(q3−h)2<rt2 with q=A𝖳(x−c) its axis: the third axis of component.axes A through component.center_km c (the shape-model z-axis unless set)
Layer sbtk.interior.layer(name, top_depth_km, bottom_depth_km, drho_kgm3) dtop≤ts−r<dbottom rays from 𝐨
Sector sbtk.interior.sector(name, frac, lat_deg, lon_deg, drho_kgm3) fin≤r/ts<fout, ϕ1≤ϕ<ϕ2 (≤90° if ϕ2=90°), λ in [λ1,λ2) modulo 360° rays from 𝐨

Notes on the types:

  • Sphere. A sphere entirely inside the body is integrated exactly as a point mass; one that crosses the surface is clipped. Its center can be estimated in an inversion (component.estimate_position).
  • Ellipsoid. R=Rz(yaw)Ry(pitch)Rx(roll) (Coordinate systems).
  • Torus. Lies about its axis, the shape-model z-axis through the origin as constructed; set component.center_km to move it (for example to the center of figure) and turn it with sbtk.interior.set_axis. It may be buried, cross the surface or extend outside the body. Only the part inside the body counts.
  • In another frame. sbtk.interior.to_frame moves and turns every component with the frame: centers, the axes of ellipsoids, the axis of a torus and the axes in which a sector's latitude and longitude are measured (component.axes), and the random field. The density at every point is unchanged (Frames of a gravity field).
  • Layer. Depth is measured along the ray from the expansion origin, not along the surface normal; layer("regolith", 0, 0.012, …) is the outermost 12 m along each ray.
  • Sector. Radial fractions follow the shape: sector("shell", [0.5 0.75], [-90 90], [-180 180], …) is a shell between half and three quarters of the way to the surface. sbtk.interior.sector stops with sbtk:interior:sectorRange unless each range increases and the longitude range spans at most 360°.

sbtk.interior.latlon converts latitude, longitude and distance to a position, for example to place a sphere. sbtk.interior.summary prints a list of components.

Where to place components#

Spheres, ellipsoids and tori are placed in the coordinates of the shape-model file, so a center [0 0 0] is the origin of the file. Layers and sectors are measured along rays from the expansion origin, which in a simulation is the center of mass. The center of figure is the centroid of the shape model (body.centroid_km), the center of mass of a homogeneous body (Coordinate systems).

Place components from the center of figure:

  • It depends only on the shape. The center of mass of a model depends on its components, so positions measured from it would depend on what they define.
  • "Central" means concentric with the figure. An offset of a component from the center of figure is what moves the center of mass away from it, which the data measure (degree 1). That offset should be chosen, not inherited from where the file has its origin.
  • The origin of a shape-model file can be far from the body's center. It is 57 m from the center of figure in the DART Didymos model v003 (13% of its radius), 0.7 m in the DART Dimorphos model v004, and 1.4 m in the OSIRIS-REx Bennu model, whose origin is the center of mass found from the tracking data.
MATLAB fragment. Requires the variables defined in An interior model of Didymos.
cof = body.centroid_km;                                  % center of figure
core = sbtk.interior.sphere("core", cof + [0.010 0 0], 0.170, +450);   % 10 m from the center of figure along x
t = sbtk.interior.torus("torus", 0.370, 0.055, 0, -500);
t.center_km = cof;                                       % about the z-axis through the center of figure

In the interior of Cavale et al. (Icarus) for Bennu (Bennu) every position is from the origin of the Bennu shape model, which is its measured center of mass: there the two choices differ by 1.4 m. With a pre-mission model such as the DART Didymos v003 they differ by 57 m. A central core placed at the origin is then 57 m off center, and in a Didymos model it moves the center of mass about 2 m from the center of figure.

Axes of components#

The axis of a torus, the axes of an ellipsoid and the axes in which a sector's latitude and longitude are measured are component.axes; their third axis is "the axis" of the component.

  • sbtk.interior.set_axis(c, direction) turns a component so that its axis points along a direction (the smallest rotation, about its center).
  • sbtk.interior.align_with_spin_axis(body, interior, names, tol_deg, max_iter) sets the axis of the named components along the axis of the largest moment of the whole model: the spin axis of a body in principal-axis rotation, about which an equatorial torus forms. That axis depends on the components themselves, so the function iterates (simulate to degree 2, take the axis, turn the components, repeat) until the axis moves less than tol_deg, at most max_iter times (sbtk.internal.fixed_point, sbtk:iteration:notConverged). Other components are not changed.
MATLAB fragment. Requires the variables defined in An interior model of Didymos.
cof = body.centroid_km;
t = sbtk.interior.torus("torus", 0.370, 0.055, 0, -500);
t.center_km = cof;
model = sbtk.interior.create([sbtk.interior.sphere("boulder", cof + sbtk.interior.latlon(25, 60, 0.250), 0.040, +900), t], ...
                             sbtk.interior.no_random_field());
[model, spin_axis, n] = sbtk.interior.align_with_spin_axis(body, model, "torus", 0.01, 20);
fprintf("torus axis %.2f deg from the shape-model z-axis after %d simulations\n", acosd(spin_axis(3)), n)

For a true model these are modeling choices. In an inversion the geometry of a torus or an ellipsoid (center, height, axis) can be estimated instead, with bounds and priors (Density estimation).

Sector grids#

sbtk.interior.sector_grid(frac_edges, lat_edges_deg, lon_edges_deg) divides the whole body into sectors, one per radial shell, latitude band and longitude band, named s<shell><lat><lon> (s111 is the innermost shell, the southernmost band, the first longitude band). This is a density model without an assumed structure. Because the sectors fill the body, the background density and a common change of all sector densities are indistinguishable: an inversion must hold the background at the bulk density (background = "bulk") or use regularization (Density estimation).

Random density field#

sbtk.interior.random_field(sigma_kgm3, corr_length_km, seed) is a Gaussian random field with standard deviation σ and correlation exp(−|Δ𝐱|2/(2L2)), represented by 300 Fourier modes (random_field). It is defined at every point independently of the expansion origin and is the same for the same seed. sbtk.interior.no_random_field gives no field. A random field is used in simulations; inversions do not estimate one.

Prescribed components#

A component with component.estimate_density set to false keeps its relative density in an inversion, for example a surface layer of known density. The constructors set it to true.

Example#

MATLAB script: An interior model of Didymos
run("/path/to/SBTK/sbtk_setup.m")
body = sbtk.body.from_mass("Didymos", sbtk.shape.bundled("didymos"), 5.273e11, 0.43);
cof = body.centroid_km;                                          % positions from the center of figure
torus = sbtk.interior.torus("torus", 0.370, 0.055, 0, -500);
torus.center_km = cof;                                           % about the z-axis through it
components = [ ...
    sbtk.interior.sphere("core", cof, 0.170, +450), ...
    torus, ...
    sbtk.interior.layer("regolith", 0, 0.012, -900), ...
    sbtk.interior.sphere("boulder", cof + sbtk.interior.latlon(25, 60, 0.250), 0.040, +900)];
interior = sbtk.interior.create(components, sbtk.interior.random_field(40, 0.06, 7));
sbtk.interior.summary(interior.components)

geo = sbtk.gravity.geometry(body, body.centroid_km, 0);          % degree 0: no coefficients needed
fm  = sbtk.gravity.forward(geo, interior, body.mass_kg);
fprintf("background density %.0f kg/m^3\n", fm.rho_bg_kgm3)
model = interior;
model.rho_bg_kgm3 = fm.rho_bg_kgm3;                               % background + components + field
rho = sbtk.interior.density_at(model, body.centroid_km + [0 0 0; 0.30 0 0], geo)

Here the geometry is built about the center of figure, so the layer is measured from it; sbtk.data.simulate uses the center of mass instead and returns the model with its background density as truth. The last line evaluates the density at the center of figure and 300 m from it along x. Further examples: Density models by component type.

Models and calculations

Gravity and moment calculations#

The forward model computes, for a density model inside a shape model, the gravity coefficients (Gravity coefficients), the center of mass and the inertia tensor (Moments of inertia) about an expansion origin 𝐨.

Facet cones#

sbtk.gravity.geometry(body, origin_km, degree) divides the body into tetrahedral cones, one per surface facet, with apex at 𝐨 and the facet as base. This partition is exact when the shape is star-shaped about 𝐨 (small overhangs count with their sign: Shape models). For every cone f it stores, per unit density (geo):

Quantity Definition Field
Spherical-harmonic integrals Tf,lm=∫f(r/Rref)lY¯lmdV, with Y¯lm=P¯lm(sinϕ){cos,sin}(mλ)/(2l+1) geo.T
Volume Vf geo.V
First moments ∫f𝐱dV geo.m1
Second moments ∫f[x2,y2,z2,xy,xz,yz]dV geo.Q

Tf,lm comes from the polyhedral kernel sbtk.internal.ComputePolyhedralCSBar_mex applied to the tetrahedron of each cone. With this definition a body of uniform density ρ has C¯lm=ρ∑fTf,lm/M (with the unit factor of Units).

Scaling within a cone#

Shrinking a cone about its apex by a factor s multiplies rldV by sl+3. The part of cone f between the scaled facets sa and sb (0≤sa<sb≤1) therefore contributes exactly

Tf,lm(sbl+3−sal+3),Vf(sb3−sa3),𝐦1,f(sb4−sa4),Qf(sb5−sa5).

The validation test testConeScaling checks this law against the kernel to a relative error below 10⁻¹³.

Integrals of components#

sbtk.gravity.component_integrals(geo, c) returns the integrals of the part of a component inside the body per unit density (integrals):

  • Sphere entirely inside the body: exact point-mass integrals.
  • Layer: along each of 9 sub-rays per facet, the radial interval between the two depths gives sa and sb directly.
  • Sector: the radial fractions give sa and sb; whether a sub-ray lies within the latitude and longitude range is tested at the middle of the interval.
  • Sphere crossing the surface, ellipsoid, torus: a sub-ray crosses the component's surface where a polynomial in the distance along it vanishes: a quadratic for a sphere or an ellipsoid, a quartic for a torus (solved as the eigenvalues of its companion matrix). Its real roots between the expansion origin and the body's surface split the sub-ray, and each piece whose midpoint is inside the component contributes sbp−sap, so a ray may enter and leave the component several times, and a ray that only grazes it contributes a correspondingly short piece.

For each facet the contributions are averaged over its 9 sub-rays and multiplied by the cone's integrals. The result is exact when the radial interval is the same along every sub-ray of a cone, and converges with mesh resolution otherwise (Assumptions and limitations).

sbtk.gravity.random_field_integrals evaluates the random field at the centroid of each of 24 radial shells of every cone (samples) and integrates each shell exactly with that value.

Coefficients, center of mass and inertia#
