sbtk.gravity.forward(geo, interior, mass_kg) combines the integrals of the body (U, V, 𝐦1, Q), of the components (Uc, Vc, …) and of the random field (Uδ, …):

U=ρbgUbody+∑cΔρcUc+Uδ,C¯lm,S¯lm=UlmM, 𝐱cm=𝐨+ρbg𝐦1,body+∑cΔρc𝐦1,c+𝐦1,δM,Ixx=Qyy+Qzz, Ixy=−Qxy, …

with ρbg chosen so that the mass is M (Density distributions). It returns the coefficients to degree L, the center of mass and [Ixx,Iyy,Izz,Ixy,Ixz,Iyz]/(MRref2) (fm).

Simulated measurements#

sbtk.data.simulate(body, interior, degree, name) runs the forward model about the center of mass:

  1. geometry and forward model about the shape-model origin;
  2. geometry and forward model about the resulting center of mass, repeated until the center of mass and the expansion origin differ by less than 1 mm (layers and sectors depend on the origin);
  3. a check that the density is not negative at the sample points of sbtk.internal.body_samples (24 radial shells per cone), otherwise sbtk:data:negativeDensity;
  4. the exact coefficients of degree 1 to L, the six inertia elements and the libration row, with the ratio k=(Iyy−Ixx)2+4Ixy2/Izz of the principal moments, as a measurement set without uncertainties (obs), and the true model (truth).

No measurement uncertainties enter the forward model. To make measurements of the true model, sbtk.data.set_uncertainties (or sbtk.data.use_uncertainties, sbtk.data.set_covariance, sbtk.data.set_moi_sigma) gives the exact values uncertainties and sbtk.data.add_noise draws one noisy realization (Measurement sets). Selecting which inertia quantities a data set contains: sbtk.data.select_moi.

Potential and acceleration at points#

The spherical-harmonic expansion converges only outside the sphere about its expansion point that encloses the body, and slowly near it. For points closer in, or on the surface, SBTK computes the potential and the acceleration from the shape model directly:

  • sbtk.gravity.polyhedron: a homogeneous polyhedron, exactly, with the closed form of Werner and Scheeres (1997, Celestial Mechanics and Dynamical Astronomy 65, 313–344), a sum over the edges and faces of the shape model. It holds outside, on and inside the body; on an edge the edge terms are zero.
  • sbtk.gravity.field_at: any model. The background density fills the polyhedron, exactly; the departures from it (components, random field) are taken on the density grid of sbtk.exchange.density_grid, each cell a uniform cube with the closed form of Nagy, Papp and Benedek (2000, Journal of Geodesy 74, 552–560). A homogeneous model is exact; otherwise the cubes follow the boundaries of the components to within a cell.

The potential is positive, U=G∫ρ/|r−r′|dV, and the acceleration is its gradient; the rotation of the body is not included. tests/unit/test_gravity.m checks that the two closed forms give the same cube to 10−10, that the divergence of the acceleration is −4πGρ inside the body, and that the acceleration is the gradient of the potential.

For the homogeneous Didymos (1.165 m model, 2600 kg/m³, Rref = 410 m), the expansion about the origin of the file compared with the exact potential (the sphere that encloses the body has a radius of 449.7 m):

Distance from the origin Expansion to degree 10 to degree 30
492 m (1.2 Rref) 1.5 × 10⁻⁴ 7.8 × 10⁻⁷
600 m 6.7 × 10⁻⁶ 2.2 × 10⁻¹⁰
707 m 1.9 × 10⁻⁷ 1.9 × 10⁻¹²
2449 m 5.8 × 10⁻¹³ 8 × 10⁻¹⁵

(relative difference of the potential at one point each). The polyhedron takes about 1 s per point for 3 million facets.

Computation time#

Times measured by tools/benchmark.m on Didymos (49,152 facets, degree 4), MATLAB R2025a on an Apple-silicon laptop:

Step Time
Geometry, degree 4 0.22 s
Simulation: 4 components and a random field, center-of-mass frame 3.6 s
Inversion setup: 3 components 1.3 s
Inversion run 0.25 s
Comparison with the true model 0.53 s

The geometry scales with the number of facets and with the number of coefficients: the agreed 3,145,728-facet Didymos model takes 4 s to read and 56 s to integrate to degree 10 (4.5 GB), and a forward model with four components then 14 s. On that model the comparison with a true model (sbtk.compare.with_truth) takes 16 s and a 20 m density grid 14 s: the surface along a direction is found among the facets sorted by direction (sbtk.internal.surface_distance_indexed), not among all 3 million.

Example#

MATLAB script: Coefficients, center of mass and inertia of a model
run("/path/to/SBTK/sbtk_setup.m")
body = sbtk.body.from_mass("Didymos", sbtk.shape.bundled("didymos"), 5.273e11, 0.43);
interior = sbtk.interior.create(sbtk.interior.sphere("core", [0 0 0], 0.170, +450));

geo = sbtk.gravity.geometry(body, body.centroid_km, 4);       % about the center of figure, to degree 4
fm  = sbtk.gravity.forward(geo, interior, body.mass_kg);
lab = sbtk.gravity.labels(4);
fprintf("C20 = %.5e, C22 = %.5e\n", fm.coef(strcmp(lab, "C20")), fm.coef(strcmp(lab, "C22")))
fprintf("center of mass - center of figure = [%.2f %.2f %.2f] m\n", 1e3*(fm.com_km - body.centroid_km))
fprintf("Izz / (M R_ref^2) = %.4f\n", fm.inertia_norm(3))

The core is centered at the shape-model origin, 57 m from the center of figure, so the center of mass moves toward it and the degree-1 coefficients about the center of figure are not zero.

Measurements and inversion

Measurement sets#

A measurement set (obs) holds fully normalized gravity coefficients with their covariance, moment-of-inertia measurement rows, the total mass, the reference radius and the expansion origin.

Sources#

Source Function Notes
A simulated interior sbtk.data.simulate Exact values about the true center of mass, without uncertainties (they are NaN until set, below); coef_about = 'origin'.
An SBTK measurement package sbtk.exchange.read_data Coefficients about the measured center of mass with their full covariance; returns the body as well (Exchange packages).
A gravity file in the PDS SHADR layout sbtk.exchange.read_shadr Header row (R, GM, σGM, degree, order, normalization state, …) then rows l, m, C, S, sigma_C, sigma_S; diagonal covariance. The caller gives the shape model and the point the coefficients are about.
A JPL SSD gravity file sbtk.io.read_jpl_gravity MATLAB-assignment form with NAMES, VALS, COV; parsed as text; full covariance; Jl converted to C¯l0.
Coefficient matrices sbtk.data.from_coefficients C(l+1, m+1), S(l+1, m+1) and their 1σ; diagonal covariance.
The SBTK text format sbtk.io.read_measurements, sbtk.io.load_measurements One keyword per line; diagonal covariance only (Results folders).

Uncertainties and covariance#

  • Exact values have none. sbtk.data.simulate returns the true model's exact values without uncertainties: coef_cov and every inertia σ are NaN. Measurements need them: sbtk.data.add_noise, sbtk.invert.setup and sbtk.exchange.write_data stop with sbtk:data:noUncertainties otherwise.
  • By degree. sbtk.data.set_uncertainties(obs, unc) gives every coefficient of degree l the 1σ of sbtk.data.uncertainties for that degree (a diagonal covariance), every inertia element its 1σ (as a fraction of MRref2), and the libration row the 1σ of the ratio times Izz/(MRref2).
  • From another data set. sbtk.data.use_uncertainties gives every coefficient that a reference data set also contains the reference's variances and covariances, converted to the reference radius of the target by (R/R′)l. Coefficients the reference lacks keep their variances and become uncorrelated with the others.
  • Full covariance. sbtk.data.set_covariance replaces the coefficient covariance with any symmetric positive definite matrix in the order of obs.coef_labels.
  • Inertia rows. sbtk.data.set_moi_sigma sets the σ of named rows; the field libration gives the 1σ of the ratio.

Noise#

sbtk.data.add_noise(obs, seed) returns one realization: the coefficients plus L𝐳, with L the lower Cholesky factor of the coefficient covariance and 𝐳 standard normal; each inertia row plus its σ times a standard normal variable. The same seed gives the same noise; obs.noise_seed records it.

Inertia measurements and the center of mass#

Function Adds
sbtk.data.add_moi One element Ixx … Iyz as I/(MRref2) (sbtk.units.moi_to_norm converts from kg m²).
sbtk.data.add_moi_row Any linear combination of the six elements.
sbtk.data.add_libration The libration ratio (B−A)/C as a linear row (Moments of inertia). Requires C¯22 and S¯22.
sbtk.data.libration_ratio_from_amplitude Computes the ratio and its 1σ from a forced libration amplitude.
sbtk.data.add_center_of_mass The measured center of mass as degree-1 coefficients; sets coef_about to 'center_of_mass'.

Selecting measurements#

sbtk.data.select_degree keeps the coefficients up to a degree, sbtk.data.select_coefficients a list of coefficients, and sbtk.data.select_moi a list of inertia rows; the covariance keeps the matching rows and columns. sbtk.data.move_origin changes the expansion origin of data about the center of mass. sbtk.data.summary prints the contents of a measurement set.

Example#

MATLAB script: Measurements from coefficient matrices
run("/path/to/SBTK/sbtk_setup.m")
body = sbtk.body.from_mass("Dimorphos", sbtk.shape.bundled("dimorphos"), 2.700e9, 0.10);

% coefficient matrices, C(l+1, m+1) = C_lm, fully normalized, about the shape-model origin
L = 2;
C = zeros(L + 1);  S = zeros(L + 1);
C(1,1) = 1;  C(3,1) = -0.08;  C(3,3) = 0.03;  S(3,3) = 0.002;     % C00, C20, C22, S22
Cs = 1e-3*ones(L + 1);  Ss = 1e-3*ones(L + 1);                     % 1-sigma of each
obs = sbtk.data.from_coefficients(body, "example", [0 0 0], C, S, Cs, Ss);

% a polar moment given in kg m^2, and a libration ratio
Izz = sbtk.units.moi_to_norm(1.6e14, body.mass_kg, body.R_ref_km);
obs = sbtk.data.add_moi(obs, "Izz", Izz, 0.01*Izz);
obs = sbtk.data.add_libration(obs, 0.20, 0.03, Izz);

% 30% correlation between all coefficients
sig = sqrt(diag(obs.coef_cov));
obs = sbtk.data.set_covariance(obs, (0.3 + 0.7*eye(numel(sig))).*(sig*sig'));
sbtk.data.summary(obs)

Calculations has further examples: simulated data with uncertainties from another data set, selection of inertia rows, and reading files.

Measurements and inversion

Uncertainties and the expansion point#

A gravity field can be written about any point, and its coefficients depend on that point. So do their uncertainties. The Hera radio-science (RSE) team gives the uncertainties of a field about the center of mass; the HLP6 packages give coefficients about the origin of the shape model file, 56 m from the center of mass of Didymos in UCB-DATA1. This lesson starts from what a coefficient measures, derives how the coefficients and their uncertainties change when the expansion point moves, works the Didymos and Dimorphos cases by hand, and ends with the intuition and what to do.

1. What a coefficient measures#

A coefficient of degree l is a moment of the mass distribution of order l, taken about the expansion point. With x,y,z measured from that point, M the mass and R the reference radius, the coefficients of degree 0 to 2 are (unnormalized):

Coefficient Moment Meaning
C00=1 1M∫ρdV the mass
C10, C11, S11 1MR∫ρzdV, 1MR∫ρxdV, 1MR∫ρydV the center of mass from the point, z¯/R, x¯/R, y¯/R
C20 1MR2∫ρ(z2−12(x2+y2))dV flattening along z
C22 14MR2∫ρ(x2−y2)dV elongation along x

The fully normalized coefficients of the packages are C¯lm=Clm/Nlm, with N10=N11=3, N20=5 and N22=5/12 (Gravity coefficients). About the center of mass, degree 1 is zero by definition; about any other point it gives where the center of mass is.

2. Moving the point: a warm-up in one dimension#

Take mass along a line and its second moment about the origin, ∫ρx2dx. About a point at x=h instead:

∫ρ(x−h)2dx=∫ρx2dx−2h∫ρxdx+h2∫ρdx.

The second moment about the new point is the old second moment, plus the old first moment times h, plus the old zeroth moment (the mass) times h2. This is the parallel-axis theorem. Two things follow, and they hold for every degree:

  • a moment about the new point mixes in the moments of lower order about the old one, weighted by powers of the offset; never higher ones;
  • if a lower moment is uncertain, the higher moments about the new point inherit that uncertainty, multiplied by the offset (the lever arm).

3. The rules for degrees 1 and 2#

Let h=(hx,hy,hz) be the new expansion point minus the old one, so that the coordinates about the new point are x−hx, y−hy, z−hz. Putting these into the moments of section 1:

Degree 1 picks up only the mass:

C10′=C10−hzR,C11′=C11−hxR,S11′=S11−hyR.

Degree 2 picks up degree 1 and the mass. Expanding (z−hz)2−12((x−hx)2+(y−hy)2) and (x−hx)2−(y−hy)2:

C20′=C20−2hzRC10+hxRC11+hyRS11+hz2−12(hx2+hy2)R2, C22′=C22−hx2RC11+hy2RS11+hx2−hy24R2.

In fully normalized coefficients (divide each side by its Nlm):

C¯20′=C¯20+35(−2hzRC¯10+hxRC¯11+hyRS¯11)+const, C¯22′=C¯22+35(−hxRC¯11+hyRS¯11)+const.

The constants hold only h and C00=1. For every degree at once the rule is linear, c′=Tc, with T the translation matrix of solid harmonics (sbtk.internal.sh_translation): degree l about the new point is a combination of degrees 0 to l about the old one, with powers of h/R.

4. From values to uncertainties#

A linear map carries a covariance K to K′=TKT𝖳. For one coefficient this means: the variance of a sum of independent terms is the sum of their variances, each with the square of its weight, and a constant adds nothing. The offset h is known exactly (the shape model file is agreed) and C00=1, so only the uncertain coefficients count. With uncorrelated inputs:

σ2(C¯1m′)=σ2(C¯1m)(degree 1 does not change) σ2(C¯20′)=σ2(C¯20)+125(hzR)2σ2(C¯10)+35(hxR)2σ2(C¯11)+35(hyR)2σ2(S¯11) σ2(C¯22′)=σ2(C¯22)+95(hxR)2σ2(C¯11)+95(hyR)2σ2(S¯11)

The 1σ of degree 1 is the uncertainty of the center of mass: σx=3Rσ(C¯11), σy=3Rσ(S¯11), σz=3Rσ(C¯10). With it the added terms read as a lever arm times a position error, over R2; for example the z term of C¯20 is 25hzσz/R2.

If the inputs are correlated, each pair adds twice its covariance times the two weights; TKT𝖳 includes that. The RSE .tab files give only one 1σ per coefficient, so the examples below treat them as uncorrelated, as sbtk.data.use_uncertainties does.

5. Example: the zonal coefficient of degree 2 of Didymos (UCB-DATA1)#

The package gives degree 1 about the origin of the file; it puts the center of mass at c=(15.03, 42.27, −33.98) m. The RSE field is about the center of mass, so the expansion point moves from the center of mass to the origin: h=−c=(−15.03, −42.27, 33.98) m, and with R=410 m, h/R=(−0.0367, −0.1031, 0.0829). The RSE 1σ, converted to R=410 m (factor (430/410)l):

σ(C¯20) σ(C¯10) σ(C¯11) σ(S¯11)
RSE, R = 410 m 8.70 × 10⁻⁶ 1.378 × 10⁻⁴ (σz = 9.8 cm) 1.240 × 10⁻⁵ (σx = 0.9 cm) 1.304 × 10⁻⁵ (σy = 0.9 cm)

The terms of σ(C¯20′):

Term Value
own, σ(C¯20) 8.70 × 10⁻⁶
z: 12/5(0.0829)(1.378×10−4) 1.77 × 10⁻⁵
x: 3/5(0.0367)(1.240×10−5) 3.5 × 10⁻⁷
y: 3/5(0.1031)(1.304×10−5) 1.04 × 10⁻⁶
total, sum of squares 1.97 × 10⁻⁵, 2.27 times the RSE value

The z term dominates: the 34 m height of the origin above the center of mass is the lever arm, and the center of mass is least certain along z (9.8 cm against 0.9 cm in x and y).

6. Example: the sectoral coefficient of degree 2 of Dimorphos (UCB-DATA4)#

The center of mass is at c=(−1.11, −2.26, −0.25) m from the origin of the Dimorphos file, so h=(1.11, 2.26, 0.25) m and, with R=100 m, h/R=(0.0111, 0.0226, 0.0025).

σ(C¯22) σ(C¯11) σ(S¯11)
RSE 4.04 × 10⁻⁶ 2.462 × 10⁻³ (σx = 0.43 m) 3.380 × 10⁻³ (σy = 0.59 m)
Term Value
own, σ(C¯22) 4.04 × 10⁻⁶
x: 35(0.0111)(2.462×10−3) 3.67 × 10⁻⁵
y: 35(0.0226)(3.380×10−3) 1.03 × 10⁻⁴
total 1.09 × 10⁻⁴, 27 times the RSE value

The offset is only 2.5 m, but the center of mass of Dimorphos is known to about half a meter, and C¯22 itself is known very well (4×10−6). A small lever arm on a large position error swamps a small own uncertainty.

The other coefficients, worked the same way (answers in section 10): Dimorphos C¯20 grows 1.60 times, Didymos C¯22 only 1.003 times, because C¯22 couples only to x and y, where the center of mass of Didymos is known to a centimeter.

7. Example: degree 1 does not change#

C¯10′=C¯10−hz/(3R), and hz is known exactly. For UCB-DATA1 the value goes from about zero (about the center of mass) to −33.98 m/(3·410 m)=−0.0478, the C¯10 in the package, while the 1σ stays 1.378×10−4. Degree 1 is the position of the center of mass; measuring it from a different fixed point changes the number, not how well it is known.

8. Example: the moments of inertia#

The inertia elements move by the parallel-axis theorem, Iij(origin)=Iij(c.m.)+M(|c|2δij−cicj), so Ixx(origin)=Ixx(c.m.)+M(cy2+cz2). An error in c changes it by 2M(cyδcy+czδcz), and in units of MR2 the added 1σ is

2R2(cyσy)2+(czσz)2.

For Dimorphos (UCB-DATA4): 2(100 m)2(2.26·0.585)2+(0.25·0.418)2 m2=2.65×10−4, against the RSE 1σ of Ixx, 1.1081×104 kg km² /(MR2)=4.10×10−4 (the file labels it kg m²; Didymos and Dimorphos values): the total is 4.89×10−4, 19% more than the RSE 1σ. For Didymos the added term is 4×10−5 against an RSE 1σ of 2.8×10−2, which is negligible. (The inertia errors are also correlated with degree 1, which SBTK, keeping inertia and coefficients uncorrelated, cannot carry; it adds the variance only.)

9. The intuition#

  • Coefficients describe the mass as seen from a point. About the center of mass, the RSE measures the shape of the field very well and the position of the center of mass separately. About another point, every coefficient also encodes where the center of mass sits relative to that point, so the position error enters them.
  • The offset is a lever arm. As in the parallel-axis theorem, the error a position uncertainty causes grows with the distance: no offset, no added uncertainty. That is why the field is best described about the center of mass.
  • It reaches every higher degree. Degree l mixes in all lower degrees with powers of h/R, so the uncertainty of the center of mass reaches degree 2, 3 and above, with weights that fall as h/R is small.
  • It matters most where a coefficient is known best. A coefficient whose own 1σ is tiny (Dimorphos C¯22) is overwhelmed; one with a large own 1σ hardly changes.
  • Nothing is lost. K′=TKT𝖳 has correlations between degree 1 and the rest. A fit that uses the full covariance gives the same answer about the origin as about the center of mass. The mistake is to keep the RSE 1σ, which belong to the center of mass, for coefficients about the origin: that claims those coefficients are known up to 27 times better than they are, and a fit then weights them too much.

10. What to do, and answers#

To weight data about a fixed point with uncertainties given about the center of mass, do one of these two; they give the same fit:

  1. move the covariance to the point of the data, K′=TKT𝖳: sbtk.data.use_uncertainties does it when the reference set is about another point, and projects/hera_hlp6/hlp6_uncertainties.m gives the RSE field the center of mass the package's degree 1 gives;
  2. move the coefficients to that center of mass (sbtk.data.expand_about) and use the RSE 1σ there.

The numbers of sections 5 to 8 can be reproduced with the formulas of section 4:

MATLAB
R = 0.41;  h = [-15.03 -42.27 33.98]/1e3;                       % Didymos, UCB-DATA1 [km]
s20 = 8.70e-6;  s10 = 1.378e-4;  s11 = 1.240e-5;  t11 = 1.304e-5;  % RSE 1-sigma at R = 0.41 km
c20 = sqrt(s20^2 + 12/5*(h(3)/R)^2*s10^2 + 3/5*(h(1)/R)^2*s11^2 + 3/5*(h(2)/R)^2*t11^2);
fprintf('Didymos C20: %.3g, %.2f times the RSE value\n', c20, c20/s20)          % 1.97e-05, 2.27
R = 0.10;  h = [1.11 2.26 0.25]/1e3;                            % Dimorphos, UCB-DATA4 [km]
s22 = 4.04e-6;  s11 = 2.462e-3;  t11 = 3.380e-3;
c22 = sqrt(s22^2 + 9/5*(h(1)/R)^2*s11^2 + 9/5*(h(2)/R)^2*t11^2);
fprintf('Dimorphos C22: %.3g, %.1f times the RSE value\n', c22, c22/s22)        % 1.09e-04, 27.0

and for any package, with the full covariance, by SBTK:

MATLAB
[obs, body] = sbtk.exchange.read_data("UCB-DATA1-Didymos");
addpath(fullfile(sbtk.root, "projects", "hera_hlp6"));
obs = hlp6_uncertainties(obs, body);      % RSE covariance moved from the center of mass to the file origin

Exercises. Answers below each.

  1. Dimorphos C¯20 (UCB-DATA4). With σ(C¯20)=5.09×10−5, σ(C¯10)=2.41×10−3 and the rest from section 6: terms z 9.3×10−6, x 2.12×10−5, y 5.92×10−5; total 8.14×10−5, 1.60 times the RSE value.
  2. Didymos C¯22 (UCB-DATA1). With σ(C¯22)=2.645×10−5: terms x 6.1×10−7, y 1.8×10−6; total 2.652×10−5, 1.003 times: the center of mass of Didymos is known to 0.9 cm in x and y.
  3. How high above the center of mass must the expansion point of Didymos be for σ(C¯20) to double? Doubling means the added variance is three times the own: $\tfrac{12}{5}(h_z/R)^2\sigma^2(\bar C_{10}) = 3\sigma^2(\bar C_{20})$, so $h_z = R\,\sqrt3\,\sigma(\bar C_{20})/(\sqrt{12/5}\,\sigma(\bar C_{10})) = 410\ \text{m} \times 0.0706 \approx$ 29 m. The origin of the file is 34 m above it, hence a little more than double.
  4. Why does σ(C¯10) not change? Its only new term is hz/(3R) times C00=1, and both are exact (section 7).

Measurements and inversion

Reading the gravity coefficients#

An inversion estimates the densities of the components it is given; it does not say which components to give it. This page is the step before: how to read the gravity coefficients of an unknown body to decide which components to model, and where to start them. It derives what each kind of structure does to the coefficients, gives a procedure with the SBTK functions for each step, works an example, and reports how well the procedure finds known interiors (What the study found). The procedure applies to any body with a shape model; the examples use Didymos.

The anomaly: what the interior adds#

The coefficients of a body of constant density follow from its shape alone. The density structure is in the difference between the measured coefficients and those of the homogeneous body, the same shape with the bulk density ρ¯=M/V everywhere. Write the density as ρ(r)=ρ¯+δρ(r); since the mass is known, ∫δρdV=0. About a fixed point, the fully normalized coefficients are linear in the density, so the difference is

ΔC¯lm=C¯lm−C¯lmhom=1MRl∫δρ(r)|r−rf|lY¯lm(r−rf)dV,

the anomaly of each coefficient. SBTK expresses it about the center of figure rf, the homogeneous body's center of mass and a fixed point of the shape, so that the anomaly of a model is the sum of the anomalies of its components. Measurements about another point (a package about the origin of its shape-model file, or a field about the measured center of mass) are moved there exactly, with their covariance (Uncertainties and the expansion point). sbtk.interpret.anomaly computes it, for measurements or for a model:

  • an.value the anomaly, an.sigma its 1σ (the homogeneous field is exact), an.significance the ratio;
  • an.com_offset_km the degree-1 part as the center of mass minus the center of figure;
  • per degree, the RMS of the anomaly and of its 1σ (an.signal_rms, an.sigma_rms): a degree whose anomaly is not well above its 1σ carries no information about the interior;
  • the inertia rows of the measurements with the homogeneous body's values about the same point.

sbtk.plot.significance draws every measurement with its ±1σ interval against the constant-density value, and counts those that differ from it by more than 1σ and 3σ. sbtk.interpret.summary prints the rest of this page's quantities.

Signatures of components#

A relative density Δρc in a component of volume Vc lowers the density of the rest of the body by ΔρcVc/V, because the mass is fixed. The anomaly it makes is Δρc times the component's signature

sc=1M(Uc−VcVUbody),

with U the integrals ∫(r/R)lY¯lmdV of the component and of the body about the center of figure (sbtk.gravity.component_integrals). The anomaly of any model is ∑cΔρcsc (checked to 10⁻¹² in testSignaturesAddUp). sbtk.interpret.signatures computes the signatures of candidate components, and fits each one alone to the measured anomaly: its density, the reduction of χ2 from the homogeneous body, and the correlation of its signature with the anomaly.

What each kind of structure does#

The homogeneous body's own coefficients set the scale. Each degree l≥2 of a field can be split into a scaled homogeneous field and the rest:

C¯l·=klC¯l·hom+restl,kl=hl·clhl·hl,

with hl and cl the 2l+1 coefficients of degree l of the homogeneous body and of the field (an.ratio, an.residual). Structure that is symmetric about the center of figure changes only kl; everything else shows in the rest.

Structure Degree 1 Scaling kl The rest
Dense core at the center of figure, mass excess qM 0 1−q at every degree none
The same core moved by d qd/(3R) 1−q, to order (d/R)2 qpl(d), of order q(d/R)l
Light core (q<0) qd/(3R) 1+|q| as above
Surface layer, thickness t, relative density Δρ 0 1+Δρρ¯(s3−sl+3)≈1+Δρρ¯ltr¯ small
Ring or torus about the z-axis, radius a 0 changes the even degrees J2,J4,… only
The same, raised by h C10=qth/(3R) as above adds J3≈0.98(a/R)2C¯10
Elongated core (ellipsoid) as a core as a core C¯22,S¯22: its elongation and direction
Boulder of mass qbM at db qbdb/(3R) small every order, falling as (db/R)l

A compact mass. A sphere inside the body is a point mass: its integrals are Vcp(d), with pl(d) the coefficients of a unit point mass at d from the center of figure (sbtk.internal.point_mass_sh). With q=ΔρcVc/M, the field is exactly

cl=(1−q)hl+qpl(d)for every l≥1.

At degree 1, h1=0 and p1(d)=d/(3R) (as C11,S11,C10): the center of mass moves by qd. At degree l the core's own term is of order q(d/R)l; for d→0 it vanishes and every degree is the homogeneous one scaled by 1−q. A dense core makes every coefficient smaller in the same proportion; a light core makes them larger.

A surface layer. SBTK's layers are defined along rays from the center, so a layer from depth 0 to t is the body minus the body scaled by s=1−t/r along each ray (r the distance to the surface). In the cone of each facet the integrals of degree l scale with sl+3; for a layer thin compared with the radius of a nearly round body, s is about the same on every ray, the layer's signature is 1M(s3−sl+3)Ubody, and

kl=1+Δρρ¯(s3−sl+3)≈1+Δρρ¯ltr¯.

A light layer (Δρ<0) scales the coefficients down like a dense core, but more at higher degree: a ratio kl that falls with degree is a surface layer, a constant one a central mass.

A ring or torus. A thin ring of mass qtM and radius a about the z-axis through the center of figure, at height h, has only zonal terms, C¯l0=qt(r/R)lPl(sinφ)/2l+1 with r2=a2+h2, sinφ=h/r. In the equatorial plane only the even degrees remain: P2(0)=−12, P4(0)=38, so a dense ring raises J2 and lowers J4, a light one does the opposite, and the sectoral and tesseral coefficients are untouched. Raised by h, the ring adds C¯10=qth/(3R) and C¯30≈−32qtha2/(7R3), so J3≈3327(a/R)2C¯10. A core moved by the same amount along z makes the same C¯10 with a J3 of order (d/R)3: J3 beside C10 tells a raised torus from a raised core.

An elongated core has a degree-2 field of its own, C¯22 and S¯22 in proportion to the difference of its two equatorial axes; the angle 12atan2(S22,C22) of the rest of degree 2 is the direction of its long axis (or short axis, if it is light).

A boulder far from the center makes degree 1 and a rest in every degree and order, falling as (db/R)l; its direction is the direction of the degree-1 anomaly when nothing else moves the center of mass.

Degree 1 and the core#

Degree 1 is the first moment of the density anomaly:

M(rcm−rf)=∑cΔρcVc(r¯c−rf),

with r¯c the centroid of component c. It fixes the product of a core's mass excess and its offset, not either alone: a dense core at d and a light core at −d give the same degree 1, and so does a lighter core farther out. The mass excess must come from elsewhere, and degree 2 gives it if the core is the only central mass. sbtk.interpret.central_mass solves the two equations of a single compact mass,

qd=rcm−rf,c2−h2=q(p2(d)−h2),

by iteration from q=1−k2 and d=(rcm−rf)/q, with their 1σ from the full covariance. For a sphere alone the answer is exact (testCentralMassOfOneSphere). With other structure, q is the net central condensation of all of it: a light surface layer adds to it, a light torus too, and d then comes out too short. That is why a model fit does not end the question of the core's position:

  • sbtk.invert.scan_position fits the densities with the core placed at each of a list of points, here along the measured center-of-mass offset, and returns the χ2 profile. It shows both sides of the ambiguity (a dense core on one side, a light one on the other) and how flat the valley between core mass and offset is;
  • Gauss–Newton on the core position (component.estimate_position), started from the lowest point of the profile, refines it with every coefficient at once;
  • sbtk.invert.recenter instead moves the core so that the model's center of mass equals the measured one at the fitted densities, s=M(rcm−rcmmodel)/(ΔρcVc), and repeated with new densities it is a fixed-point iteration. It converges in a few steps when the core is the only component that can move the center of mass; when other components can match degree 1 themselves, it stops where it starts (What the study found).

Procedure#

  1. Read. an = sbtk.interpret.anomaly(obs, body, L) with every coefficient to degree L and the uncertainties you will use; sbtk.interpret.summary, sbtk.plot.significance. Note which degrees carry signal, whether the center of mass is off the center of figure, and the inertia rows.
  2. Scaling and rest. sbtk.plot.degree_ratio: kl below 1 at every degree is central mass, falling with degree a light surface, above 1 a light center or a dense surface. The rest, coefficient by coefficient (an.residual_significance): only even zonal terms point to a ring or torus about z; J3 with C10 to a raised torus; C22,S22 to an elongated center; every order in degrees 2–4 to something off center. The geometry (sbtk.interpret.geometry, sbtk.plot.anomaly_map): the center-of-mass offset as a direction; the principal axes of the second moment of degree 2 (C20, C21, S21, C22, S22), the axis mass was moved toward and the one it was moved away from, with their 1σ; and each degree as a map on the sphere with its directions of strongest excess and deficit. A compact mass gives one direction at every degree, a ring or belt the even degrees with extremes along the equator and at the poles. This is the reading that places components: a core along the offset, a torus about the axis degree 2 moved mass away from, a boulder where degrees 2–4 agree.
  3. One compact mass. sbtk.interpret.central_mass: the size and offset of the central mass if it were alone.
  4. Candidates. sbtk.interpret.signatures for the component types step 2 suggests, at several sizes and positions (sbtk.interior.sphere_grid for positions anywhere); sbtk.interpret.select adds them one at a time by the largest reduction of χ2, with an a priori 1σ of each density. It is a guide: similar signatures (a core and a surface layer) can share the anomaly between them.
  5. Model and core position. Set up the model (sbtk.invert.setup); sbtk.invert.scan_position along the center-of-mass offset; Gauss–Newton from the lowest point, with the geometry the rest points to free (torus height, ellipsoid axes).
  6. Test. The χ2 test (Goodness of fit); the anomaly of the fit against the measured one (sbtk.plot.anomaly); and a fit to the low degrees only, predicting the others (sbtk.invert.predict, sbtk.plot.coefficient_residuals; Fitting part of the coefficients).

Example#

examples/ex10_reading_coefficients.m runs the procedure on a hidden Didymos interior: a dense core (+500 kg/m³, radius 140 m) 30 m from the center of figure, a light torus (−400 kg/m³) 12 m above the equator and a light 15 m surface layer (−600 kg/m³), with coefficients to degree 5 about the origin of the shape-model file and 1σ close to the Hera radio-science values.

MATLAB script: Reading the coefficients of a hidden interior
run("/path/to/SBTK/sbtk_setup.m")
body = sbtk.body.create("Didymos", sbtk.shape.bundled("didymos"), 2600, 0.41);
cof  = body.centroid_km;
torus = sbtk.interior.torus("torus", 0.36, 0.05, 0, -400);
torus.center_km = cof + [0 0 0.012];
hidden = [sbtk.interior.sphere("core", cof + [0.025 -0.015 0.008], 0.14, +500), torus, ...
          sbtk.interior.layer("regolith", 0, 0.015, -600)];
exact = sbtk.data.simulate(body, sbtk.interior.create(hidden), 5, "reading example");
exact = sbtk.data.expand_about(sbtk.data.select_moi(exact, {}), [0 0 0]);
obs = sbtk.data.set_uncertainties(exact, sbtk.data.uncertainties([1.3e-5 2e-5 3e-5 3e-5 3e-5], 1, 0.02));

an = sbtk.interpret.anomaly(obs, body, 5);              % 1. read
sbtk.interpret.summary(an);
cm = sbtk.interpret.central_mass(an);                   % 3. one compact mass

model = [sbtk.interior.sphere("core", cof, 0.15, 0), sbtk.interior.torus("torus", 0.37, 0.055, 0, 0), ...
         sbtk.interior.layer("regolith", 0, 0.012, 0)];
model(2).center_km = cof;
opts = sbtk.invert.options(moi_labels={});
prob = sbtk.invert.setup(body, model, obs, opts);
u  = an.com_offset_km/norm(an.com_offset_km);           % 5. the core along the center-of-mass offset
sc = sbtk.invert.scan_position(prob, "core", cof + (-0.10:0.005:0.10)'*u);
model(1).center_km = sc.centers_km(sc.best, :);
model(1).estimate_position = true;
model(2).estimate_position = [false false true];
fit = sbtk.invert.solve(body, model, obs, opts);
sbtk.invert.summary(fit)
Output: sbtk.interpret.summary(an)
Didymos (reading example): anomaly about the center of figure, degrees 1 to 5
  center of mass - center of figure: [0.26 -0.15 -0.07] m +- [0.01 0.01 0.01] m, |offset| 0.31 m
  chi-square of the offset: 1096 for 3 degrees of freedom
  degree  RMS anomaly  RMS 1-sigma     ratio k_l +- 1-sigma      residual chi2 / dof
  1         2.485e-04    1.300e-05
  2         1.079e-03    2.010e-05       0.94114 +- 0.00050                348.8 / 4
  3         6.282e-05    3.045e-05       0.98676 +- 0.00670                25.95 / 6
  4         3.283e-04    3.202e-05       0.81902 +- 0.00607                58.65 / 8
  5         3.766e-05    3.345e-05       0.97409 +- 0.02249               12.97 / 10
  one compact mass with the same degrees 1 and 2: 5.893% +- 0.050% of the mass (3.12e+10 kg) at [4.4 -2.5 -1.1] m +- [0.2 0.2 0.2] m from the center of figure

1. Read. 15 of the 35 coefficients differ from constant density by more than 1σ and 9 by more than 3σ. The center of mass is 0.31 m from the center of figure, measured to 1 cm: something is off center. J2 is 120σ below the homogeneous value and J4 30σ above it.

2. Scaling and rest. Degree 2 is scaled down by 5.9%, degree 4 by 18%, degrees 3 and 5 by about 1–3%: the even degrees much more than the odd ones. A central mass alone would scale every degree alike and a surface layer would scale degree 4 more than degree 2 but degree 3 in between; the even–odd alternation is the signature of a ring about the z-axis. The rest confirms it: χ2 of 349 for the 4 degrees of freedom of degree 2 and 59 for the 8 of degree 4, against 26 and 13 for degrees 3 and 5, and in degree 2 most of it is J2. J3 (−4σ) and J5 (+3σ) point to a ring that is not in the equatorial plane.

3. One compact mass. Degrees 1 and 2 as one mass give 5.9% of the mass, 4.4 m from the center of figure. The hidden core is 1.1% of the mass 30 m from it: the 5.9% is the net central condensation of the core, the light torus and the light surface layer together, and the offset divided by it comes out about 6 times too short (5 m instead of 30 m). On its own, a compact mass is the wrong reading here, as step 2 already said.

5. Model and core position. The model has the three components step 2 points to, with the sizes a receiving team would guess (core radius 150 m, torus radii 370 and 55 m about the z-axis, a 12 m layer). The χ2 profile of the core along the center-of-mass offset has two valleys: a light core 45 m on the negative side (χ2≈160) and a dense core on the positive side, flat from 40 to 100 m (χ2≈93). The hidden core is at 27 m along this line.

Gauss–Newton from the lowest point, with the torus height free, ends at a reduced χ2 of 0.65 (p=0.92): the model is consistent with the measurements. It puts the torus 12.2 m above the equator (hidden: 12 m, ±1.9 m) with a relative density of −359 ± 15 kg/m³ (hidden: −400). The core, however, has +122 ± 22 kg/m³ at 127 m from the center of figure, and the layer −1418 ± 184 kg/m³: a weak core far out and a very light surface explain the measurements as well as the hidden dense core and lighter surface, within the 1σ of the measurements and with this model's slightly wrong sizes. With the hidden sizes the fit recovers every density exactly (χ2=6×10−12). Degree 1 fixes the core's first moment; how it splits into mass and offset depends on the degree-2 scaling, which the layer shares. The position 1σ of Gauss–Newton (18 m) describes the valley near the solution, not the length of the valley: read the χ2 profile.

6. Test. Fitted to degrees 1–3 only, the same model predicts the 16 coefficients of degrees 4 and 5 with a χ2 of 1.2 per coefficient: the model passes a test on coefficients it was not fitted to. The test does not separate the core from the layer either: at this precision degrees 4 and 5 do not tell the two explanations apart.

What the study found#

tests/studies/coefficient_reading_study.m applies the procedure to 110 random Didymos interiors whose answers are known, and tests/studies/coefficient_reading_figures.m summarizes it. Each true interior gives the exact coefficients to degree 5 about the origin of the shape-model file, weighted by the Hera radio-science 1σ (hlp6_uncertainties.m), and the same with one realization of noise. The interiors come in four families:

Family True models Contents (random)
no core 20 a torus about the z-axis (ring radius 300–400 m, tube 35–65 m, ±150 to ±700 kg/m³, up to 25 m above or below the equator) and a light surface layer (8–30 m, −200 to −1100 kg/m³)
core 30 one sphere (radius 100–200 m, +200 to +900 kg/m³, or −200 to −700 in one case of four) up to 60 m from the center of figure
core, torus, layer 30 the three together
with unmodeled structure 30 the three, the torus tilted up to 4°, 1 to 3 dense boulders (25–50 m) and a Gaussian random field

Each data set is fitted with 8 sets of coefficients, from degree 1 and J2 to every coefficient to degree 5, with two models of fixed sizes, the sizes a team would have to guess: a core of radius 150 m, and that core with a torus (radii 370 and 55 m) and a 12 m layer. The core is placed by up to five procedures: at the center of figure; Gauss–Newton from there; the χ2 profile along the center-of-mass offset, then Gauss–Newton (also with the torus height free); the fixed-point iteration of sbtk.invert.recenter. That is 15,840 fits; on the 49,152-facet model a fit takes 2 s (core fixed) to 8 s (profile and Gauss–Newton), 50 s with the torus height free, and the study 3 hours on 10 workers.

Reading without a fit#

  • A core alone scales every degree by the same factor (kl=0.992, the median 1−q), leaves no rest, and sbtk.interpret.central_mass returns its mass excess and position exactly in all 30 models.
  • A torus and a layer scale degree 4 down most (median k4=0.89, against k2=0.96 and k3=0.96) and leave a rest in degrees 2 and 4 (median χ2 108 and 154) much larger than in degrees 3 and 5 (9 and 6): the signature of the even degrees. The compact mass from degrees 1 and 2 is then the net central condensation: it converges in 90% of the models, its mass is off by a factor (median 1.25 of the core's, with 10% of the models below −2.9 and 10% above 9.3) and its position 20 m (median) from the core.
  • Boulders and a random field add a rest in the odd degrees: median χ2 84 in degree 3 and 24 in degree 5, against 9 and 6 without them. A rest in the odd degrees is the sign that a core, a torus and a layer will not be enough.

Degree 1 and the core#

  • Degree 1 and J2 determine a core that is alone. The four numbers fix its four unknowns: without noise the core is recovered exactly; at the Hera precision it is 4.6 m from the true core (median), within 10 m in 83% of the models, with its mass excess within 2%. More coefficients do not move it closer (4.1–4.6 m with every set to degree 5): the position is limited by how well degree 1 and J2 are measured relative to the core's mass. Gauss–Newton, the profile and the fixed-point iteration give the same result.
  • Matching degree 1 by moving the core is an iteration that converges when the core is the only component that moves the center of mass. With the core model, sbtk.invert.recenter converges in all 240 fits with noise, in 3 steps (median). With the three-component model, fitted to degree 1 and J2, it stops at its first step with the core at the center of figure: the torus and the layer, cut by the irregular surface, have their own degree 1, and their fitted densities already match the measured one. With more coefficients it converges in 53–77% of the fits, after 6–32 steps, and ends 15–30 m from the core.
  • Gauss–Newton from the center of figure with the three-component model finds a lone core within 10 m in 17% of the models with degree 1 and J2 (its mass excess wrong by about 300%); from the lowest point of the χ2 profile, in 83%.
  • The χ2 profile chooses the side. Its lowest point is on the side of the true core in every model of a lone core without noise and in 93% with noise; with a torus and a layer in 79%, with unmodeled structure in 80%. Most profiles (64–81%) have two valleys, a dense core on one side and a light one on the other.

Which coefficients#

With the right model (a lone core fitted with the core model) every set predicts the coefficients it was not fitted to with χ2 of 1.0 per coefficient, as the noise: degree 1 and J2 are enough. With a torus and a layer, the three-component model of guessed sizes, placed by the profile and Gauss–Newton, with noise:

Coefficients fitted Number Core within 10 m Core error (median) Mass excess error (median) Consistent χ2 per coefficient of the others
degree 1 + J2 4 23% 22 m 151% (underdetermined) 21.5
+ J3 5 20% 47 m 134% (underdetermined) 13.5
+ J4 6 30% 22 m 53% (no degree of freedom) 3.8
degrees 1–2 8 27% 22 m 77% 63% 16.3
degrees 1–2 + J3 + J4 10 27% 14 m 47% 40% 3.1
degrees 1–3 15 20% 20 m 88% 47% 5.3
degrees 1–4 24 37% 14 m 56% 37% 1.5
degrees 1–5 35 33% 15 m 46% 33% –

Without noise the same model places the core within 10 m in 53–60% of the models from degrees 1–4 or 1–5 (median 8–10 m).

  • J4 is the coefficient that separates a torus and a layer from a core. Added to degree 1 and J2, it lowers the χ2 of the other coefficients from 21.5 to 3.8 per coefficient and the error of the core's mass excess from 151% to 53%. J3 adds little: at this precision it is mostly noise, and fitting it moves the core to fit the noise (47 m).
  • A fit to degrees 1–2 can be consistent and wrong. Degree 2 has five numbers; 63% of these fits pass the χ2 test and still predict the other coefficients at 16 per coefficient. For interiors without any core the same model passes on degrees 1–2 in 60% of the models and predicts the rest at 45. Test a model on coefficients it was not fitted to (Fitting part of the coefficients).
  • The low degrees predict the high ones once J4 is in: fitted to degrees 1–4, the model predicts degree 5 at 1.5 per coefficient.

What limits the finding#

  • The sizes of the components. The models' sizes are fixed and the true ones random. With the true sizes the fit recovers every density exactly (the Example); with guessed sizes the densities and the core position absorb the difference, and the core is found within 10 m in about a third of the models with noise and the mass excess to 50%. Search the sizes as well as the densities (Searching the geometry), as in ROB-DATA3.
  • Structure the model does not have. With boulders and a random field the three-component model places the core within 10 m in at most a fifth of the fits, and is consistent with the coefficients in at most 7% of the fits to degrees 1–2 + J3 + J4 or 1–3 and in none of the fits to degrees 1–4 or 1–5. The rest in the odd degrees says so before any fit.
  • Noise costs about a factor two in the core position with three components (8–10 m without noise, 14–15 m with).

In practice#

  1. If every degree is scaled alike and there is no rest, the interior is a core: fit a core to degree 1 and J2, and test it on the rest.
  2. If degree 4 is scaled down more than degree 2 and the rest is in the even degrees, add a torus and a layer, and fit at least degree 1, J2 and J4; degrees 1–4 when the low degrees are not enough.
  3. If there is a rest in the odd degrees, three components are not enough; do not trust a core position from them.
  4. Place the core by its χ2 profile, not by Gauss–Newton from the center of figure; the fixed-point iteration only for a core that is alone.
  5. Vary the sizes of the components, and add compact masses only where the measurements ask for them (Searching the geometry).
  6. Accept a model only if it predicts coefficients it was not fitted to.

Measurements and inversion

Density estimation#

The inversion estimates the background density and the relative densities of a set of components from a measurement set, and optionally parts of their geometry: the position of spheres, ellipsoids and tori and the axis of ellipsoids and tori (Estimated geometry).

Procedure#

sbtk.invert.setup(body, components, obs, opts) builds the geometry about obs.origin_km and the design matrix once (prob); sbtk.invert.run(prob) solves. sbtk.invert.solve does both. Reusing prob is faster when the same problem is solved more than once:

  • with other settings that do not select measurements (prob.opts.regularization, bounds, positions);
  • for a homogeneous body (sbtk.invert.homogeneous);
  • for other realizations of the same measurements (sbtk.invert.replace_data).

Estimation problem#

Let 𝐲 be the n measurements (the selected coefficients followed by the inertia rows named in opts.moi_labels) with covariance Σ=LL𝖳. The predictions are linear in the densities:

𝐲pred=ρbg𝐠body+∑c=1ncΔρc𝐠c,

where 𝐠body and 𝐠c are the measurements of a unit density in the whole body and in component c (prob.gbody, prob.G). The unknowns 𝐱=(ρbg,Δρ1,…,Δρnc) minimize

\lVertL−1(𝐲pred−𝐲)\rVert2+λ∑c(Δρcρ¯)2

subject to

  • the mass constraint ρbgV+∑cΔρcVc=M, with Vc the volume of component c inside the body and M = obs.mass_kg;
  • the bounds 0≤ρbg≤ρmax and 0≤ρbg+Δρc≤ρmax for every component, with ρmax = opts.rho_max_kgm3;
  • fixed parameters: with opts.background = "bulk" the background is held at the bulk density ρ¯=M/V; components with component.estimate_density false keep their relative density.

λ is the Tikhonov parameter opts.regularization. The problem is solved with lsqlin, first with the active-set algorithm and, if that does not converge, with the interior-point algorithm; if neither converges the run stops with sbtk:invert:solver.

Estimated geometry#

Besides the densities, an inversion can estimate the geometry of components. The geometry parameters are listed by sbtk.internal.geometry_parameters:

Field of the component Components Parameters
component.estimate_position = true sphere, ellipsoid, torus the three center coordinates, km (<name>_x, _y, _z)
component.estimate_position = [false false true] sphere, ellipsoid, torus only the coordinates of the mask, for example the height of a torus
component.estimate_axis = true torus the direction of its axis: two tilts about its own first and second axes, deg (<name>_tilt1, _tilt2)
component.estimate_axis = true ellipsoid its orientation: the two tilts of its third axis and the turn about it, deg (<name>_tilt1, _tilt2, _turn)

Setting either field on a component without a center or an axis stops the inversion with sbtk:invert:geometryParameter. The geometry is found by Gauss–Newton iteration:

  • Each step linearizes the measurements in the geometry parameters and solves the bounded problem. The derivatives are central differences of the integrals: 10⁻⁶ km for a sphere inside the body (a point mass), 10⁻⁴ km and 10⁻² deg for components integrated along rays, whose integrals are smooth only on scales larger than the ray spacing (Assumptions and limitations).
  • Trust region. The steps are limited to opts.step_km for a center coordinate and opts.step_deg for a tilt or turn. A step that does not lower the objective is undone and the trust region halved; a successful step restores it.
  • A priori constraints. With opts.position_sigma_km or opts.axis_sigma_deg finite, each center coordinate, tilt or turn has an a priori constraint of that 1σ about its starting value. These are needed when the measurements do not determine all of the geometry, and they keep a component from absorbing structure the model lacks (below).
  • Hard limits. opts.max_shift_km bounds the distance of an estimated center from its start, opts.max_tilt_deg the angle of an estimated axis from its starting direction, and opts.max_turn_deg the turn of an ellipsoid about its axis. Spheres are always kept inside the body.
  • Stopping. Iteration stops after opts.max_iter steps, or earlier when any of these holds:
  • the objective changes by less than 10⁻¹⁰ relative;
  • an accepted step changes every parameter by less than opts.geometry_tol of its step limit;
  • the trust region falls below 10⁻⁶ km.

Without the step test, a model that lacks structure the data contain keeps lowering χ2 by ever smaller steps. That runs every repetition about the center of mass to its limit.

For data about the center of mass the fit is repeated about the model's own center of mass (below), and each repetition continues from the geometry of the previous one. The priors and limits always refer to the geometry the components were given.

Absorbed structure. An estimated geometry can absorb structure the model lacks, so freeing it can lower χ2 while moving the component away from the truth. Example: a Didymos true model has a torus about its spin axis at the center of figure, plus a boulder and a random density field. The data are its exact values weighted by the Hera radio-science precision, in the frame and about the origin of the DART file. An inversion model with a core, the torus (about the z-axis through the center of figure, 3.7° from the true torus axis) and the regolith has a reduced χ2 of 157 (R2=0.49) with fixed geometry. With the torus axis and height estimated (a priori 1σ of 1° and 10 m, limits of 10° and 50 m), χ2 drops to 49 while R2 falls to −1.95: the torus moves 50 m up, to its limit, and tilts 6.9° from z to stand in for the boulder, and the regolith density falls to its lower bound. At this precision such priors are weak. Priors, or limits tight enough to bind, must express how well the geometry is actually known.

Local minima. A fit whose geometry absorbs structure can have more than one local minimum. The same Didymos fit, in the frame with the center of mass as origin and the spin axes, settled with the torus 41 m above the center of figure (reduced χ2 39) or, with the derivatives taken over smaller steps, 47 m below it (reduced χ2 37); which minimum Gauss–Newton reaches depends on its path. Compare fits started from different geometries before reading a position or an axis as a result.

sbtk.interior.align_with_spin_axis is the counterpart for making a true model: it sets the axis of tori, ellipsoids or sectors along the model's own axis of the largest moment by fixed-point iteration (Density distributions).

Uncertainties#

The covariance of the parameters is the linearized one at the solution, with the mass constraint and the fixed parameters eliminated:

P=Z(Z𝖳J𝖳JZ)−1Z𝖳,

where J is the whitened Jacobian of the measurements with the regularization and a priori rows appended, and the columns of Z span the null space of the mass constraint and the fixed parameters. If Z𝖳J𝖳JZ is singular (the measurements do not determine every free parameter), the pseudo-inverse is used and fit.determined is false. The bounds are not included in P; fit.at_bound marks densities at a bound.

The density of a component and its 1σ are ρbg+Δρc and Pbg,bg+Pcc+2Pbg,c (fit.rho_kgm3, fit.rho_sigma_kgm3). fit.resolved marks components whose relative density exceeds its 1σ. The validation tests check over 40 noise realizations that the standard deviation of (estimate − truth)/σ is within 0.25 of 1, with diagonal and with strongly correlated covariances (Validation).

Regularization#

Models with many components, such as a sector grid, or weak data need Tikhonov regularization to keep noise from producing large alternating densities. sbtk.invert.choose_regularization returns the largest λ for which

χ2≤max(n, χmin2+2n),

with n the number of measurements and χmin2 the value at λ=10−2 (the discrepancy principle): χ2 may rise by about one standard deviation of its distribution. It searches log10λ∈[−2,8] by bisection with 9 solves; the result is returned, not stored, so set prob.opts.regularization before the final run.

Data about a fixed point or about the center of mass#

When obs.coef_about is 'origin', the coefficients, degree 1 included, and the inertia are about the fixed point obs.origin_km: for a package in the frame and about the origin of its shape model file, as the HLP6 makers send, [0 0 0]. Layers and sectors are measured along rays from the center of mass, as in sbtk.data.simulate, so the model's geometry is built about the center of mass the degree-1 coefficients give (fit.origin_km; if that is within 3σ of obs.origin_km, the data do not tell the two apart and obs.origin_km is used). Its coefficients, degree 1 included, and its inertia are moved to obs.origin_km exactly (sbtk.internal.sh_translation, the parallel-axis theorem; fit.com_shift_km is that point minus fit.origin_km). Degree 1 then compares the model's center of mass with the measured one, and no iteration is needed. Measuring layers and sectors from the origin of the file instead, 52 to 57 m from the center of mass of Didymos, changes a sector by about 25% of its volume, and a fit with exactly the components of the true model no longer recovers it (testLayersFromMeasuredCenterOfMass).

When obs.coef_about is 'center_of_mass', the coefficients of degree 2 and higher are about the body's center of mass, which is known only through its measurement (the degree-1 rows). Expanding the model about the measured center of mass would carry the error of that measurement into the predictions: a translation of the expansion point changes the coefficients of degree l by terms proportional to those of lower degrees (Uncertainties and the expansion point). sbtk.invert.run therefore

  1. keeps the model where it is: its geometry is built about the measured center of mass (fit.origin_km), from which layers and sectors are measured;
  2. moves its predicted coefficients of degree ≥ 2 and inertia to the model's own center of mass, by the exact translation of solid harmonics (sbtk.internal.sh_translation) and the parallel-axis theorem;
  3. iterates (Gauss–Newton, including the dependence of the center of mass on the densities, prob.D) until that center moves by less than 1 mm (fit.frame_iterations, fit.frame_offset_km);
  4. compares the model's center of mass with the measured one through the degree-1 rows.

Here fit.com_shift_km is the model's center of mass minus fit.origin_km. The tests testCenterOfMassFrameMatchesTheTrueFrame and testPredictionsAboutTheModelCenterOfMass check that the densities agree with an inversion about the true center of mass to within 0.2σ and that the predictions equal a forward model computed from scratch about the fitted center of mass (Validation).

Settings#

Setting (opts) Standard value Meaning
opts.moi_labels {'Ixx','Iyy','Izz'} Inertia rows fitted; {} for gravity coefficients only.
opts.regularization 0 Tikhonov parameter λ.
opts.background "estimate" "bulk" holds the background at M/V.
opts.rho_max_kgm3 4500 Upper bound on every density, kg/m³.
opts.max_iter 20 Gauss–Newton iterations for estimated geometry.
opts.step_km 0.010 Trust-region radius of a center coordinate, km.
opts.step_deg 1 Trust-region radius of an axis tilt or turn, deg.
opts.position_sigma_km Inf A priori 1σ of center coordinates, km.
opts.axis_sigma_deg Inf A priori 1σ of axis tilts and turns, deg.
opts.max_shift_km Inf Largest distance of an estimated center from its start, km.
opts.max_tilt_deg Inf Largest angle of an estimated axis from its start, deg.
opts.max_turn_deg Inf Largest turn of an estimated ellipsoid about its axis from its start, deg.
opts.geometry_tol 10⁻³ Converged when every geometry step is below this fraction of its step limit.

sbtk.invert.options(Name=Value) changes any of them; the fields can also be set afterwards.

Example#

MATLAB script: Estimation with several settings
run("/path/to/SBTK/sbtk_setup.m")
body = sbtk.body.from_mass("Didymos", sbtk.shape.bundled("didymos"), 5.273e11, 0.43);
unc  = sbtk.data.uncertainties([sbtk.units.offset_to_degree1(0.002, 0.43), 1e-4, 2e-4, 4e-4], 2e-3, 0.02);
cof = body.centroid_km;                                                % positions from the center of figure
true_components = [sbtk.interior.sphere("core", cof + [0.03 -0.02 0.01], 0.17, +500), ...
                   sbtk.interior.torus("torus", 0.37, 0.055, 0.015, -500), ...
                   sbtk.interior.layer("regolith", 0, 0.012, -900)];
true_components(2).center_km = cof;                                    % the torus about the z-axis through cof
[exact, truth] = sbtk.data.simulate(body, sbtk.interior.create(true_components), 4, "estimation");
obs = sbtk.data.add_noise(sbtk.data.set_uncertainties(exact, unc), 1);

components = [sbtk.interior.sphere("core", cof, 0.17, 0), ...         % geometry fixed, densities estimated
              sbtk.interior.torus("torus", 0.37, 0.055, 0, 0), ...
              sbtk.interior.layer("regolith", 0, 0.012, 0)];
components(2).center_km = cof;
prob = sbtk.invert.setup(body, components, obs, sbtk.invert.options());
hom  = sbtk.invert.homogeneous(prob);                                  % is structure required?
fit  = sbtk.invert.run(prob);
sbtk.invert.summary(fit)

moving = components;  moving(1).estimate_position = true;              % estimate the core center as well
fit_p  = sbtk.invert.solve(body, moving, obs);
fprintf("core center [%.0f %.0f %.0f] m from the center of figure +- [%.0f %.0f %.0f] m\n", ...
        1e3*(fit_p.components(1).center_km - cof), 1e3*fit_p.center_sigma_km(1, :))

raised = components;  raised(2).estimate_position = [false false true];  % estimate the height of the torus
fit_z  = sbtk.invert.solve(body, raised, obs, sbtk.invert.options(max_shift_km=0.030));
fprintf("torus height %.1f m +- %.1f m (true 15 m)\n", 1e3*(fit_z.components(2).center_km(3) - cof(3)), 1e3*fit_z.center_sigma_km(2, 3))

The true core is at (30, −20, 10) m from the center of figure and the true torus 15 m above it; the fixed-geometry fit places both at the center of figure. More examples: Calculations.

Measurements and inversion

Searching the geometry#

The densities of a model are linear in the measurements; its geometry is not. sbtk.invert.run estimates the densities, and by Gauss–Newton the centers and axes it is asked to, from where the model starts. It does not estimate sizes (the radii of a torus, the thickness of a layer), it finds the minimum of the valley it starts in, and it fits only the components it is given. What the study found showed what that costs: with guessed sizes a core is placed within 10 m in about a third of the interiors, and with boulders the model does not fit at all. sbtk.search searches the geometry systematically, for any model and any set of measurements.

The method#

For fixed geometry, the densities cost one small least-squares solve. With every center, size and axis fixed, the measurements are linear in the densities, and with the mass constraint one density follows from the others. The χ2 of a geometry is then the minimum over the densities, from the component integrals alone. The integrals of a component depend only on its own geometry: a grid that varies the ring and tube radii and the axis of a torus, the thickness of a layer and the position of a core needs integrals for each value of each component's own parameters, and then a least-squares solve for every combination. 140 torus shapes, 4 layer thicknesses and 17 core positions are 9,520 combinations from 161 integrals; on the 49,152-facet Didymos model a torus integral takes 0.9 s and a solve a fraction of a millisecond.

The search goes from the coarse to the fine and adds parameters only where the measurements need them:

  1. Grid (sbtk.search.grid): every combination of the values of the searched parameters, densities without bounds; the best few fitted again with the bounds of sbtk.invert.run. The χ2 profile of each parameter, the lowest χ2 over all others at each of its values, shows which values the measurements allow (sbtk.plot.search_profiles).
  2. Gauss–Newton from the best points (sbtk.search.refine): the centers and axes with derivatives refined from each of the best combinations, which start in different valleys; the fits ranked by χ2.
  3. Compact masses (sbtk.search.add_masses): the residuals of the model tell where one more mass would lower χ2 most. For every position of a grid of candidates inside the body, a point mass (a sphere inside the body is exactly one) is added and the densities fitted again: one solve per position, a map of where and with which sign the measurements ask for mass. The best few positions are refined by Gauss–Newton with the position derivatives, then with all the estimated geometry free, and the mass is kept only if it lowers χ2 by at least the 1−α quantile of χ2 with 4 degrees of freedom, the likelihood-ratio test for a model with a center and a density more (9.49 for α=0.05). The step repeats until the model is consistent with the measurements (p≥0.05), a mass is not significant, or a largest number is reached (sbtk.plot.search_masses).

sbtk.search.run does the three steps in order, each from the best result of the one before, and logs each.

What can be searched#

Any component of any model, by name, with sbtk.search.parameter:

Component Fields Gauss–Newton
sphere center_km, radius_km center
ellipsoid center_km, semi_axes_km, axis center, orientation
torus center_km, ring_radius_km, tube_radius_km, height_km, axis center (height), axis
layer depth_km (top and bottom) –
sector frac, lat_deg, lon_deg, axis –

Sizes have no derivatives in SBTK and are searched on the grid; centers and axes are searched coarsely on the grid (the side of a core, the tilt of a torus) and refined by Gauss–Newton. sbtk.search.directions spreads axis directions evenly in a cone. Several parameters of one component vary together. The measurements can be any set: all coefficients, a subset (sbtk.data.select_coefficients), inertia rows; the search targets whatever obs contains.

Two limits hold for any search:

  • A sphere inside the body is a point mass. The coefficients see its mass and position, not its radius: a dense small sphere and a less dense large one give the same coefficients. Its radius matters only through the density bounds (opts.rho_max_kgm3 caps its mass).
  • A thin layer is seen through its mass per area, thickness times density, unless the measurements are precise enough to separate them. Its profile is then flat along the thickness.

Functions#

Step Function
Parameters and axis directions sbtk.search.parameter, sbtk.search.directions
Grid sbtk.search.grid, sbtk.plot.search_profiles
Gauss–Newton from several starts sbtk.search.refine
Compact masses sbtk.search.add_masses, sbtk.plot.search_masses
All steps sbtk.search.run, sbtk.search.settings

What the search finds#

tests/studies/geometry_search_study.m searches the 60 interiors of the coefficient reading study that have a torus and a layer, exact and with the Hera radio-science noise, with a core, a torus and a layer: the core along the center-of-mass offset (−80 to 80 m), the ring radius (300 to 400 m) and tube radius (35 to 65 m), 7 axis directions up to 4° from z and 4 layer thicknesses on the grid (9,520 combinations from 161 integrals), Gauss–Newton on the core position and the torus height and axis from the best three starts, then up to four compact masses. It compares the result with the true interior and with the same model of guessed sizes. 120 searches took 2.7 hours on 10 workers, 7 to 17 minutes each.

Interiors of a core, a torus and a layer. The search fits the coefficients in every interior (p≥0.05 in all 30, against 10 of 30 with guessed sizes), places the core within 10 m in 43% (83% without noise, against 33% and 53%), and determines the core's mass excess to 18% (11%), against 46% (38%). The torus comes out with its ring radius within 7 m, its height within 2 m and its axis within 0.6° (median, with noise). Its tube radius and the thickness of the layer are not determined: at degree 5 a thin torus and a thin layer are seen through their mass (cross-section or thickness times density), and the grid ends at its first or last value as often as near the true one.

Interiors with boulders and a random field. The search fits the coefficients in 27% of them with noise (none with guessed sizes) and 57% without, but the core is no better placed (within 10 m in 10% and 13%), and the compact masses do not find the boulders: about three are added per interior, each passing the likelihood-ratio test, at a median 230 m from the nearest true boulder (2% within 40 m), with masses up to tens of times the boulders' and of either sign. They fit the coefficients, and the density moves further from the true one (median R2 of the density −0.10 before them, −0.21 after). The boulders are 25 to 50 m across, at most 10⁻³ of the mass, 120 to 260 m from the center: to degree 5 their fields are smooth, and other components (the torus's tilt, the random field, a mass elsewhere) make the same coefficients. A compact mass that passes the test says that the model lacks something the coefficients see, not where a boulder is.

In short: search the sizes and the axis on a grid and refine by Gauss–Newton from each valley; it finds the parameters the coefficients determine (the core, the ring radius, the axis) and shows by its profiles which they do not (a thin tube or layer). Add compact masses to see whether the model lacks structure, not to locate boulders, unless they are large and shallow enough to dominate a degree.

Every solution, and the true interior, is averaged over the same 40 m cells, the resolution of the point masses, and compared by the R2 of the cell averages (the fraction of the variance of the true cell averages explained):
