With few measurements, the smoothest solution that fits puts the mass where the coefficients are most sensitive to it, near the surface, not where it is.
  • The models with components recover 60–76% of the cell variance where their kinds of component are right (the core, torus and layer interiors), with 6 to 9 parameters; with boulders and a random field, which they do not have, 30–38% (fixed sizes) and less after the search's compact masses.
  • The discrepancy principle leaves χ² at the number of measurements (reduced χ² about 4): not a consistent fit.

The point masses show the side and the depth range of an anomaly (the ROB pages compare them with every other solution), but not its shape; a model whose components are the right kind does far better with far fewer parameters.

Measurements and inversion

Fitting part of the coefficients#

A model can be fitted to some of the coefficients and tested on the others. This answers two questions: which coefficients determine which parts of a model (can degree 1 and J2 alone place a core?), and whether a model fitted to the well-measured low degrees predicts the higher ones, which is a test on data it was not fitted to.

Functions#

Step Function
Keep some coefficients sbtk.data.select_coefficients(obs, labels), sbtk.data.select_degree(obs, L)
Fit them sbtk.invert.setup, sbtk.invert.run (or sbtk.invert.solve)
Predict every coefficient from the fit sbtk.invert.predict(fit, body, obs) with the full set
Map the residuals of several fits sbtk.plot.coefficient_residuals
Compare anomalies coefficient by coefficient sbtk.plot.anomaly with sbtk.interpret.anomaly of each fit

sbtk.invert.predict evaluates the fitted model (its components with their fitted geometry and densities) for every measurement of the full set: for the fitted rows it gives the fit's own predictions, for the others new ones. It reports the χ2 of each group with its own covariance (pred.chi2_fitted, pred.chi2_other). The fit and the full set must give the same measured center of mass, so keep degree 1 in every subset of data about a fixed point; otherwise the model's layers and sectors would be measured from another point and sbtk:invert:predictOrigin stops the prediction.

A subset with fewer coefficients than free parameters leaves the fit underdetermined: fit.determined is false, the solution is one of many, and its χ2 is 0 by construction. A core alone has four unknowns (its relative density and three coordinates), which degree 1 and J2 determine exactly; a core, a torus and a layer have six.

MATLAB fragment. Requires the variables defined in Reading the coefficients of a hidden interior.
part = sbtk.data.select_coefficients(obs, ["C10" "C11" "S11" "C20"]);   % degree 1 and J2
core = sbtk.interior.sphere("core", cm.center_km, 0.15, 0);
core.estimate_position = true;
fit1 = sbtk.invert.solve(body, core, part, opts);
pred1 = sbtk.invert.predict(fit1, body, obs);
fit3 = sbtk.invert.solve(body, model, sbtk.data.select_degree(obs, 3), opts);
pred3 = sbtk.invert.predict(fit3, body, obs);
fprintf('degree 1 + J2: chi2 per coefficient of the others %.3g\n', pred1.chi2_other/pred1.n_other);
fprintf('degrees 1-3:   chi2 per coefficient of degrees 4-5 %.3g\n', pred3.chi2_other/pred3.n_other);
fig = sbtk.plot.coefficient_residuals({pred1, pred3}, ["core, degree 1 + J2", "three components, degrees 1-3"]);

How well the fitted coefficients are matched#

A fit to part of the coefficients has to be judged on two groups: the coefficients it was fitted to, which it matches by construction as well as its parameters allow, and the others, which it predicts. sbtk.plot.coefficient_residuals shows both for several fits at once, one row per fit and one column per measurement, with the fitted cells outlined; sbtk.plot.anomaly shows the anomaly of a few fits against the measured one, filled where fitted and open where predicted.

tests/studies/coefficient_reading_figures.m does this for one of the study's true interiors (the first of the family "core, torus, layer": a core of +776 kg/m³ and radius 121 m, 54 m from the center of figure, a torus of −652 kg/m³ and a layer of −421 kg/m³), with noise at the Hera precision, fitted with the three-component model of guessed sizes to each of the eight sets, the core placed by its χ2 profile and Gauss–Newton:

Output
truth_051: core +776 kg/m^3, radius 121 m, 53.6 m from the center of figure; torus -652; layer -421
coefficients               fitted  chi2/n fitted  chi2/n others    core drho core error m
degree 1 + J2                   4       4.67e-15           34.5         1799         38.6
+ J3                            5       1.84e-14           9.92          883         28.5
+ J4                            6         0.0058           12.2         -121        187.0
degrees 1-2                     8           1.89           16.8          388         45.7
degrees 1-2 + J3 + J4          10           3.01            3.3          189         78.1
degrees 1-3                    15           2.58           5.58          300         34.9
degrees 1-4                    24           3.32           1.87          560          9.4
degrees 1-5                    35           2.87              -          433         16.8
  • With 4, 5 or 6 coefficients for 6 unknowns, the fit matches its coefficients exactly (χ2 per coefficient 10⁻¹⁵ to 10⁻²): the row is white where it is outlined. That says nothing about the model; the other coefficients do (34.5, 9.9 and 12.2 per coefficient), and the core ends 29 to 187 m from the true one.
  • From degrees 1–2 the fit has more coefficients than unknowns and its own χ2 rises (1.9 to 3.3 per coefficient): the model with these sizes cannot match the coefficients to their 1σ. J4 brings the prediction of the others from 16.8 to 3.3; degrees 1–4 predict degree 5 at 1.9, and the core is then 9 m from the true one.
  • S¯22 is several σ off in every fit. The true interior has the same three kinds of component; the model's, of other sizes, do not make its S¯22 at any densities and core position.

Results of the study#

What the study found reports the 15,840 fits of tests/studies/coefficient_reading_study.m. For the choice of coefficients:

  • A core that is alone is determined by degree 1 and J2, and the fit predicts every other coefficient as well as the noise allows (1.0 per coefficient). More coefficients do not improve its position (4–5 m at the Hera precision).
  • A core with a torus and a layer needs J4: degree 1 + J2 + J4 predicts the others at 3.8 per coefficient against 21.5 without J4; degrees 1–2 + J3 + J4 at 3.1; degrees 1–4 predict degree 5 at 1.5. J3 adds little and, with noise, moves the core to fit the noise.
  • Degrees 1–2 alone are not a test: 63% of those fits are consistent with their coefficients and still predict the others at 16 per coefficient; for interiors with no core at all, 60% and 45.
  • The fixed-point iteration that moves the core to match degree 1 (sbtk.invert.recenter) converges in about 3 steps for a core alone, and not at all when other components can match degree 1 themselves.

Measurements and inversion

Goodness of fit and model comparison#

Chi-square test#

For a fit with residuals 𝐫=𝐲pred−𝐲 and measurement covariance Σ:

Quantity Definition Field
χ2 𝐫𝖳Σ−1𝐫, with the full covariance fit.chi2
Effective number of parameters peff=tr(JdPJd𝖳), the trace of the data resolution matrix (Jd whitened measurement Jacobian, P parameter covariance); it accounts for fixed parameters and regularization
Degrees of freedom ν=n−peff fit.dof
Reduced χ2 χ2/ν; close to 1 when the model and the stated uncertainties are correct fit.chi2_reduced
p-value P(χν2≥χ2), the probability that a correct model gives a χ2 at least as large, computed as the upper regularized incomplete gamma function Q(ν/2,χ2/2) fit.p_value
Consistent p≥0.05: the model is consistent with the measurements at the 5% significance level fit.consistent

sbtk.invert.goodness_of_fit computes the last three from χ2 and ν. When ν≤10−6 (at least as many parameters as measurements) the test is undefined: the reduced χ2 and the p-value are NaN and consistent is false.

Homogeneous body#

sbtk.invert.homogeneous fits a body of uniform density M/V to the same measurements; it has no free parameters (ν=n). If this fit is already consistent with the measurements, the data do not require internal structure at their precision.

Normalized residuals#

(ypred−y)/σ for every measurement (fit.normalized_residual, sbtk.plot.residuals). For a correct model about 68% lie within ±1. Large residuals concentrated in one group indicate structure that the model lacks: in the degree-1 rows, a model that cannot place the center of mass; at one degree, structure at the corresponding scale.

When a fit is rejected (p<0.05), its densities and uncertainties describe the best model of the chosen form, not the body. At high measurement precision, small structures that a component model omits, such as a random density field of a few percent of the bulk density or a boulder tens of meters across, can be enough to reject an otherwise correct model (Hera blind test).

Comparison with a true model#

In synthetic tests the true model is known. sbtk.compare.with_truth(body, truth, fit) evaluates both densities at the centroids of 24 radial shells of every facet cone (1,179,648 points for the 49,152-facet Didymos model), each weighted by the shell volume wi, with each model's layers and sectors measured from its own origin. A model with more than 50,000 facets is sampled in the cones of every k-th facet, k=⌈nf/50,000⌉, which fills the volume as evenly (1.2 million points for the 3,145,728-facet model instead of 75 million). It returns (cmp):

R2=1−∑iwi(ρest,i−ρtrue,i)2∑iwi(ρtrue,i−ρ¯true)2,

the fraction of the volume-weighted variance of the true density about its mean that the estimate explains: 1 for an exact estimate, 0 for one no better than a uniform density, negative for a worse one.

  • Rmax2: the largest R2 attainable with the same components, from a weighted least-squares fit of the true density by the background and the components. It measures the limit set by the choice of components; R2 close to Rmax2 means the measurements determined the densities as well as that geometry allows.
  • The volume-weighted RMS error and the standard deviation of the true density.
  • For each component present in both models: estimate, 1σ, true density and |estimate−true|/σ.

For many fits of the same components against one true model, sbtk.compare.reference samples the true model once and sbtk.compare.evaluate compares each fit in milliseconds. sbtk.compare.summary prints a comparison and sbtk.plot.comparison plots it.

Comparison of density grids#

Any two models can be compared on a common cubic grid, independently of how they are parametrized. sbtk.exchange.density_grid(body, model, spacing_km) evaluates a model at cell centers that lie at integer multiples of the spacing along the axes of the shape-model frame; cells whose center is inside the shape model (tested along rays from the center of figure) are kept, so all models of a body have the same cells (grid). sbtk.compare.grids(truth, estimate) compares the cells present in both grids (gridcmp): R2 with equal weights, RMS and mean error, and the fraction of cells whose error is at most twice the 1σ of the estimate. Both grids must have the same spacing (sbtk:compare:gridSpacing). This is how solutions in exchange packages are compared with interior-model packages.

Calibration of the uncertainties#

The uncertainties of a fit can be checked with repeated noise realizations: if they are correct, the standard deviation of (ρ^−ρtrue)/σ over many realizations is close to 1.

MATLAB script: Calibration over noise realizations
run("/path/to/SBTK/sbtk_setup.m")
body = sbtk.body.from_mass("Didymos", sbtk.shape.bundled("didymos"), 5.273e11, 0.43);
unc  = sbtk.data.uncertainties([sbtk.units.offset_to_degree1(0.002, 0.43), 1e-4, 2e-4, 4e-4], 2e-3, 0.02);
components = [sbtk.interior.sphere("core", body.centroid_km, 0.17, +450), sbtk.interior.layer("regolith", 0, 0.012, -900)];
[exact, truth] = sbtk.data.simulate(body, sbtk.interior.create(components), 4, "calibration");
exact = sbtk.data.set_uncertainties(exact, unc);

prob = sbtk.invert.setup(body, components, sbtk.data.add_noise(exact, 1), sbtk.invert.options());
z = zeros(30, 3);
for k = 1:30
    f = sbtk.invert.run(sbtk.invert.replace_data(prob, sbtk.data.add_noise(exact, 100 + k)));
    z(k, :) = ([f.rho_bg_kgm3, [f.components.drho_kgm3]] - [truth.rho_bg_kgm3, [components.drho_kgm3]]) ...
              ./[f.rho_bg_sigma_kgm3, f.drho_sigma_kgm3];
end
fprintf("standard deviation of (estimate - truth)/sigma: %.2f\n", std(z(:)))

Files

Results folders and figures#

Run folders#

sbtk.io.new_run(project, name) creates the folder results/<project>/<yyyy-mm-dd_HHMMSS>_<name>/ in the repository and starts recording everything printed in the Command Window to log.txt in it, until sbtk.io.finish_run closes the log. It returns an out structure, which every save and report function takes. A new run never overwrites an earlier one.

  • sbtk.io.latest_run(project, name) returns the newest folder whose name after the time stamp equals name exactly: "didymos_T1" does not match didymos_T1_inversion. Inversion scripts use it to find the newest simulation.
  • sbtk.io.subfolder(out, name) makes the save and report functions write into a subfolder while the log stays in the run folder. The Hera simulation runners use it to keep the true model apart from the data package (Hera blind test).
MATLAB
out = sbtk.io.new_run("my_project", "T1_inversion");     % results/my_project/<date_time>_T1_inversion/
prob = sbtk.invert.setup(body, components, obs, sbtk.invert.options());
sbtk.io.report_inversion(out, body, sbtk.invert.run(prob), sbtk.invert.homogeneous(prob));
sbtk.io.finish_run(out);

This fragment requires body, components and obs as defined in the first script.

Files#

File Written by Contents Read with
log.txt sbtk.io.new_run Everything printed during the run. a text editor
settings.json sbtk.io.save_settings, called by the report functions Body, degree, uncertainties, components, random field, noise seed and inversion settings of the run. jsondecode(fileread(file))
measurements.txt, .mat sbtk.io.save_measurements The measurement set (obs); the text has only the diagonal of the coefficient covariance. sbtk.io.load_measurements
truth.txt, .mat sbtk.io.save_truth The true model of a simulation (truth). sbtk.io.load_truth
fit.txt, .mat sbtk.io.save_fit Densities with 1σ, χ2 test, every residual (fit). sbtk.io.load_fit
homogeneous.txt sbtk.io.report_inversion The same data fitted by a homogeneous body.
comparison.txt, .mat sbtk.io.save_comparison R2, Rmax2, RMS error, per-component comparison (cmp). load
figures/*.png sbtk.io.save_figure (200 dpi) The figures below.

The report functions write a standard set in one call:

Function Writes
sbtk.io.report_simulation(out, body, obs, truth) measurements.*, truth.*, settings.json, figures/truth_3d.png, truth_slices.png, measurements.png
sbtk.io.report_inversion(out, body, fit, homogeneous) fit.*, homogeneous.txt, settings.json, figures/residuals.png, densities.png, estimate_3d.png, estimate_slices.png
sbtk.io.report_comparison(out, body, truth, fit, cmp) comparison.*, settings.json, figures/comparison.png, truth_vs_estimate.png

True models (sbtk.io.write_truth) and comparisons (sbtk.io.write_comparison) use the same layout.

Figures#

Every plot function returns a figure handle. sbtk.io.save_figure(out, fig, name) saves it as figures/<name>.png at 200 dpi in a run folder; exportgraphics saves it anywhere. Densities are drawn with a sequential color map (dark blue to yellow); signed differences with blue for lower and red for higher density.

The figures below come from one synthetic Didymos run, made by documentation/tools/make_samples.m: a core (+450 kg/m³) at the center of figure, an equatorial torus (−500) about the z-axis through it, a 12 m regolith layer (−900), a boulder of radius 40 m (+900) and a random field of 40 kg/m³ with a 60 m correlation length; measurements to degree 4 with the uncertainties of the first script; an inversion for core, torus and regolith (the boulder and the field are not in the inversion model). The fit has χ2/ν=1.08 (p=0.36), the homogeneous body χ2/ν=45.0; R2=0.93 with Rmax2=0.98.

Shape model#

sbtk.plot.shape(body): the mesh with its center of figure and axes.

Interior in three dimensions#

sbtk.plot.interior3d(body, model, title): the surface drawn translucent; spheres, ellipsoids and tori drawn where they lie inside the body, layers by their lower boundary; color is the relative density. Sectors are not drawn (use slices). Saved as truth_3d.png and estimate_3d.png by the report functions.

Density slices#

sbtk.plot.slices(body, {models}, {titles}): the density on the plane z=0 (left) and the plane y=0 (right), both through the first model's origin, one row per model with a common color scale. Saved as truth_slices.png and estimate_slices.png.

Measurements#

sbtk.plot.measurements(obs): left, the root-mean-square size of the coefficients of each degree (points) and of their 1σ uncertainties (line); degrees where the points lie well above the line carry information about the interior. Degree 1 is close to zero about the center of mass. Right, each inertia measurement with its 1σ. Saved as measurements.png.

Normalized residuals#

sbtk.plot.residuals(fit): (predicted − measured)/σ for every measurement; gray band ±1σ, dashed lines ±2σ. Saved as residuals.png.

Estimated densities#

sbtk.plot.densities(fit): the density of the background and each component with its ±1σ interval; the dashed line is the background. Components whose relative density is smaller than its 1σ are drawn in gray. Saved as densities.png.

Comparison with the true model#

sbtk.plot.comparison(cmp): left, R2 of the estimate and Rmax2; right, each component's estimate with ±1σ and its true density (cross). Saved as comparison.png.

sbtk.plot.truth_vs_estimate(body, truth, fit): rows for the true density, the estimate (same color scale) and their difference, on the two planes through the true center of mass. Saved as truth_vs_estimate.png.

Difference from the homogeneous body#

sbtk.plot.difference_from_homogeneous(body, sets, names, scale, frame): for each set of gravity coefficients (a measurement set, a true model or an inversion result), the coefficients minus those of the homogeneous body (density M/V), both about their own center of mass, as radio-science fields are. Degree 1 shows the set's center of mass minus the center of figure. A measurement set about another point (for example a field about the shape-model origin) is first moved to its center of mass by the exact translation of solid harmonics. Zonal coefficients are shown as Jl=−C¯l0. With scale = "linear" the signed difference has ±3σ bars for sets with uncertainties; with "log" the absolute difference is drawn with 3σ as a separate line, which shows which departures from a uniform density the measurements resolve. With frame = "shape" both fields are in the shape-model axes; with "spin" in the spin axes of the set (z along its axis of the largest moment), where the set's C¯21, S¯21 vanish; with "principal" in its principal axes, where also S¯22 vanishes. The differences in the vanishing terms are the homogeneous body's own terms in those axes: they measure how far the principal axes of the interior are tilted and turned from those of the homogeneous body (Frames of a gravity field). Not saved by the report functions; save it with sbtk.io.save_figure.

Files

Exchange packages#

Exchange packages carry measurements, interior models and solutions between teams, for example in a blind test where one team simulates measurements of an interior it keeps hidden and other teams invert them. They are plain text with the units, frame and normalization written in them, and can be read without SBTK.

Package Name Written by Contents Released
Measurements <team>-DATA<n>-<comment> sbtk.exchange.write_data Gravity field, covariance, center of mass, moments of inertia, shape model with the data set
Interior model <team>-MOD<n>-<comment> sbtk.exchange.write_model True model, density grid, noise-free measurements, figures after the solutions
Solution <team>-SOL_<data team><n> sbtk.exchange.write_solution Estimated densities, covariance, fitted measurements, density grid, figures with the solution

sbtk.exchange.solution_name forms solution names; sbtk.exchange.locate finds the package of a given kind in a run folder and its redacted/ and unredacted/ subfolders.

File layout#

Each file starts with metadata lines # key: value, followed by one line of column names and comma-separated rows. Every column and key with a unit ends with it; NaN marks a value that is not provided.

Reader Statement
MATLAB T = readtable('gravity_field.txt', 'FileType', 'text', 'CommentStyle', '#');
Python with pandas T = pandas.read_csv('gravity_field.txt', comment='#')
Python, standard library rows = list(csv.DictReader(l for l in open('gravity_field.txt') if not l.startswith('#')))
SBTK sbtk.exchange.read_data(folder), sbtk.exchange.read_grid(file)

Measurement package#

File Contents
README.txt Summary (GM and mass, bulk density, degree and reference radius of the field; the uncertainties and the noise when the values have them) and the list of files.
gravity_field.txt l,m,C,S, fully normalized, with sigma_C,sigma_S when the values have uncertainties: from degree 1 about the origin of the shape model file, or from degree 2 about the center of mass (Expansion point).
gravity_field_unnormalized.txt The same coefficients unnormalized, Clm=NlmC¯lm, Slm=NlmS¯lm (Gravity coefficients), and their 1σ when they have one.
gravity_covariance.txt Full covariance of the normalized coefficients; rows and columns labeled. Only when the values have uncertainties.
center_of_mass.txt Center of mass in the shape-model frame (with its 3 × 3 covariance when it has one) and the center of figure.
moments_of_inertia.txt quantity,value,unit (and sigma): inertia elements as I/(MRref2) about the same point as the gravity field and/or the libration ratio. The products of inertia are tensor elements, Ixy=−∫ρxydV (Moments of inertia); the definition of the libration ratio is given when the file has it.
conventions.txt Units; the frame (what its origin and axes are, and any change of frame from the original shape-model file); the normalization, with MATLAB and Python code; degree 1 and the center of mass.
<shape>.obj The shape model the data were made with, in km, in the frame of every position of the package (The shape model of a package). Not included when it is one of SBTK's shape model files as distributed (data/shapes/), such as the agreed HLP6 models: the files then name it.
potential_acceleration.txt Optional (sbtk.exchange.write_potential): the gravitational potential and acceleration at given points, in SI units (Potential and acceleration at points).

The package contains nothing about the interior: not the noise seed, the model name or any component; testNothingAboutTheInterior checks this (Validation).

Expansion point#

The gravity field and the moments of inertia are given about one of two points, chosen by the measurement set that sbtk.exchange.write_data writes:

Point Measurement set gravity_field.txt sbtk.exchange.read_data returns
The origin of the shape model file (the HLP6 choice) about [0 0 0], e.g. from sbtk.data.expand_about degree 1 and above; degree 1 gives the center of mass the coefficients as given, coef_about = 'origin', origin_km = [0 0 0]
The center of mass, as a radio-science solution any other set degree 2 and above; degree 1 is zero and not listed degree ≥ 2 about the measured center of mass, degree 1 as 0 ± σ (the uncertainty of the center of mass), coef_about = 'center_of_mass'

center_of_mass.txt gives the center of mass and the center of figure in both, and conventions.txt states which point the package uses. The body is built from the package's shape model and GM; sbtk.exchange.read_data reads the shape model from the package, or from data/shapes/ when the package names a file it does not include. A libration ratio, which is defined about the center of mass, becomes the row (B−A)−kIzz=0 with σ = σkIzz, using the measured Izz if the package has one and that of a homogeneous body otherwise.

The files state only what applies to the package. Those of a measurement package with uncertainties and noise, made by documentation/tools/make_samples.m:

Output

The shape model of a package#

A package's shape model is the one the data were made with, in the frame of every position of the package. The HLP6 makers use the agreed shape model file as distributed, unchanged, in its own frame (Frames of a gravity field). Every team has that file, and it never changes, so a package made with it does not include it: README.txt and the header of every file name it. ex09) sends the original shape model moved and rotated into the new frame with sbtk.body.to_frame: every vertex becomes x′=(x−c)A, with c the center of mass of the true model and the columns of A the new axes, both in the frame of the original file. The shape itself does not change, only its coordinates.

Example Shape model of the package Origin Axes
Didymos, spin axes TEAM-DATA1-Didymos_didymos_v003_com_spin_axes.obj center of mass z the axis of the largest moment, x the DART x-axis projected onto the plane normal to z
Dimorphos, principal axes TEAM-DATA2-Dimorphos_dimorphos_v004_com_principal_axes.obj center of mass principal axes: x the axis of the smallest and z of the largest moment

Each true model has its own center of mass and axes, so each package has its own shape model, and its file name starts with the name of the package: <package>_<shape name>.obj (sbtk.internal.shape_file_name). The interior-model package of the data set and a solution of it use the same name. A shape model taken unchanged from a file keeps the file's name.

The center of mass is then at the origin (to rounding), and the center of figure at −(rCoM−rCoF)A. The gravity field, the moments of inertia and center_of_mass.txt, and in the interior-model package every component and the density grid, are in this frame, so a receiving team uses the shape model as it is, with nothing to move or rotate. The FRAME section of conventions.txt states the origin and the axes, and the change of frame from the original file (o=c and A), so the coordinates of the original file are x=x′AT+c. The shape model records this change as shape.frame_origin_km and shape.frame_axes, combined over successive changes of frame. The FRAME section of such a package, made by documentation/tools/make_samples.m:

Output
FRAME
  All positions, the gravity field and the moments of inertia of this package are given
  in the frame of its shape model file, DOC-DATA3-Didymos_didymos_v003_com_spin_axes.obj:
    origin  the center of mass of the body
    z       the axis of the largest moment of inertia
    x       the x-axis of the original file projected onto the plane normal to z
    y       completes the right-handed frame (y = z cross x)
  The shape model file was made by moving and rotating the original file,
    didymos_g_9309mm_spc_obj_0000n00000_v003.obj
  into this frame:
    x' = (x - o) A
    o = [0.015281496 0.042884748 -0.034053123] km  (the center of mass, in the original file)
    A = [  0.997920540676  0.000000000000 -0.064456143974
          -0.001688015795  0.999657019950 -0.026134136041
           0.064434036803  0.026188594157  0.997578273840 ]
  where x and x' are the coordinates of a point (row vectors, km) in the original file and
  in this one, and o and the columns of A are the origin and the axes of this frame in the
  original file.

Potential and acceleration at points#

sbtk.exchange.write_potential adds potential_acceleration.txt to a package: one row per point with its position x_m,y_m,z_m in the frame of the shape model file, the potential U_m2_s2 and the acceleration ax_m_s2,ay_m_s2,az_m_s2, in SI units as the HLP6 makers' cross-validation asks. The potential is positive, U=G∫ρ/|r−r′|dV, the acceleration is its gradient, and the rotation of the body is not included. The header states how the values were computed (sbtk.gravity.field_at): exactly for a homogeneous body, otherwise with the departures from the background density on a grid of cubes (Potential and acceleration at points). The function works for any model; the HLP6 makers give it for the homogeneous Didymos (examples/make_didymos_homogeneous.m).

Packages of exact values#

A set without any uncertainties, such as the exact values of a true model (sbtk.data.simulate), is written as a package of exact values:

  • gravity_field.txt has the columns l,m,C,S, center_of_mass.txt the columns axis,center_of_mass_km,center_of_figure_km, and moments_of_inertia.txt the columns quantity,value,unit;
  • there is no gravity_covariance.txt;
  • no file has an uncertainties or noise line.

A maker's package of exact values in the frame and about the origin of the shape model file, as the HLP6 makers send them, made by documentation/tools/make_samples.m:

Output

y,0.042884747979,0.042313853148
z,-0.034053123055,-0.033978532721

In a blind test the makers send such packages, and each receiving team applies uncertainties of its own choosing. sbtk.exchange.read_data reads them with NaN uncertainties. The inversion then stops with sbtk:data:noUncertainties until uncertainties are given, for example with sbtk.data.use_uncertainties from a precision file and sbtk.data.set_moi_sigma, after truncating with sbtk.data.select_degree to the degrees the precision covers. A set with some uncertainties but not all is not written (sbtk:data:noUncertainties).

Interior-model package#

File Contents
README.txt Summary (mass, bulk and background density, number of components, random field, density grid) and the list of files.
interior_model.txt name,type,relative_density_kgm3,density_kgm3,geometry for the background and every component; metadata: mass, bulk and background density, the point layers and sectors are measured from, the random field, the principal axes of inertia (unit vectors in the shape-model axes) and the principal moments A≤B≤C (Frames of a gravity field).
density_grid.txt x_km,y_km,z_km,density_kgm3,density_sigma_kgm3: the true density at the cell centers (σ = 0), random field included.
noise_free_data/ The measurement files without noise.
figures/ true_density_3d.png, true_density_slices.png.
Output
# product: true interior model
# model: DOC-MOD1-Didymos
# data_set: DOC-DATA1-Didymos
# body: Didymos
# shape_model: didymos_g_9309mm_spc_obj_0000n00000_v003.obj (24578 vertices, 49152 facets, lengths in km)
# frame: shape model frame
# mass_kg: 5.273000e+11
# bulk_density_kgm3: 2592.984
# background_density_kgm3: 2672.002

# layers_and_sectors_from_km: 0.015281 0.042885 -0.034053
# overlaps: relative densities add; components are clipped to the shape model

# principal_moments: A B C = 0.253270820 0.271737242 0.335835620 (I / (M R_ref^2))
# random_field: Gaussian, standard deviation 40.0 kg/m^3, correlation exp(-d^2/(2 L^2)) with L = 0.0600 km, seed 7

Solution package#

File Contents
README.txt Method, the χ2 test of the fit and of a homogeneous body, the measurements used.
solution.txt Background and each component: density and relative density with 1σ, estimated or prescribed, geometry.
solution_covariance.txt Covariance of the estimated parameters.
fitted_measurements.txt label,measured,predicted,sigma,normalized_residual; degree-1 rows are the center of mass.
density_grid.txt Estimated density and its 1σ at the cell centers, propagated from the parameter covariance.
figures/ Residuals, densities, 3-D view, slices.

Density grid#

Cell centers lie at integer multiples of spacing_km along each axis of the shape-model frame, so grids of the same spacing coincide regardless of who made them. A cell is listed when its center is inside the shape model, tested along rays from the center of figure, so all models of a body have the same cells. Each cell stands for the volume spacing_km³ and carries the density at its center. sbtk.compare.grids compares two grids (Comparison of density grids); the comparison of the example solution with its model:

Output
density grids: 3179 common cells (3179 true, 3179 estimated)
  R2 = 0.922 (fraction of the variance of the true density explained)
  RMS error 98.3 kg/m^3, mean error +1.2 kg/m^3, standard deviation of the true density 351.3 kg/m^3
  97.9% of the common cells have abs(estimate - true) <= 2 sigma of the estimate

conventions.txt#

Every measurement package includes this file, written by sbtk.internal.exchange_conventions; the tests check the normalization code it prints. That of the maker's package above, in the frame and about the origin of the shape model file:

Output
UNITS
  Lengths and positions in km, mass in kg, time in s, GM in km^3/s^2, densities in kg/m^3,
  angles in degrees.

FRAME
  All positions, the gravity field and the moments of inertia of this package are given
  in the frame of its shape model file, didymos_g_9309mm_spc_obj_0000n00000_v003.obj:
    origin  the origin of the shape model file (different from the CoF and CoM)
    axes    those of the shape model file as distributed

GRAVITY FIELD COEFFICIENT NORMALIZATION
  The files give fully normalized coefficients:
    Cbar_lm = C_lm / N_lm,   Sbar_lm = S_lm / N_lm,   Pbar_lm = N_lm P_lm,
    N_lm = sqrt( (2 - delta_m0) (2l + 1) (l - m)! / (l + m)! )
  where P_lm are the associated Legendre functions without the factor (-1)^m. For example,
    N_20 = sqrt(5), N_21 = sqrt(5/3), N_22 = sqrt(5/12), N_30 = sqrt(7).
  Zonal coefficients: J_l = -C_l0 = -sqrt(2l + 1) Cbar_l0.
  gravity_field_unnormalized.txt gives the same coefficients unnormalized:
    C_lm = N_lm Cbar_lm,   S_lm = N_lm Sbar_lm.

  MATLAB
    N = sqrt((2 - (m == 0)) .* (2*l + 1) .* factorial(l - m) ./ factorial(l + m));
  Python
    N = math.sqrt((2 - (m == 0)) * (2*l + 1) * math.factorial(l - m) / math.factorial(l + m))

DEGREE 1 AND THE CENTER OF MASS
  The gravity field is expanded about the origin of the shape model file. Its degree-1
  coefficients give the center of mass (xc, yc, zc) relative to that origin. The moments
  of inertia are about the same origin.

Other formats#

Format Function Notes
PDS SHADR layout sbtk.exchange.read_shadr Header row then l, m, C, S, sigma_C, sigma_S; commas or spaces; # comments. The caller gives the shape model and the point the coefficients are about.
JPL SSD gravity file sbtk.io.read_jpl_gravity Full covariance; Jl converted.
Coefficient matrices sbtk.data.from_coefficients
Uncertainties of another data set sbtk.data.use_uncertainties Converted to the target reference radius by (R/R′)l.

Examples

Density models by component type#

One example per component type and model feature. Each example after the first is a fragment: it uses the body and uncertainties defined in the setup script below, which must be run first. Building a true model and its exact values (sbtk.data.simulate) needs no uncertainties; only the examples that make measurements and estimate densities use unc. Geometry definitions: Density distributions.

Setup#

MATLAB script: Body and uncertainties used by the examples on this page
run("/path/to/SBTK/sbtk_setup.m")
body = sbtk.body.from_mass("Didymos", sbtk.shape.bundled("didymos"), 5.273e11, 0.43);    % mass [kg], R_ref [km]
unc  = sbtk.data.uncertainties([sbtk.units.offset_to_degree1(0.002, 0.43), 1e-4, 2e-4, 4e-4], 2e-3, 0.02);   % for measurements

Sphere#

A sphere is given by its center (shape-model frame, km), radius and relative density. A sphere entirely inside the body is integrated as a point mass. sbtk.interior.latlon gives a position by latitude, longitude and distance; added to the center of figure, as here, it is measured from there (Where to place components).

MATLAB fragment. Requires the variables defined in Body and uncertainties used by the examples on this page.
core    = sbtk.interior.sphere("core", body.centroid_km, 0.170, +450);
boulder = sbtk.interior.sphere("boulder", body.centroid_km + sbtk.interior.latlon(25, 60, 0.250), 0.040, +900);
[exact, truth] = sbtk.data.simulate(body, sbtk.interior.create([core, boulder]), 4, "spheres");
fprintf("center of mass - center of figure: [%.1f %.1f %.1f] m\n", 1e3*exact.com_minus_cof_km)

Ellipsoid#

Semi-axes along x, y, z before the rotation by yaw (about z), pitch (about y) and roll (about x), in degrees.

MATLAB fragment. Requires the variables defined in Body and uncertainties used by the examples on this page.
lens = sbtk.interior.ellipsoid("lens", body.centroid_km + [0.05 0.10 0.12], [0.20 0.08 0.05], [40 -30 15], +300);
disp(lens.axes)                                   % columns: the ellipsoid axes in the shape-model frame
[exact, truth] = sbtk.data.simulate(body, sbtk.interior.create(lens), 4, "ellipsoid");
sbtk.plot.slices(body, {truth}, {'ellipsoid'});

Torus#

A torus about the z-axis: ring radius, tube radius, height of its plane. Only the part inside the body counts, so a torus that crosses the surface at the equator represents a belt of different density along the equator. Set its center_km to place it about the center of figure, and align it with the spin axis with sbtk.interior.align_with_spin_axis (Axes of components).

MATLAB fragment. Requires the variables defined in Body and uncertainties used by the examples on this page.
torus = sbtk.interior.torus("torus", 0.370, 0.055, 0, -500);
torus.center_km = body.centroid_km;                          % about the z-axis through the center of figure
geo = sbtk.gravity.geometry(body, body.centroid_km, 0);
I = sbtk.gravity.component_integrals(geo, torus);
fprintf("torus volume inside the body: %.5f km^3 (%.1f%% of the body)\n", I.V, 100*I.V/body.volume_km3)

Layer#

Top and bottom depth below the surface, along rays from the expansion origin.

MATLAB fragment. Requires the variables defined in Body and uncertainties used by the examples on this page.
regolith = sbtk.interior.layer("regolith", 0, 0.012, -900);          % the outermost 12 m
mantle   = sbtk.interior.layer("mantle", 0.012, 0.080, -200);        % from 12 m to 80 m deep
[exact, truth] = sbtk.data.simulate(body, sbtk.interior.create([regolith, mantle]), 4, "layers");
fprintf("background density %.0f kg/m^3\n", truth.rho_bg_kgm3)

Sector#

Radial fractions of the distance from the expansion origin to the surface, a latitude range and a longitude range (degrees). Longitude ranges may extend beyond ±180°.

MATLAB fragment. Requires the variables defined in Body and uncertainties used by the examples on this page.
block = sbtk.interior.sector("block", [0.3 0.9], [40 90], [150 240], +200);    % northern block across 180 deg
shell = sbtk.interior.sector("shell", [0.5 0.75], [-90 90], [-180 180], -300); % a shell that follows the shape
[exact, truth] = sbtk.data.simulate(body, sbtk.interior.create([block, shell]), 4, "sectors");
sbtk.plot.slices(body, {truth}, {'sectors'});

Sector grid#

A grid of sectors that fills the body is a model without assumed structure. As an estimation model it needs the background held at the bulk density and, with many sectors, regularization. Here the true interior is a dense core and the estimate uses 36 sectors.

MATLAB fragment. Requires the variables defined in Body and uncertainties used by the examples on this page.
[exact, truth] = sbtk.data.simulate(body, sbtk.interior.create(sbtk.interior.sphere("core", body.centroid_km, 0.17, +450)), ...
                                    4, "core");
obs = sbtk.data.add_noise(sbtk.data.set_uncertainties(exact, unc), 1);       % measurements of it
sectors = sbtk.interior.sector_grid([0 0.5 0.85 1], [-90 -30 30 90], [-180 -90 0 90 180]);   % 3 x 3 x 4
prob = sbtk.invert.setup(body, sectors, obs, sbtk.invert.options(background="bulk"));
prob.opts.regularization = sbtk.invert.choose_regularization(prob);
fit = sbtk.invert.run(prob);
fprintf("lambda %.3g, reduced chi2 %.2f, dof %.1f\n", fit.regularization, fit.chi2_reduced, fit.dof)
sbtk.plot.slices(body, {truth, fit}, {'true density', 'sector estimate'});

Random density field#

Standard deviation (kg/m³), correlation length (km) and seed. The field is added to the components; it is used in simulations and is not estimated by the inversion.

MATLAB fragment. Requires the variables defined in Body and uncertainties used by the examples on this page.
field = sbtk.interior.random_field(40, 0.06, 7);                     % sigma 40 kg/m^3, correlation length 60 m
[exact, truth] = sbtk.data.simulate(body, sbtk.interior.create(sbtk.interior.no_components(), field), 4, "field");
grid = sbtk.exchange.density_grid(body, truth, 0.020);              % density at 20 m cell centers inside the body
fprintf("%d cells: mean %.0f, standard deviation %.1f kg/m^3\n", numel(grid.density_kgm3), ...
        mean(grid.density_kgm3), std(grid.density_kgm3))

Homogeneous body#

sbtk.interior.no_components without a random field gives a uniform density M/V.

MATLAB fragment. Requires the variables defined in Body and uncertainties used by the examples on this page.
[exact, truth] = sbtk.data.simulate(body, sbtk.interior.create(sbtk.interior.no_components()), 4, "uniform");
fprintf("background %.1f kg/m^3, bulk density %.1f kg/m^3\n", truth.rho_bg_kgm3, body.bulk_density_kgm3)

Prescribed component#

A component with estimate_density = false keeps its relative density in the inversion; here a regolith layer of known density while the core is estimated.

MATLAB fragment. Requires the variables defined in Body and uncertainties used by the examples on this page.
truth_components = [sbtk.interior.sphere("core", body.centroid_km, 0.17, +450), sbtk.interior.layer("regolith", 0, 0.012, -900)];
exact = sbtk.data.simulate(body, sbtk.interior.create(truth_components), 4, "prescribed");
obs = sbtk.data.add_noise(sbtk.data.set_uncertainties(exact, unc), 1);
model = truth_components;
model(1).drho_kgm3 = 0;                  % estimated: the value is not used
model(2).estimate_density = false;       % prescribed: -900 kg/m^3 is kept
fit = sbtk.invert.solve(body, model, obs);
sbtk.invert.summary(fit)

Estimated sphere position#

The center of a sphere with estimate_position = true is estimated with its density; position_sigma_km adds an a priori constraint about the starting position. The center, height and orientation of tori and ellipsoids can be estimated the same way (Estimated geometry).

MATLAB fragment. Requires the variables defined in Body and uncertainties used by the examples on this page.
truth_components = sbtk.interior.sphere("core", body.centroid_km + [0.03 -0.02 0.01], 0.17, +500);
exact = sbtk.data.simulate(body, sbtk.interior.create(truth_components), 4, "position");
obs = sbtk.data.add_noise(sbtk.data.set_uncertainties(exact, unc), 1);
model = sbtk.interior.sphere("core", body.centroid_km, 0.17, 0);       % started at the center of figure
model.estimate_position = true;
fit = sbtk.invert.solve(body, model, obs, sbtk.invert.options(position_sigma_km=0.050));
fprintf("center [%.1f %.1f %.1f] m from the center of figure +- [%.1f %.1f %.1f] m after %d iterations\n", ...
        1e3*(fit.components(1).center_km - body.centroid_km), 1e3*fit.center_sigma_km(1, :), fit.iterations)

Examples

Calculations#

Short examples of individual calculations. Fragments on this page use the variables of the setup script below.

Setup#

MATLAB script: Body, interior and measurements used by the examples on this page
run("/path/to/SBTK/sbtk_setup.m")
body = sbtk.body.from_mass("Didymos", sbtk.shape.bundled("didymos"), 5.273e11, 0.43);
components = [sbtk.interior.sphere("core", body.centroid_km, 0.170, +450), sbtk.interior.layer("regolith", 0, 0.012, -900)];
[exact, truth] = sbtk.data.simulate(body, sbtk.interior.create(components), 4, "calculations");   % the true model
unc  = sbtk.data.uncertainties([sbtk.units.offset_to_degree1(0.002, 0.43), 1e-4, 2e-4, 4e-4], 2e-3, 0.02);
exact = sbtk.data.set_uncertainties(exact, unc);                     % exact values with uncertainties
obs = sbtk.data.add_noise(exact, 1);                                 % one noisy realization

Unit conversions#

MATLAB fragment. Requires the variables defined in Body, interior and measurements used by the examples on this page.
Izz = sbtk.units.moi_to_norm(1.6e16, body.mass_kg, body.R_ref_km)    % kg m^2 -> I / (M R_ref^2)
I_kgm2 = sbtk.units.norm_to_moi(Izz, body.mass_kg, body.R_ref_km)    % and back
c = sbtk.units.offset_to_degree1(0.002, body.R_ref_km)               % 2 m center-of-mass offset -> degree 1
f = sbtk.units.length_scale("m")                                     % m -> km: 1e-3

Volume and moments of one component#

sbtk.gravity.component_integrals returns the integrals of the part of a component inside the body, per unit density, about the origin of the geometry.

MATLAB fragment. Requires the variables defined in Body, interior and measurements used by the examples on this page.
geo = sbtk.gravity.geometry(body, truth.origin_km, 4);
I = sbtk.gravity.component_integrals(geo, components(2));            % the regolith layer
fprintf("regolith volume %.5f km^3 = %.1f%% of the body\n", I.V, 100*I.V/geo.V_body)
mass_deficit_kg = components(2).drho_kgm3*I.V*1e9                   % its mass relative to the background

Coefficients and inertia about another origin#

MATLAB fragment. Requires the variables defined in Body, interior and measurements used by the examples on this page.
geo0 = sbtk.gravity.geometry(body, [0 0 0], 4);                       % about the shape-model origin
fm = sbtk.gravity.forward(geo0, sbtk.interior.create(components), body.mass_kg);
lab = sbtk.gravity.labels(4);
fprintf("C11 about the shape origin %.4e; about the center of mass %.1e\n", ...
        fm.coef(strcmp(lab, "C11")), truth.coef(strcmp(lab, "C11")))

Difference from the homogeneous body#

The gravity coefficients of the true model and of the measurements, minus those of a body of uniform density, with the 3σ of the measurements (Figures). The second output holds the plotted values; axes_deg gives the angles between the principal axes of each set and of the homogeneous body.

MATLAB fragment. Requires the variables defined in Body, interior and measurements used by the examples on this page.
[fig, d] = sbtk.plot.difference_from_homogeneous(body, {obs, truth}, ["measured" "true model"], "linear", "shape");
fprintf("%s: %+.2e\n", [d(2).labels(1:4); string(d(2).difference(1:4))])   % C10, C11, S11, J2 of the true model
sbtk.plot.difference_from_homogeneous(body, {obs, truth}, ["measured" "true model"], "log", "shape");
[~, dp] = sbtk.plot.difference_from_homogeneous(body, {truth}, "true model", "linear", "principal");
fprintf("principal axes of the true model vs the homogeneous body: tilt %.2f deg, turn %.2f deg\n", dp.axes_deg)

Field about the center of mass, in spin and principal axes#

sbtk.gravity.center_of_mass_frame moves a field to its center of mass (degree 1 becomes 0) and, with "spin", turns its axis of the largest moment to z (C¯21=S¯21=0) or, with "principal", rotates it into its principal axes of inertia (C¯21=S¯21=S¯22=0) (Frames of a gravity field).

MATLAB fragment. Requires the variables defined in Body, interior and measurements used by the examples on this page.
cs = sbtk.gravity.center_of_mass_frame(truth, body, "shape");
cz = sbtk.gravity.center_of_mass_frame(truth, body, "spin");
cp = sbtk.gravity.center_of_mass_frame(truth, body, "principal");
disp(table(cs.labels(1:8)', cs.coef(1:8)', cz.coef(1:8)', cp.coef(1:8)', 'VariableNames', ...
           ["coefficient" "shape axes" "spin axes" "principal axes"]))
fprintf("axis of the largest moment %.2f deg from the shape-model z-axis\n", acosd(cp.principal(3, 3)))
mo = sbtk.gravity.center_of_mass_frame(obs, body, "principal");      % a measurement set: with its covariance
fprintf("C22 in principal axes %.4e +- %.1e\n", mo.coef(mo.labels == "C22"), mo.sigma(mo.labels == "C22"))

A body and its true model in another frame#

sbtk.body.to_frame and sbtk.interior.to_frame carry the shape model and the true model into the frame with the center of mass as origin and the spin axes; the density grid is then on cells of that frame (Frames of a gravity field).

MATLAB fragment. Requires the variables defined in Body, interior and measurements used by the examples on this page.
spin = sbtk.gravity.center_of_mass_frame(truth, body, "spin");
body_s  = sbtk.body.to_frame(body, spin.com_km, spin.axes, "didymos_v003_com_spin_axes");
truth_s = sbtk.interior.to_frame(truth, spin.com_km, spin.axes);
fprintf("center of mass %s km in the shape-model file, %s km in the new frame\n", mat2str(truth.com_km, 4), ...
        mat2str(truth_s.com_km, 4))
fprintf("center of figure %s km in the new frame\n", mat2str(body_s.centroid_km, 4))
grid_s = sbtk.exchange.density_grid(body_s, truth_s, 0.040);
fprintf("%d cells of 40 m in the spin axes\n", numel(grid_s.density_kgm3))

Density at points and on a grid#

MATLAB fragment. Requires the variables defined in Body, interior and measurements used by the examples on this page.
geo = sbtk.gravity.geometry(body, truth.origin_km, 0);               % geometry in the model's frame
x = linspace(-0.3, 0.3, 61)';
rho = sbtk.interior.density_at(truth, truth.origin_km + [x, 0*x, 0*x], geo);
plot(1e3*x, rho); xlabel("x from the center of mass [m]"); ylabel("density [kg/m^3]");

grid = sbtk.exchange.density_grid(body, truth, 0.040);              % 40 m cells
fprintf("%d cells, mean density %.0f kg/m^3\n", numel(grid.density_kgm3), mean(grid.density_kgm3))

Uncertainties from another data set#

sbtk.data.use_uncertainties gives simulated coefficients the covariance of a reference data set, converted to the target reference radius. Here the reference has Rref=0.40 km.

MATLAB fragment. Requires the variables defined in Body, interior and measurements used by the examples on this page.
L = 4;
[C, S] = deal(zeros(L + 1));  C(1, 1) = 1;
sig = 5e-5*ones(L + 1);
reference = sbtk.data.from_coefficients(sbtk.body.from_mass("Didymos", body.shape, body.mass_kg, 0.40), ...
                                        "precision", [0 0 0], C, S, sig, sig);
noisy = sbtk.data.add_noise(sbtk.data.use_uncertainties(exact, reference), 2);
fprintf("1-sigma of C20: %.3e (reference %.1e at 0.40 km)\n", sqrt(noisy.coef_cov(4, 4)), 5e-5)

Inertia measurements#

sbtk.data.select_moi chooses the inertia rows of a data set; opts.moi_labels the rows a fit uses. sbtk.data.libration_ratio_from_amplitude converts a libration amplitude into a libration ratio.

MATLAB fragment. Requires the variables defined in Body, interior and measurements used by the examples on this page.
gravity_only = sbtk.data.select_moi(obs, {});
with_izz = sbtk.data.add_moi(gravity_only, "Izz", exact.moi(3).value, 2e-3);
with_lib = sbtk.data.add_libration(gravity_only, exact.libration_ratio, 0.001, exact.moi(3).value);
[k, sk] = sbtk.data.libration_ratio_from_amplitude(-12, 0.2, 0.027, 0.001)   % G [deg], its sigma, e, its sigma

f0 = sbtk.invert.solve(body, components, gravity_only, sbtk.invert.options(moi_labels={}));
f1 = sbtk.invert.solve(body, components, with_izz, sbtk.invert.options(moi_labels={'Izz'}));
f2 = sbtk.invert.solve(body, components, with_lib, sbtk.invert.options(moi_labels={'libration'}));
fprintf("regolith density 1-sigma: gravity only %.0f, with Izz %.0f, with the libration ratio %.0f kg/m^3\n", ...
        f0.rho_sigma_kgm3(2), f1.rho_sigma_kgm3(2), f2.rho_sigma_kgm3(2))

Measured center of mass#

A gravity field about the center of mass has no degree-1 terms; sbtk.data.add_center_of_mass adds the measured position, after which the inversion expands about the model's own center of mass (Density estimation).

MATLAB fragment. Requires the variables defined in Body, interior and measurements used by the examples on this page.
field = sbtk.data.select_coefficients(obs, setdiff(obs.coef_labels, {'C10', 'C11', 'S11'}, "stable"));
field = sbtk.data.add_center_of_mass(field, obs.origin_km + [0.0005 0 0], 0.002);   % measured 0.5 m off
fit = sbtk.invert.solve(body, components, field);
fprintf("frame iterations %d, model center of mass - origin: [%.2f %.2f %.2f] m\n", fit.frame_iterations, 1e3*fit.com_shift_km)

Reading a SHADR-layout gravity file#

The example writes a small file in the PDS SHADR layout and reads it back. The coefficients are about the shape-model origin, so the file includes degree-1 terms and origin_km = [0 0 0].

MATLAB fragment. Requires the variables defined in Body, interior and measurements used by the examples on this page.
geo0 = sbtk.gravity.geometry(body, [0 0 0], 2);
fm = sbtk.gravity.forward(geo0, sbtk.interior.create(components), body.mass_kg);
lab = sbtk.gravity.labels(2);
coef = @(name) fm.coef(strcmp(lab, name));
file = [tempname '.tab'];
rows = sprintf("%.4f, %.6e, 0, 2, 2, 1, 0, 0", body.R_ref_km, body.GM_km3_s2);   % R, GM, sigma GM, degree, order, normalized
rows(2) = sprintf("1, 0, %.10e, 0, 1e-5, 1e-5", coef("C10"));
rows(3) = sprintf("1, 1, %.10e, %.10e, 1e-5, 1e-5", coef("C11"), coef("S11"));
rows(4) = sprintf("2, 0, %.10e, 0, 1e-5, 1e-5", coef("C20"));
rows(5) = sprintf("2, 1, %.10e, %.10e, 1e-5, 1e-5", coef("C21"), coef("S21"));
rows(6) = sprintf("2, 2, %.10e, %.10e, 1e-5, 1e-5", coef("C22"), coef("S22"));
writelines(rows, file);
[shadr, shadr_body] = sbtk.exchange.read_shadr(file, "Didymos", body.shape, [0 0 0], 2);
sbtk.data.summary(shadr)

Packages for another team#

MATLAB fragment. Requires the variables defined in Body, interior and measurements used by the examples on this page.
folder = tempname;
data  = sbtk.exchange.write_data(folder, "TEAM-DATA1-Didymos", body, obs, "Team name");
model = sbtk.exchange.write_model(folder, "TEAM-MOD1-Didymos", "TEAM-DATA1-Didymos", body, truth, exact, 0.040, "Team name");
[obs2, body2] = sbtk.exchange.read_data(data);                       % what the other team reads
prob = sbtk.invert.setup(body2, components, obs2, sbtk.invert.options());
solution = sbtk.exchange.write_solution(folder, sbtk.exchange.solution_name("OTHER", obs2.name), body2, ...
                                        sbtk.invert.run(prob), sbtk.invert.homogeneous(prob), 0.040, "Other team");
cmp = sbtk.compare.grids(sbtk.exchange.read_grid(fullfile(model, "density_grid.txt")), ...
                         sbtk.exchange.read_grid(fullfile(solution, "density_grid.txt")));
sbtk.compare.grid_summary(cmp);

Many fits against one true model#

sbtk.compare.reference samples the true model once; sbtk.compare.evaluate then compares each fit in milliseconds. sbtk.invert.replace_data reuses the setup for each noise realization.

MATLAB fragment. Requires the variables defined in Body, interior and measurements used by the examples on this page.
prob = sbtk.invert.setup(body, components, obs, sbtk.invert.options());
ref = sbtk.compare.reference(body, truth, components, prob.geo.origin_km);
R2 = zeros(1, 20);
for k = 1:20
    fit = sbtk.invert.run(sbtk.invert.replace_data(prob, sbtk.data.add_noise(exact, 10 + k)));
    R2(k) = sbtk.compare.evaluate(ref, fit).R2;
end
fprintf("R2 over 20 noise realizations: %.2f +- %.2f\n", mean(R2), std(R2))

Examples

Tutorial scripts#

The repository folder examples/ contains nine tutorial scripts with sections. Each adds toolbox/ to the path itself and can be run whole or section by section. All nine run in the test suite (tests/integration/test_examples.m, also section by section for ex01). The code below is included from the repository files.

Script Topic Run time
ex01_quick_start.m Body, interior, simulation, inversion, comparison on the 1.165 m Didymos model about 90 s
ex02_shapes_and_bodies.m Shape models from files, arrays and ellipsoids; checks; bodies about 5 s
ex03_forward_model.m Every component type, a random field, the simulated measurements, plots about 20 s
ex04_inversion.m Homogeneous test, inertia data, sphere positions, regularization, calibration about 30 s
ex05_import_data.m Measurements from matrices, kg m², a full covariance, the text format about 5 s
ex06_results_folders.m Run folders, reports, logs, settings about 30 s
ex07_exchange_packages.m Measurement, interior-model and solution packages about 40 s
ex08_moments_of_inertia.m What inertia data and the libration ratio add to the gravity field about 20 s
ex09_moved_and_rotated_package.m A package with its shape model moved to the center of mass and rotated into the spin axes about 40 s
ex10_reading_coefficients.m Reading the coefficients of a hidden interior, placing the core along the center-of-mass offset, testing on coefficients not fitted about 30 s
ex11_geometry_search.m Searching the geometry of a model: a grid over sizes, axis and core position, Gauss–Newton from each valley, compact masses about 10 min

The same folder has the maker models of the Hera blind test, make_didymos_1.m to make_dimorphos_3.m, and the homogeneous reference make_didymos_homogeneous.m (Maker models).

ex01: quick start#

The sequence of the first script on the full-resolution Didymos model (3,145,728 facets), which is not in the repository (Installation). With "didymos" instead of "didymos_highres" it runs in about 15 s.

MATLAB script: examples/ex01_quick_start.m
%% EX01_QUICK_START  Simulate measurements of an interior, invert them, compare with the true model. (~90 s with the 1.165 m shape model)
%
% The SBTK workflow on the Didymos shape model:
%   1. a body: shape model, bulk density, reference radius
%   2. forward model: components -> gravity coefficients and moments of inertia
%   3. inversion: measurements + component geometry -> densities with 1-sigma uncertainties
%   4. comparison with the true model

addpath(fullfile(fileparts(fileparts(which('ex01_quick_start'))), 'toolbox'));

%% 1. Body
body = sbtk.body.from_mass("Didymos", sbtk.shape.bundled("didymos_highres"), 5.273e11, 0.43);   % mass [kg], R_ref [km] (Hera end-to-end test)
sbtk.body.summary(body)

%% 2. Forward model: a dense core and a low-density surface layer
components = [sbtk.interior.sphere("core", body.centroid_km, 0.170, +450), ...  % center [km] (the center of figure), radius [km], relative density [kg/m^3]
              sbtk.interior.layer("regolith", 0, 0.012, -900)];           % from 0 to 12 m below the surface
[exact, truth] = sbtk.data.simulate(body, sbtk.interior.create(components), 4, "quick_start");   % exact values

% measurements: 1-sigma uncertainties, then one noise realization
unc = sbtk.data.uncertainties([sbtk.units.offset_to_degree1(0.002, 0.43), ...  % degree 1: 2 m center of mass
                               1e-4, 2e-4, 4e-4], ...                          % degrees 2, 3, 4
                              2e-3, ...                                        % each MOI / (M R_ref^2)
                              0.02);                                           % libration ratio
obs = sbtk.data.add_noise(sbtk.data.set_uncertainties(exact, unc), 1);
sbtk.data.summary(obs)

%% 3. Inversion: the same components, relative densities unknown
% (the relative densities given with the components are not used: they are estimated)
fit = sbtk.invert.solve(body, components, obs);
sbtk.invert.summary(fit)

%% 4. Comparison with the true model
cmp = sbtk.compare.with_truth(body, truth, fit);
sbtk.compare.summary(cmp)
sbtk.plot.densities(fit);
sbtk.plot.truth_vs_estimate(body, truth, fit);

ex02: shapes and bodies#

Shape models from an OBJ file with a stated unit, from arrays (a tetrahedron in meters) and as an ellipsoid; the checks of sbtk.shape.properties; writing OBJ; a body; the unit table.

MATLAB script: examples/ex02_shapes_and_bodies.m
%% EX02_SHAPES_AND_BODIES  Shape models from files or arrays, units, checks. (~5 s)
%
% Any closed polyhedral shape works if it is star-shaped about its center of
% mass (every facet visible from it). Lengths are converted to km on input:
% the unit of the file must be given.

addpath(fullfile(fileparts(fileparts(which('ex02_shapes_and_bodies'))), 'toolbox'));

%% From an OBJ file (unit stated explicitly)
didymos = sbtk.shape.load(fullfile(sbtk.root, "data", "shapes", "didymos_g_9309mm_spc_obj_0000n00000_v003.obj"), "km");
% the shape models that ship with SBTK also load by name:
%   sbtk.shape.bundled("didymos"), ("bennu"), ("dimorphos_placeholder"), ("example_asteroid")
props = sbtk.shape.properties(didymos);
fprintf('%s: %d facets, volume %.5f km^3, centroid [%.1f %.1f %.1f] m, star-shaped: %d\n', didymos.name, ...
        props.n_facets, props.volume_km3, 1e3*props.centroid_km, props.star_shaped_about_centroid);

%% From arrays (here a tetrahedron given in meters)
V = [0 0 0; 100 0 0; 0 100 0; 0 0 100] - 25;          % vertices [m]
F = [1 3 2; 1 2 4; 1 4 3; 2 3 4];                      % facets, outward
tetra = sbtk.shape.from_arrays("tetra", F, V, "m");
disp(sbtk.shape.properties(tetra))

%% A triaxial ellipsoid (exact test shape), saved to OBJ
ell = sbtk.shape.ellipsoid("test_ellipsoid", [0.40 0.35 0.30], 4);     % 5,120 facets
file = fullfile(tempdir, 'test_ellipsoid.obj');
sbtk.shape.write_obj(ell, file);
ell2 = sbtk.shape.load(file, "km");

%% Bodies: shape + bulk density + reference radius of the gravity field
body = sbtk.body.create("Ellipsoid", ell2, 2200, 0.40);
sbtk.body.summary(body)
sbtk.plot.shape(body);
sbtk.units.table()

ex03: forward model#

Every component type and a random field, the simulated measurements as a table, the density at given points, and the three-dimensional, slice and measurement figures.

MATLAB script: examples/ex03_forward_model.m
%% EX03_FORWARD_MODEL  Every component type, a random density field, and the simulated measurements. (~20 s)
%
% Components are regions of uniform relative density (density minus the
% background density). Overlapping relative densities add and components are
% clipped to the body. The background density follows from the total mass.

addpath(fullfile(fileparts(fileparts(which('ex03_forward_model'))), 'toolbox'));
body = sbtk.body.from_mass("Didymos", sbtk.shape.bundled("didymos"), 5.273e11, 0.43);

%% Components
% Spheres, ellipsoids and tori are placed in shape-model coordinates, here from the center of
% figure (the origin of this shape-model file is 57 m from it); layers and sectors are
% measured from the center of mass.
cof = body.centroid_km;
components = [ ...
  sbtk.interior.sphere("core", cof, 0.170, +250), ...                                         % center, radius
  sbtk.interior.ellipsoid("lens", cof + [0.05 0.10 0.12], [0.20 0.08 0.05], [40 -30 15], +300), ... % center, semi-axes, yaw/pitch/roll
  sbtk.interior.torus("torus", 0.370, 0.055, 0.000, -500), ...                                % ring radius, tube radius, height
  sbtk.interior.layer("regolith", 0.000, 0.012, -900), ...                                    % top, bottom depth
  sbtk.interior.sector("block", [0.3 0.9], [40 90], [150 240], +200), ...                     % radial fraction, lat, lon
  sbtk.interior.sphere("boulder", cof + sbtk.interior.latlon(25, 60, 0.250), 0.040, +900)];   % position from lat/lon/distance
components(3).center_km = cof;                                                                % the torus about the z-axis through cof
sbtk.interior.summary(components)

%% Gaussian random density field (standard deviation 40 kg/m^3, correlation length 60 m, seed 7)
interior = sbtk.interior.create(components, sbtk.interior.random_field(40, 0.06, 7));

%% Forward model: the true model and its exact gravity coefficients and moments of inertia
[exact, truth, geo] = sbtk.data.simulate(body, interior, 4, "example_interior");

%% Measurements of it: uncertainties, then noise drawn from them
unc = sbtk.data.uncertainties([sbtk.units.offset_to_degree1(0.002, 0.43), 1e-4, 2e-4, 4e-4], 2e-3, 0.02);
obs = sbtk.data.add_noise(sbtk.data.set_uncertainties(exact, unc), 1);
fprintf('background density %.0f kg/m^3, center of mass %.1f m from the center of figure\n', ...
        truth.rho_bg_kgm3, 1e3*norm(obs.com_minus_cof_km));

% What the measurements look like
disp(table(obs.coef_labels(1:8), obs.coef(1:8), sqrt(diag(obs.coef_cov(1:8, 1:8))), ...
           'VariableNames', {'label', 'value', 'sigma'}))
disp(struct2table(obs.moi))

%% Density anywhere inside (truth frame = center of mass)
rho = sbtk.interior.density_at(truth, [0 0 0; 0.3 0 0] + truth.origin_km, geo);
fprintf('density at the center %.0f, 300 m out along x %.0f kg/m^3\n', rho);

%% Plots
sbtk.plot.interior3d(body, truth, "example interior");
sbtk.plot.slices(body, {truth}, {'truth'});
sbtk.plot.measurements(obs);

ex04: inversion options#

The homogeneous test; fits with and without inertia data; estimation of a sphere center; a 36-sector grid with Tikhonov regularization chosen by the discrepancy principle; and the standard deviation of (estimate − truth)/σ over 50 noise realizations using sbtk.invert.replace_data.

MATLAB script: examples/ex04_inversion.m
%% EX04_INVERSION  Inversion options: homogeneous model, MOI, sphere positions, regularization. (~30 s)
%
% setup does the slow part once (geometry and each component's effect on every
% measurement); run solves in milliseconds, so trying options is cheap.

addpath(fullfile(fileparts(fileparts(which('ex04_inversion'))), 'toolbox'));
body  = sbtk.body.from_mass("Didymos", sbtk.shape.bundled("didymos"), 5.273e11, 0.43);
unc   = sbtk.data.uncertainties([sbtk.units.offset_to_degree1(0.002, 0.43), 1e-4, 2e-4, 4e-4], 2e-3, 0.02);
cof   = body.centroid_km;                  % components are placed from the center of figure
truth_components = [sbtk.interior.sphere("core", cof + [0.03 -0.02 0.01], 0.17, +500), ...
               sbtk.interior.torus("torus", 0.37, 0.055, 0, -500), sbtk.interior.layer("regolith", 0, 0.012, -900)];
truth_components(2).center_km = cof;       % the torus about the z-axis through the center of figure
[exact, truth] = sbtk.data.simulate(body, sbtk.interior.create(truth_components), 4, "ex04");
exact = sbtk.data.set_uncertainties(exact, unc);
obs = sbtk.data.add_noise(exact, 1);

%% Set up once
% Component geometry is fixed (the core is placed at the center of figure, 37 m from the true
% center); relative densities are estimated, so their values here are not used.
components = [sbtk.interior.sphere("core", cof, 0.17, 0), sbtk.interior.torus("torus", 0.37, 0.055, 0, 0), ...
              sbtk.interior.layer("regolith", 0, 0.012, 0)];
components(2).center_km = cof;
opts = sbtk.invert.options();             % every setting and its standard value
disp(opts)
prob = sbtk.invert.setup(body, components, obs, opts);

%% Is a homogeneous body consistent with the measurements?
u = sbtk.invert.homogeneous(prob);
fprintf('homogeneous body: reduced chi2 %.2f, p = %.2g\n', u.chi2_reduced, u.p_value);

%% Fit, and the same with gravity only (no MOI): MOI shrink the uncertainties
fit = sbtk.invert.run(prob);
sbtk.invert.summary(fit)
fit_g = sbtk.invert.solve(body, components, obs, sbtk.invert.options(moi_labels={}));
fprintf('core 1-sigma: %.0f kg/m^3 with MOI, %.0f without\n', fit.rho_sigma_kgm3(1), fit_g.rho_sigma_kgm3(1));

%% Estimate the core position as well
moving = components;  moving(1).estimate_position = true;
fit_p = sbtk.invert.solve(body, moving, obs);
fprintf('core center [%.0f %.0f %.0f] m +- [%.0f %.0f %.0f] m (truth [30 -20 10] m from the shape origin)\n', ...
        1e3*fit_p.components(1).center_km, 1e3*fit_p.center_sigma_km(1, :));

%% Tikhonov regularization for many components (36-sector grid), parameter by the discrepancy principle
% The sectors fill the body, so the background is held at the bulk density.
sectors = sbtk.interior.sector_grid([0 0.5 0.85 1], [-90 -30 30 90], [-180 -90 0 90 180]);
probc = sbtk.invert.setup(body, sectors, obs, sbtk.invert.options(background="bulk"));
probc.opts.regularization = sbtk.invert.choose_regularization(probc);
fitc = sbtk.invert.run(probc);
fprintf('sector grid: lambda %.3g, reduced chi2 %.2f (dof %.1f)\n', fitc.regularization, fitc.chi2_reduced, fitc.dof);

%% Calibration of the uncertainties: 50 noise realizations
z = zeros(50, 4);
for k = 1:50
    f = sbtk.invert.run(sbtk.invert.replace_data(prob, sbtk.data.add_noise(exact, 100 + k)));
    z(k, :) = ([f.rho_bg_kgm3, [f.components.drho_kgm3]] - [truth.rho_bg_kgm3, [truth_components.drho_kgm3]]) ...
              ./[f.rho_bg_sigma_kgm3, f.drho_sigma_kgm3];
end
fprintf('standard deviation of (estimate - truth)/sigma: %.2f (1 for calibrated uncertainties)\n', std(z(:)));
sbtk.plot.residuals(fit);

ex05: importing data#

A measurement set from coefficient matrices; inertia given in kg m²; a libration ratio; a full covariance; the text format written and read back; selection of degrees.

MATLAB script: examples/ex05_import_data.m
%% EX05_IMPORT_DATA  Measurements from arrays, kg m^2, a full covariance, and text files. (~5 s)
%
% Real data arrive as coefficient matrices with uncertainties (and maybe a full
% covariance) and as moments of inertia. This builds an SBTK measurement set
% from them, in the units SBTK uses.

addpath(fullfile(fileparts(fileparts(which('ex05_import_data'))), 'toolbox'));
body = sbtk.body.from_mass("Dimorphos", sbtk.shape.bundled("dimorphos"), 2.700e9, 0.10);

%% Coefficient matrices: C(l+1, m+1) = C_lm, fully normalized about origin_km
L = 2;
C = zeros(L + 1);  S = zeros(L + 1);
C(1,1) = 1;  C(3,1) = -0.08;  C(3,3) = 0.03;  S(3,3) = 0.002;     % C00, C20, C22, S22
Cs = 1e-3*ones(L + 1);  Ss = 1e-3*ones(L + 1);                     % 1-sigma of each
obs = sbtk.data.from_coefficients(body, "example_import", [0 0 0], C, S, Cs, Ss);

%% Moments of inertia, given in kg m^2 -> I/(M R_ref^2)
Izz_kgm2 = 1.6e14;
Izz = sbtk.units.moi_to_norm(Izz_kgm2, body.mass_kg, body.R_ref_km);
obs = sbtk.data.add_moi(obs, "Izz", Izz, 0.01*Izz);
obs = sbtk.data.add_libration(obs, 0.20, 0.03, Izz);                % (B-A)/C and its 1-sigma

%% A full covariance (here: 30% correlation between all coefficients)
sig = sqrt(diag(obs.coef_cov));
corr = 0.3*ones(numel(sig)) + 0.7*eye(numel(sig));
obs = sbtk.data.set_covariance(obs, corr.*(sig*sig'));
sbtk.data.summary(obs)

%% The SBTK text format: write it, read it back
% (for data to send to other teams see ex07_exchange_packages.m)
file = fullfile(tempdir, 'example_measurements.txt');
sbtk.io.write_measurements(obs, file);
type(file)
back = sbtk.io.load_measurements(file);     % (the text keeps only the diagonal of the covariance)

%% Use fewer degrees
obs1 = sbtk.data.select_degree(obs, 1);
fprintf('%d coefficients up to degree 1\n', numel(obs1.coef));

ex06: results folders#

A simulation, an inversion of the newest simulation found with sbtk.io.latest_run, and a comparison, each in its own run folder with log, settings and figures (Results folders).

MATLAB script: examples/ex06_results_folders.m
%% EX06_RESULTS_FOLDERS  Standard outputs: run folders, reports, logs, settings. (~30 s)
%
% Every run gets results/<project>/<date_time>_<name>/ with standard file names,
% settings.json (every number used) and log.txt (everything printed). The
% report_* functions save, print and plot the standard set in one call.

addpath(fullfile(fileparts(fileparts(which('ex06_results_folders'))), 'toolbox'));
shape = sbtk.shape.ellipsoid("ellipsoid", [0.40 0.35 0.30], 4);
body  = sbtk.body.create("Ellipsoid", shape, 2200, 0.40);
unc   = sbtk.data.uncertainties([sbtk.units.offset_to_degree1(0.002, 0.40), 1e-4, 2e-4], 2e-3, 0.02);

%% Simulation
components = [sbtk.interior.sphere("core", [0.03 0 0], 0.15, +600), sbtk.interior.layer("regolith", 0, 0.02, -700)];
out = sbtk.io.new_run("examples", "ellipsoid_T1");
[exact, truth] = sbtk.data.simulate(body, sbtk.interior.create(components), 3, "ellipsoid_T1");
obs = sbtk.data.add_noise(sbtk.data.set_uncertainties(exact, unc), 1);
sbtk.io.report_simulation(out, body, obs, truth);
sbtk.io.finish_run(out);

%% Inversion of the newest simulation
obs = sbtk.io.load_measurements(sbtk.io.latest_run("examples", "ellipsoid_T1"));
out = sbtk.io.new_run("examples", "ellipsoid_T1_inversion");
prob = sbtk.invert.setup(body, components, obs, sbtk.invert.options());
fit = sbtk.invert.run(prob);
sbtk.io.report_inversion(out, body, fit, sbtk.invert.homogeneous(prob));
sbtk.io.finish_run(out);

%% Comparison with the true model
truth = sbtk.io.load_truth(sbtk.io.latest_run("examples", "ellipsoid_T1"));
out = sbtk.io.new_run("examples", "ellipsoid_T1_comparison");
sbtk.io.report_comparison(out, body, truth, fit, sbtk.compare.with_truth(body, truth, fit));
sbtk.io.finish_run(out);
dir(out.folder)

ex07: exchange packages#

A blind test in miniature: one team writes a measurement package and an interior-model package; another reads the measurement package, inverts it and writes a solution package; the solution is compared with the hidden model on the density grid (Exchange packages).

MATLAB script: examples/ex07_exchange_packages.m
%% EX07_EXCHANGE_PACKAGES  Data for other teams: measurement, interior-model and solution packages. (~40 s)
%
% A blind test: one team simulates measurements of an interior it keeps hidden and
% sends only the measurement package, of exact values; another team gives them its own
% uncertainties, inverts them and sends a
% solution package; at the end both are compared with the hidden model on a common
% density grid. Every package is plain text with its units, frame and normalization
% written in it (docs/exchange_format.md). projects/hera_hlp6 does the same with
% results folders.

addpath(fullfile(fileparts(fileparts(which('ex07_exchange_packages'))), 'toolbox'));
body = sbtk.body.create("Example asteroid", sbtk.shape.bundled("example_asteroid"), 2000, 0.60);
unc  = sbtk.data.uncertainties([sbtk.units.offset_to_degree1(0.005, 0.60), 1e-4, 2e-4, 4e-4], 2e-3, 0.02);
folder = tempname;                         % where the packages go (normally a results folder)

%% The team that makes the data
hidden = [sbtk.interior.sphere("core", body.centroid_km + [0.03 0 0], 0.25, +500), ...   % 30 m from the center of figure
          sbtk.interior.layer("regolith", 0, 0.02, -800)];
[exact, truth] = sbtk.data.simulate(body, sbtk.interior.create(hidden), 4, "hidden_model");
data = sbtk.exchange.write_data(folder, "TEAM-DATA1-example", body, exact, "Team, contact");       % send now: exact values
model = sbtk.exchange.write_model(folder, "TEAM-MOD1-example", "TEAM-DATA1-example", body, truth, ...
                                  exact, 0.04, "Team, contact");                                     % send at the end
type(fullfile(data, 'README.txt'))

%% The team that inverts it: everything comes from the package
[obs2, body2] = sbtk.exchange.read_data(data);          % shape model, GM and reference radius included
obs2 = sbtk.data.add_noise(sbtk.data.set_uncertainties(obs2, unc), 1);   % its own uncertainties (and noise, optionally)
components = [sbtk.interior.sphere("core", body2.centroid_km, 0.25, 0), sbtk.interior.layer("regolith", 0, 0.02, 0)];
prob = sbtk.invert.setup(body2, components, obs2, sbtk.invert.options());
fit  = sbtk.invert.run(prob);
sbtk.invert.summary(fit)
solution = sbtk.exchange.write_solution(folder, sbtk.exchange.solution_name("OTHER", obs2.name), body2, fit, ...
                                        sbtk.invert.homogeneous(prob), 0.04, "Other team, contact");

%% At the end: the solution against the hidden model, cell by cell
cmp = sbtk.compare.grids(sbtk.exchange.read_grid(fullfile(model, 'density_grid.txt')), ...
                         sbtk.exchange.read_grid(fullfile(solution, 'density_grid.txt')));
sbtk.compare.grid_summary(cmp);

ex08: moments of inertia and the libration ratio#

The same inversion with no inertia data, Izz, the libration ratio at two precisions, and Ixx, Iyy, Izz; the libration ratio from an observed libration amplitude; adding measured inertia values (Moments of inertia).

MATLAB script: examples/ex08_moments_of_inertia.m
%% EX08_MOMENTS_OF_INERTIA  What moments of inertia and the libration ratio add to the gravity field. (~20 s)
%
% The degree-2 gravity coefficients fix five combinations of the inertia tensor
% (C20 ~ (Ixx + Iyy - 2 Izz), C22 ~ (Iyy - Ixx), C21, S21, S22 ~ products of inertia),
% but not its trace. A dense core and a light surface layer can therefore give the
% same gravity field, and the inversion cannot separate them. A moment of inertia
% such as the polar moment Izz (from the spin state) adds the missing combination:
% it measures how concentrated the mass is toward the center.
%
% The libration ratio (B - A)/C (principal moments: A <= B about the axes in the
% xy-plane, C = Izz) comes from the libration amplitude of a synchronously rotating body
% (e.g. Dimorphos). The degree-2 field gives B - A, so the ratio gives C: it carries the
% same information as a polar moment, with a relative precision of sigma/ratio.

addpath(fullfile(fileparts(fileparts(which('ex08_moments_of_inertia'))), 'toolbox'));
body = sbtk.body.from_mass("Didymos", sbtk.shape.bundled("didymos"), 5.273e11, 0.43);

%% Simulated measurements: every inertia quantity is available
truth_components = [sbtk.interior.sphere("core", body.centroid_km, 0.170, +450), ...   % at the center of figure
                    sbtk.interior.layer("regolith", 0, 0.012, -900)];
[exact, truth] = sbtk.data.simulate(body, sbtk.interior.create(truth_components), 4, "ex08");
unc = sbtk.data.uncertainties([sbtk.units.offset_to_degree1(0.002, 0.43), 1e-4, 2e-4, 4e-4], ...
                              2e-3, ...        % 1-sigma of each inertia element, as a fraction of M R_ref^2
                              0.02);           % 1-sigma of the libration ratio
exact = sbtk.data.set_uncertainties(exact, unc);
obs = sbtk.data.add_noise(exact, 1);
disp(struct2table(rmfield(obs.moi, 'weights')))    % Ixx Iyy Izz Ixy Ixz Iyz libration, as I/(M R_ref^2)

%% The same inversion with different inertia measurements
% opts.moi_labels chooses which of the data's inertia rows are fitted. The libration
% ratio of this body is about 0.056, so the simulated 1-sigma of 0.02 (36%) says little;
% a ratio measured to 0.001 (1.8%) is added as a separate data set (sbtk.data.add_libration).
gravity  = sbtk.data.select_moi(obs, {});                                % gravity coefficients only
precise  = sbtk.data.add_libration(gravity, exact.libration_ratio, 0.001, obs.moi(3).value);
cases = {'none (gravity only)',    obs,     {}
         'Izz',                    obs,     {'Izz'}
         'libration +- 0.02',      obs,     {'libration'}
         'libration +- 0.001',     precise, {'libration'}
         'Ixx Iyy Izz',            obs,     {'Ixx', 'Iyy', 'Izz'}};
fprintf('\n%-22s %18s %18s %12s %8s\n', 'inertia used', 'core [kg/m^3]', 'regolith [kg/m^3]', 'correlation', 'chi2/nu');
for k = 1:size(cases, 1)
    fit = sbtk.invert.solve(body, truth_components, cases{k, 2}, sbtk.invert.options(moi_labels=cases{k, 3}));
    fprintf('%-22s %10.0f +- %4.0f %10.0f +- %4.0f %12.2f %8.2f\n', cases{k, 1}, fit.rho_kgm3(1), ...
            fit.rho_sigma_kgm3(1), fit.rho_kgm3(2), fit.rho_sigma_kgm3(2), fit.corr(2, 3), fit.chi2_reduced);
end
fprintf('%-22s %10.0f %20.0f\n', 'true', truth.rho_bg_kgm3 + truth_components(1).drho_kgm3, ...
        truth.rho_bg_kgm3 + truth_components(2).drho_kgm3);
% correlation: between the core and regolith relative densities (near 1 = the data
% cannot tell them apart).
% Izz halves the regolith uncertainty. The libration ratio gives C = (B - A)/ratio, so it
% constrains C as well as the ratio is known relative to its value: +-0.001 is 1.8% of
% C and helps, Izz +-0.002 is 0.5% and helps more.

%% A libration ratio from the observed libration amplitude
% A synchronous satellite in an orbit of eccentricity e librates with amplitude
