% 2e/(3 ratio - 1) (forced libration, first order in e). Near ratio = 1/3 (elongation
% about 1.4 : 1) the amplitude is large and fixes the ratio precisely; a nearly
% axisymmetric body librates little and the ratio stays uncertain.
for amp = [-4 -12]
    [k, sk] = sbtk.data.libration_ratio_from_amplitude(amp, 0.2, 0.027, 0.001);   % deg, deg, e, sigma e
    fprintf('amplitude %5.1f +- 0.2 deg, e = 0.027 +- 0.001: (B - A)/C = %.3f +- %.4f (%.0f%%)\n', ...
            amp, k, sk, 100*sk/k);
end

%% Your own inertia measurements
% Start from the gravity coefficients (a package, a SHADR file, coefficient matrices,
% ...) and add each measured quantity. Values given in kg m^2 convert with
% sbtk.units.moi_to_norm; inertia is about the center of mass, shape-model axes.
Izz_kgm2 = sbtk.units.norm_to_moi(obs.moi(3).value, body.mass_kg, body.R_ref_km);   % e.g. a measured polar moment
mine = sbtk.data.add_moi(gravity, "Izz", sbtk.units.moi_to_norm(Izz_kgm2, body.mass_kg, body.R_ref_km), 2e-3);
mine = sbtk.data.add_libration(mine, exact.libration_ratio, 0.001, mine.moi(1).value);  % (B - A)/C, 1-sigma, Izz
fit = sbtk.invert.solve(body, truth_components, mine, sbtk.invert.options(moi_labels={'Izz', 'libration'}));
sbtk.invert.summary(fit)

ex09: moved and rotated package#

The HLP6 makers send their data in the frame and about the origin of the shape model file as distributed. This tutorial keeps the other way: the shape model, the true model and the exact values are moved to the center of mass of the true model and rotated into its spin axes (or principal axes), so degree 1 and C¯21, S¯21 are zero. The package contains the moved and rotated shape model, named after the package, and conventions.txt gives the change of frame from the original file; the original coordinates are recovered from it (Frames of a gravity field, The shape model of a package).

MATLAB script: examples/ex09_moved_and_rotated_package.m
%% EX09_MOVED_AND_ROTATED_PACKAGE  A package with the shape model moved to the center of mass and rotated. (~40 s)
%
% The HLP6 makers agreed to send their data in the frame and about the origin of the shape
% model file as distributed (examples/make_didymos_1.m): degree 1 and C21, S21 are then not
% zero. This tutorial keeps the alternative. The shape model, the true model and the exact
% values are moved to the center of mass of the true model and rotated into its spin axes
% (z the axis of the largest moment, x the shape-model x-axis projected onto the plane
% normal to z) or its principal axes, so degree 1 and C21, S21 (and S22) are zero. The
% package then contains the moved and rotated shape model, named after the package, and
% conventions.txt gives the change of frame from the original file
% (website: Frames of a gravity field; Exchange packages, "The shape model of a package").

addpath(fullfile(fileparts(fileparts(which('ex09_moved_and_rotated_package'))), 'toolbox'));
body = sbtk.body.from_mass("Didymos", sbtk.shape.bundled("didymos"), 5.273e11, 0.43);
cof  = body.centroid_km;                                   % the origin of the file is 57 m from it
folder = tempname;                                         % where the packages go (normally a results folder)

%% A true model, made in the frame of the shape model file
torus = sbtk.interior.torus("torus", 0.370, 0.055, 0, -500);
torus.center_km = cof;
interior = sbtk.interior.create([sbtk.interior.sphere("core", cof + [0.02 -0.01 0], 0.150, 400), torus]);
interior = sbtk.interior.align_with_spin_axis(body, interior, "torus", 0.01, 20);   % torus about the spin axis
[exact, truth] = sbtk.data.simulate(body, interior, 4, "moved_and_rotated");

%% Move and rotate: origin at the center of mass, spin axes ("principal" for the principal axes)
spin  = sbtk.gravity.center_of_mass_frame(truth, body, "spin");
body  = sbtk.body.to_frame(body, spin.com_km, spin.axes, "didymos_v003_com_spin_axes");
truth = sbtk.interior.to_frame(truth, spin.com_km, spin.axes);
exact = sbtk.data.to_frame(exact, spin.com_km, spin.axes);    % before select_moi: needs the full tensor
exact = sbtk.data.select_moi(exact, ["Ixx" "Iyy" "Izz"]);
fprintf('largest-moment axis %.2f deg from the DART z-axis; center of mass %.1f m from the file origin\n', ...
        acosd(spin.principal(3, 3)), 1e3*norm(spin.com_km));

%% The packages
data  = sbtk.exchange.write_data(folder, "TEAM-DATA1-Didymos", body, exact, "Team, contact");
model = sbtk.exchange.write_model(folder, "TEAM-MOD1-Didymos", "TEAM-DATA1-Didymos", body, truth, exact, ...
                                  0.040, "Team, contact");
disp(string({dir(data).name})')                           % ... TEAM-DATA1-Didymos_didymos_v003_com_spin_axes.obj
type(fullfile(data, 'conventions.txt'))

%% What a receiving team reads
[obs, rbody] = sbtk.exchange.read_data(data);
[~, i] = ismember(["C21" "S21"], string(obs.coef_labels));
fprintf('center of mass %s km; C21 %.1e, S21 %.1e\n', mat2str(obs.origin_km, 3), obs.coef(i));
% the original coordinates: x = x' A' + o
original = rbody.shape.vertices_km*body.shape.frame_axes' + body.shape.frame_origin_km;
fprintf('max difference from the DART vertices: %.1e km\n', ...
        max(abs(original - sbtk.shape.bundled("didymos").vertices_km), [], 'all'));

ex10: reading the coefficients#

The procedure of Reading the gravity coefficients on a hidden Didymos interior (a dense core 30 m from the center of figure, a light torus raised 12 m and a light surface layer): the anomaly and which coefficients differ from constant density; each degree's scaling and the rest; one compact mass from degrees 1 and 2; the core's χ2 profile along the center-of-mass offset; Gauss–Newton with the torus height free; and the model fitted to degrees 1–3 predicting degrees 4–5.

MATLAB script: examples/ex10_reading_coefficients.m
%% EX10_READING_COEFFICIENTS  Read the gravity coefficients of an unknown interior, then fit the components they point to.
%
% A worked example of the procedure in the documentation (Reading the gravity
% coefficients). The interior is hidden in the first section, as in a blind test; the
% rest uses only the measurements:
%   1. the anomaly: measured minus homogeneous coefficients, about the center of figure,
%      and which of them differ from constant density (sbtk.interpret.anomaly,
%      sbtk.interpret.summary, sbtk.plot.significance);
%   2. each degree as a scaled homogeneous field plus the rest (sbtk.plot.degree_ratio):
%      the scaling says how much mass is concentrated toward the center, the rest which
%      coefficients carry structure that is not centrally symmetric;
%   3. one compact mass from degrees 1 and 2 (sbtk.interpret.central_mass);
%   4. a model with the components the reading suggests; chi-square along the measured
%      center-of-mass offset for the core position (sbtk.invert.scan_position);
%   5. Gauss-Newton from the lowest point, with the torus height free;
%   6. the same model fitted to degrees 1-3 only predicts degrees 4-5
%      (sbtk.invert.predict): a test on coefficients it was not fitted to.
% Figures go to results/examples/<date_time>_ex10_reading_coefficients/figures/. About 30 s.

clear; close all;
root = fileparts(fileparts(mfilename('fullpath')));
addpath(fullfile(root, 'toolbox'));
out = sbtk.io.new_run("examples", "ex10_reading_coefficients");

%% The hidden interior and its measurements
body = sbtk.body.create("Didymos", sbtk.shape.bundled("didymos"), 2600, 0.41);
cof  = body.centroid_km;                                   % center of figure
torus = sbtk.interior.torus("torus", 0.36, 0.05, 0, -400);
torus.center_km = cof + [0 0 0.012];
hidden = [sbtk.interior.sphere("core", cof + [0.025 -0.015 0.008], 0.14, +500), torus, ...
          sbtk.interior.layer("regolith", 0, 0.015, -600)];
[exact, truth] = sbtk.data.simulate(body, sbtk.interior.create(hidden), 5, "reading example");
exact = sbtk.data.expand_about(sbtk.data.select_moi(exact, {}), [0 0 0]);   % about the origin of the shape model file
unc = sbtk.data.uncertainties([1.3e-5 2e-5 3e-5 3e-5 3e-5], 1, 0.02);       % 1-sigma by degree, close to the Hera RSE values
obs = sbtk.data.set_uncertainties(exact, unc);

%% 1. The anomaly
an = sbtk.interpret.anomaly(obs, body, 5);
lines = sbtk.interpret.summary(an);
sbtk.io.save_figure(out, sbtk.plot.significance(an), "significance");

%% 2. Scaling and the rest, degree by degree
sbtk.io.save_figure(out, sbtk.plot.degree_ratio(an, {}, strings(1, 0)), "degree_ratio");

%% 3. One compact mass from degrees 1 and 2
cm = sbtk.interpret.central_mass(an);

%% 4. A model and the core position along the center-of-mass offset
model = [sbtk.interior.sphere("core", cof, 0.15, 0), sbtk.interior.torus("torus", 0.37, 0.055, 0, 0), ...
         sbtk.interior.layer("regolith", 0, 0.012, 0)];
model(2).center_km = cof;
opts = sbtk.invert.options(moi_labels={});
prob = sbtk.invert.setup(body, model, obs, opts);
u  = an.com_offset_km/norm(an.com_offset_km);
t  = (-0.10:0.005:0.10)';
sc = sbtk.invert.scan_position(prob, "core", cof + t*u);
fig = figure('Color', 'w', 'Position', [100 100 700 360]);
semilogy(1e3*t, sc.chi2, 'o-');
xline(1e3*(hidden(1).center_km - cof)*u', ':', 'hidden core', 'LabelVerticalAlignment', 'middle');
xlabel('core position along the center-of-mass offset [m]');  ylabel('\chi^2');
sbtk.io.save_figure(out, fig, "scan");

%% 5. Gauss-Newton from the lowest point, the torus height free
model(1).center_km = sc.centers_km(sc.best, :);
model(1).estimate_position = true;
model(2).estimate_position = [false false true];
fit = sbtk.invert.solve(body, model, obs, opts);
sbtk.invert.summary(fit)

%% 6. Fitted to degrees 1-3, tested on degrees 4-5
fit3 = sbtk.invert.solve(body, model, sbtk.data.select_degree(obs, 3), opts);
preds = {sbtk.invert.predict(fit3, body, obs), sbtk.invert.predict(fit, body, obs)};
sbtk.io.save_figure(out, sbtk.plot.coefficient_residuals(preds, ["degrees 1-3", "degrees 1-5"]), "coefficient_residuals");
sbtk.io.save_figure(out, sbtk.plot.anomaly(an, {sbtk.interpret.anomaly(fit3, body, 5), sbtk.interpret.anomaly(fit, body, 5)}, ...
                                           ["fitted to degrees 1-3", "fitted to degrees 1-5"]), "anomaly");
fprintf('fitted to degrees 1-3: chi2 per coefficient %.2f (fitted), %.2f (degrees 4-5)\n', ...
        preds{1}.chi2_fitted/preds{1}.n_fitted, preds{1}.chi2_other/preds{1}.n_other);
sbtk.io.save_figure(out, sbtk.plot.truth_vs_estimate(body, truth, fit), "truth_vs_estimate");
sbtk.io.finish_run(out);

ex11: searching the geometry#

The search of Searching the geometry on a hidden Didymos interior (a dense core, a torus of other radii than the model's and tilted 3°, a light layer, a dense boulder and a light one): the model with guessed sizes; a grid over the core position along the center-of-mass offset, the torus radii and axis and the layer thickness, with the χ2 profile of each; Gauss–Newton from the lowest point of each valley; compact masses added while each passes the likelihood-ratio test; and the result against the hidden interior.

MATLAB script: examples/ex11_geometry_search.m
%% EX11_GEOMETRY_SEARCH  Search the geometry of a model systematically: sizes, axis, core position and compact masses.
%
% A worked example of the documentation page Searching the geometry. The interior is
% hidden in the first section, as in a blind test: a dense core, a torus of other radii
% than the model's and tilted 3 deg, a light layer, a dense boulder and a light one. The
% rest uses only the measurements (coefficients to degree 5 with 1-sigma close to the Hera
% radio-science values) and a model of a core, a torus and a layer:
%   1. the model with guessed sizes, the core placed by Gauss-Newton: the starting point;
%   2. a grid over the core position along the center-of-mass offset, the ring and tube
%      radii and the axis of the torus, and the layer thickness (sbtk.search.grid), and
%      the chi-square profile of each (sbtk.plot.search_profiles);
%   3. Gauss-Newton on the core position and the torus height and axis from the lowest
%      point of each valley of the profiles (sbtk.search.refine);
%   4. compact masses added where the residuals ask for them, each kept only if it passes
%      the likelihood-ratio test (sbtk.search.add_masses, sbtk.plot.search_masses);
%   5. the result against the hidden interior.
% sbtk.search.run does steps 2-4 in one call. The 49,152-facet Didymos model keeps the
% torus integrals at about 1 s each. Figures go to
% results/examples/<date_time>_ex11_geometry_search/figures/. About 10 minutes.

clear; close all;
root = fileparts(fileparts(mfilename('fullpath')));
addpath(fullfile(root, 'toolbox'));
out = sbtk.io.new_run("examples", "ex11_geometry_search");

%% The hidden interior and its measurements
body = sbtk.body.create("Didymos", sbtk.shape.bundled("didymos_every8"), 2600, 0.41);
cof  = body.centroid_km;                                   % center of figure
torus = sbtk.interior.torus("torus", 0.330, 0.045, 0, -450);
torus.center_km = cof + [0 0 0.010];
torus = sbtk.interior.set_axis(torus, [sind(3)*cosd(40), sind(3)*sind(40), cosd(3)]);
hidden = [sbtk.interior.sphere("core", cof + [0.035 -0.020 0.010], 0.140, +600), torus, ...
          sbtk.interior.layer("regolith", 0, 0.018, -700), ...
          sbtk.interior.sphere("boulder1", cof + sbtk.interior.latlon(20, 60, 0.200), 0.045, +1500), ...
          sbtk.interior.sphere("boulder2", cof + sbtk.interior.latlon(-30, -120, 0.180), 0.045, -1200)];
[exact, truth] = sbtk.data.simulate(body, sbtk.interior.create(hidden), 5, "search example");
exact = sbtk.data.expand_about(sbtk.data.select_moi(exact, {}), [0 0 0]);   % about the origin of the shape model file
unc = sbtk.data.uncertainties([1.3e-5 2e-5 3e-5 3e-5 3e-5], 1, 0.02);       % 1-sigma by degree, close to the Hera RSE values
obs = sbtk.data.set_uncertainties(exact, unc);

%% 1. The model with guessed sizes
an = sbtk.interpret.anomaly(obs, body, 5);
u  = an.com_offset_km/norm(an.com_offset_km);              % direction of the center-of-mass offset
core = sbtk.interior.sphere("core", cof, 0.150, 0);
core.estimate_position = true;
ring = sbtk.interior.torus("torus", 0.370, 0.055, 0, 0);
ring.center_km = cof;
ring.estimate_position = [false false true];               % its height
ring.estimate_axis = true;
model = [core, ring, sbtk.interior.layer("regolith", 0, 0.012, 0)];
opts = sbtk.invert.options(moi_labels={});
opts.max_iter = 30;
prob = sbtk.invert.setup(body, model, obs, opts);
guessed = sbtk.invert.run(prob);
fprintf('guessed sizes: chi2 %.1f for %d coefficients, p = %.2g\n', guessed.chi2, guessed.n_obs, guessed.p_value);

%% 2. Grid
t  = (-0.080:0.010:0.080)';
R  = (0.300:0.025:0.400)';
a  = (0.035:0.010:0.065)';
[d, tilt] = sbtk.search.directions([0 0 1], 4, 4);         % the z-axis and 6 directions 4 deg from it
th = [0.008; 0.015; 0.022; 0.030];
P = [sbtk.search.parameter("core", "center_km", cof + t*u, 1e3*t, "core along the offset (m)"), ...
     sbtk.search.parameter("torus", "ring_radius_km", R, R, "ring radius (km)"), ...
     sbtk.search.parameter("torus", "tube_radius_km", a, a, "tube radius (km)"), ...
     sbtk.search.parameter("torus", "axis", d, tilt, "tilt of the axis (deg)"), ...
     sbtk.search.parameter("regolith", "depth_km", [zeros(4, 1), th], 1e3*th, "thickness (m)")];
gr = sbtk.search.grid(prob, P, 3);
fprintf('grid: %d combinations from %d integrals in %.0f s; best chi2 %.1f\n', gr.n_combinations, ...
        gr.n_integrals, gr.time_s, gr.best_fit.chi2);
sbtk.io.save_figure(out, sbtk.plot.search_profiles(gr), "profiles");

%% 3. Gauss-Newton from the lowest point of each valley
rf = sbtk.search.refine(prob, gr.components);
fprintf('refined: chi2 %s\n', mat2str(rf.chi2, 4));

%% 4. Compact masses
cand = sbtk.interior.sphere_grid(body, 0.040, 0.045);     % candidate positions every 40 m
ms = sbtk.search.add_masses(prob, rf.best_fit, cand, 4, 0.05, 3);
fprintf('masses: %d kept (%s); chi2 %s\n', ms.n_masses, ms.stop_reason, mat2str(ms.chi2, 4));
sbtk.io.save_figure(out, sbtk.plot.search_masses(ms, body), "masses");

%% 5. The result against the hidden interior
fit = ms.best_fit;
sbtk.invert.summary(fit)
for c = fit.components
    fprintf('%-9s %+6.0f kg/m^3, center - cof [%5.1f %5.1f %5.1f] m\n', c.name, c.drho_kgm3, 1e3*(c.center_km - cof));
end
fprintf('torus: ring %.0f m, tube %.0f m, axis %.1f deg from z; layer %.0f m\n', 1e3*fit.components(2).ring_radius_km, ...
        1e3*fit.components(2).tube_radius_km, acosd(fit.components(2).axes(3, 3)), 1e3*fit.components(3).depth_km(2));
cmp = sbtk.compare.with_truth(body, truth, fit);
cmp0 = sbtk.compare.with_truth(body, truth, guessed);
fprintf('density R2: guessed sizes %.2f, after the search %.2f\n', cmp0.R2, cmp.R2);
sbtk.io.save_figure(out, sbtk.plot.truth_vs_estimate(body, truth, fit), "truth_vs_estimate");
sbtk.io.finish_run(out);

Projects

Project template#

A project is a folder of runner scripts for one body that write to results/<project>/. The folder projects/template/ is the starting point for a new body. Body-specific numbers are kept in one settings function, my_body.m; nothing body-specific is in the toolbox.

Files#

File Purpose
my_body.m Returns the body (shape model and its length unit, bulk density, reference radius), the gravity degree and the density-grid spacing.
simulate_measurements.m Simulates exact measurements of a prescribed interior and writes a measurement package and an interior-model package.
invert_measurements.m Gives the measurements of a package uncertainties, estimates component densities and writes a solution package.
compare_with_truth.m Compares an inversion with the true model of a simulation, by component and on the density grid.

As delivered, the template runs on data/shapes/example_asteroid.obj, a synthetic body of about 1.2 km. tests/integration/test_template_project.m runs the three scripts.

Use#

  1. Copy projects/template/ to projects/<body>/.
  2. In my_body.m, replace the shape file, its length unit, the bulk density (or use sbtk.body.from_mass), the reference radius, the degree and the grid spacing. The shape must be closed and star-shaped about its center of mass (Shape models).
  3. Set project at the top of each script.
  4. In simulate_measurements.m, edit the sections PROJECT, NAME AND DELIVERY and INTERIOR. The simulation writes exact values, without uncertainties or noise.
  5. In invert_measurements.m, edit UNCERTAINTIES (the 1σ the receiving team gives the exact values), MODEL and OPTIONS.
  6. Run the scripts in order. Each run writes its own folder (Results folders); the inversion finds the newest simulation of the given name with sbtk.io.latest_run.

A simulation run writes

Simulation run folder
results/<project>/<date_time>_<name>/
  log.txt                               everything printed (includes the true model)
  redacted/<team>-DATA<n>-<name>/       measurement package: nothing about the interior
  unredacted/<team>-MOD<n>-<name>/      interior-model package: true model, density grid, the same exact values
  unredacted/                           measurements.*, truth.*, settings.json, figures/

Code#

MATLAB: projects/template/my_body.m
function [body, degree, grid_km] = my_body()
%MY_BODY  Everything specific to your asteroid, used by every runner in this project.
%
%   [body, degree, grid_km] = my_body()
%
%   Replace the shape file (and its length unit), the bulk density, the reference
%   radius, the degree and the grid spacing with your own. The measurement
%   uncertainties are set by the receiving team in each inversion run (invert_measurements.m).

shape = sbtk.shape.load(fullfile(sbtk.root, 'data', 'shapes', 'example_asteroid.obj'), ...   % your shape model
                        "km");                                                               % its length unit: "km", "m" or "cm"
body  = sbtk.body.create("Example asteroid", shape, ...
            2000, ...       % bulk density [kg/m^3]
            0.60);          % reference radius of the gravity coefficients [km]
degree = 4;                 % highest degree of the gravity field
grid_km = 0.040;            % cell edge of the density grids in model and solution packages [km]
end
MATLAB script: projects/template/simulate_measurements.m
%% SIMULATE_MEASUREMENTS  Synthetic measurements of a prescribed interior, for any body.
%
% Edit NAME and INTERIOR; the body is defined in my_body.m. The measurements are the exact
% values of the interior, without uncertainties or noise: the receiving team applies its own
% (invert_measurements.m). Writes results/<project>/<date_time>_<name>/:
%   redacted/<team>-DATA<n>-<name>/    measurement package to send (nothing about the interior)
%   unredacted/<team>-MOD<n>-<name>/   interior-model package (true model, density grid,
%                                      the same exact values, figures)
%   unredacted/                        measurements.*, truth.*, settings.json, figures/
%   log.txt
% Package format: docs/exchange_format.md.

clear; close all;
here = fileparts(which('simulate_measurements'));
addpath(here, fullfile(fileparts(fileparts(here)), 'toolbox'));
[body, degree, grid_km] = my_body();

%% PROJECT, NAME AND DELIVERY
project     = "my_asteroid";
name        = "T1";
team        = "TEAM";                 % team identifier in package names
number      = 1;                      % package numbers: <team>-DATA<number>, <team>-MOD<number>
prepared_by = "Team name, contact";

%% INTERIOR
% Components with their relative density (density minus background, kg/m^3);
% lengths in km. See sbtk.interior: sphere, ellipsoid, torus, layer, sector. Spheres,
% ellipsoids and tori are placed from the center of figure (cof), layers and sectors are
% measured from the center of mass.
cof = body.centroid_km;
components = [ ...
    sbtk.interior.sphere("core",     cof,                                     0.250, +500), ...
    sbtk.interior.layer("regolith",  0.000, 0.020,                                   -800), ...
    sbtk.interior.sphere("boulder",  cof + sbtk.interior.latlon(10, -40, 0.35), 0.060, +900)];
field = sbtk.interior.no_random_field();     % or sbtk.interior.random_field(sigma kg/m^3, correlation length km, seed)

%% RUN
out = sbtk.io.new_run(project, name);
[exact, truth] = sbtk.data.simulate(body, sbtk.interior.create(components, field), degree, name);   % the true model
sbtk.io.report_simulation(sbtk.io.subfolder(out, "unredacted"), body, exact, truth);
data_set = sprintf("%s-DATA%d-%s", team, number, name);
sbtk.exchange.write_data(fullfile(out.folder, "redacted"), data_set, body, exact, prepared_by);
sbtk.exchange.write_model(fullfile(out.folder, "unredacted"), sprintf("%s-MOD%d-%s", team, number, name), ...
                          data_set, body, truth, exact, grid_km, prepared_by);
sbtk.io.finish_run(out);
MATLAB script: projects/template/invert_measurements.m
%% INVERT_MEASUREMENTS  Component densities from gravity coefficients and moments of inertia, for any body.
%
% Edit DATA, UNCERTAINTIES, MODEL and OPTIONS. Writes results/<project>/<date_time>_<name>_inversion/:
% fit.txt / .mat, homogeneous.txt, settings.json, log.txt, figures/.

clear; close all;
here = fileparts(which('invert_measurements'));
addpath(here, fullfile(fileparts(fileparts(here)), 'toolbox'));
[~, ~, grid_km] = my_body();
team = "TEAM";  prepared_by = "Team name, contact";

%% DATA
project = "my_asteroid";
name    = "T1";
data_folder = sbtk.exchange.locate(sbtk.io.latest_run(project, name), "DATA");   % or any package folder
[obs, body] = sbtk.exchange.read_data(data_folder);

%% UNCERTAINTIES (1-sigma): ours, since the package has exact values
unc = sbtk.data.uncertainties( ...
    [sbtk.units.offset_to_degree1(0.005, body.R_ref_km), ... % degree 1: 5 m center of mass
     1e-4, 2e-4, 4e-4], ...                                 % degrees 2..degree (fully normalized)
    2e-3, ...                                               % each moment of inertia, as a fraction of M R_ref^2
    0.02);                                                  % libration ratio (B-A)/C
obs = sbtk.data.set_uncertainties(obs, unc);
% obs = sbtk.data.add_noise(obs, 1);                         % noise drawn from them, if wanted

%% MODEL (geometry fixed; relative densities estimated)
cof = body.centroid_km;                                     % center of figure of the package's shape model
components = [ ...
    sbtk.interior.sphere("core",     cof,          0.250, 0), ...
    sbtk.interior.layer("regolith",  0.000, 0.020,        0)];
% Without assumed structure:
% components = sbtk.interior.sector_grid([0 0.45 0.8 1], [-90 0 90], [-180 -90 0 90 180]);

%% OPTIONS
opts = sbtk.invert.options();
opts.moi_labels = {'Ixx', 'Iyy', 'Izz'};   % moment-of-inertia measurements used ({} = gravity only)

%% RUN
out  = sbtk.io.new_run(project, name + "_inversion");
prob = sbtk.invert.setup(body, components, obs, opts);
if numel(components) > 6
    prob.opts.regularization = sbtk.invert.choose_regularization(prob);    % many components
end
fit = sbtk.invert.run(prob);
hom = sbtk.invert.homogeneous(prob);
sbtk.io.report_inversion(out, body, fit, hom);
sbtk.exchange.write_solution(out.folder, sbtk.exchange.solution_name(team, obs.name), body, fit, hom, grid_km, prepared_by);
sbtk.io.finish_run(out);
MATLAB script: projects/template/compare_with_truth.m
%% COMPARE_WITH_TRUTH  Compare an inversion with the true model of a simulation, for any body.
%
% Reports R2 (fraction of the variance of the true density explained by the
% estimate), R2_max for the same components, the RMS density error and each
% component's estimated and true density; then compares the density grids of the
% solution package and the interior-model package cell by cell. Writes
% results/<project>/<date_time>_<inversion>_comparison/: comparison.txt / .mat,
% grid_comparison.txt, figures/comparison.png, figures/truth_vs_estimate.png.

clear; close all;
here = fileparts(which('compare_with_truth'));
addpath(here, fullfile(fileparts(fileparts(here)), 'toolbox'));
body = my_body();

project       = "my_asteroid";
truth_run     = "T1";              % simulation
inversion_run = "T1_inversion";    % inversion

simulation = sbtk.io.latest_run(project, truth_run);
inversion  = sbtk.io.latest_run(project, inversion_run);
truth = sbtk.io.load_truth(simulation);
fit   = sbtk.io.load_fit(inversion);
out   = sbtk.io.new_run(project, inversion_run + "_comparison");
sbtk.io.report_comparison(out, body, truth, fit, sbtk.compare.with_truth(body, truth, fit));

% the solution package against the interior-model package, cell by cell
cmp = sbtk.compare.grids(sbtk.exchange.read_grid(fullfile(sbtk.exchange.locate(simulation, "MOD"), "density_grid.txt")), ...
                         sbtk.exchange.read_grid(fullfile(sbtk.exchange.locate(inversion, "SOL"), "density_grid.txt")));
writelines(sbtk.compare.grid_summary(cmp), fullfile(out.folder, "grid_comparison.txt"));
sbtk.io.finish_run(out);

Projects

Bennu#

projects/bennu/ estimates the interior of the asteroid Bennu from the OSIRIS-REx gravity field (JPL, 2019; degree 10, Rref = 0.290 km) following Cavale et al., "Constraints on the Internal Density Distribution of Bennu Using OSIRIS-REx Mission Data" (Icarus), and reproduces that paper's inversion.

Files#

File Purpose
bennu_body.m Shape model bennu_higher_qual.obj (196,608 facets, body-fixed frame with origin at the center of mass), bulk density 1190 kg/m³, Rref = 0.290 km.
bennu_measurements.m The field as a measurement set, with the paper's weighting (C10 = C11 = S11 = 0, J2, C21, S21, C22, S22, J3, J4 with equal weights) or with all coefficients of degrees 2–4 and the full JPL covariance. Reads the file with sbtk.io.read_jpl_gravity.
bennu_paper_components.m The paper's nominal model: prescribed surface (0–10 m, −297.5 kg/m³) and subsurface (10–20 m, +1190 kg/m³) layers, a core of radius 170 m with estimated center, an equatorial torus and four boulders. Positions are from the origin of the shape model, as in the paper; that origin is Bennu's center of mass from the OSIRIS-REx tracking data, 1.4 m from the center of figure (Where to place components).
invert_bennu_paper.m Reproduces the paper's inversion with the background held at the bulk density and compares the result with the paper's values (tests/reference/bennu_paper_nominal.json).
invert_bennu_boulder_positions.m The same with the centers of the two boulders that target C21/S21 and C22/S22 also estimated, with an a priori 1σ of 10 m per coordinate.
check_bennu_full_field.m Compares the reproduced interior's coefficients of degrees 2–4 with the full field and covariance.
bennu_compare_with_paper.m Prints a fit next to the paper's values.

Reproduction of the paper#

Relative densities from tools/make_readme_examples.m, which runs the paper configuration:

Relative density (kg/m³) Paper SBTK
core −241.9 −242.1
torus −239.4 −234.6
boulder C21 +664.5 +660.8
boulder C22 −1049.3 −1037.3
boulder north −148.0 −146.4
boulder south −251.5 −250.9
core center (m) (1.86, −7.89, 12.59) (2.06, −7.91, 12.56)

The paper's code counted a surface facet as part of the torus only when all three of its vertices were inside the tube; SBTK integrates the exact intersection, whose volume is 2.4% larger, which accounts for most of the torus difference. tests/integration/test_bennu_paper.m checks the reproduction: the core relative density within 1 kg/m³, the boulders within 2%, the torus mass contrast within 1%, the core center within 0.5 m, and the coefficients the paper did not fit (C31 … S44) within 0.15 of the JPL 1σ (Validation).

Projects

Hera blind test#

projects/hera_hlp6/ contains the runner scripts SBTK uses in a blind test of interior-modeling methods for the binary asteroid Didymos–Dimorphos, the target of ESA's Hera mission. In such a test one team simulates measurements of an interior it keeps hidden and shares only the measurements; other teams estimate the interior; the hidden models are released afterwards and compared with the estimates on a common density grid. The makers deliver exact values, without uncertainties or noise; each receiving team weights them with uncertainties of its own choosing. SBTK's inversion runners use those of the Hera end-to-end simulation, read from files on the Hera working-group server (Didymos and Dimorphos values); the runners need copies in data/hera_rse/.

Files#

File Purpose
hlp6_didymos.m, hlp6_dimorphos.m Settings shared by every run of one body: shape model, mass, reference radius, degree, density-grid spacing.
hlp6_team.m Team identifier and contact written into package names and files.
hlp6_uncertainties.m The receiving team's uncertainties: the Hera radio-science precision of the gravity coefficients (to degree 5 for Didymos, 3 for Dimorphos, to which the coefficients are truncated), the inertia elements and the libration ratio.
simulate_didymos.m, simulate_dimorphos.m Simulate measurements of a hidden interior; write the measurement package and the interior-model package.
invert_didymos.m, invert_dimorphos.m Invert a measurement package (by default the redacted package of the newest simulation); write a solution package.
invert_didymos_sectors.m The same with a 36-sector grid, the background held at the bulk density and regularization by the discrepancy principle.
invert_received_data.m Invert another team's package (SBTK format) or a gravity file in the PDS SHADR layout.
compare_didymos.m, compare_dimorphos.m Compare an inversion with the hidden model, by component and on the density grid.
rob_data.m Read a ROB package (shgrav.txt, moi.txt) with the receiving team's uncertainties.
analyze_rob.m, rob_candidates.m Read a ROB package, fit models of increasing detail, test how far they reach, point masses, the surface point (Testing with ROB data).
rob_surface_point.m What the Dimorphos surface point adds: a buried sphere under it.

Settings#

Setting Didymos (agreed by the makers, 21 October 2026) Dimorphos
Shape model DART v003, 1.165 m sampling, 3,145,728 facets DART v004 (before the impact), 0.243 m sampling, 3,145,728 facets
Bulk density 2600 kg/m³ 1534 kg/m³
Mass 5.299121 × 10¹¹ kg (GM 3.5367926256900638 × 10⁻⁸ km³/s²) 2.700 × 10⁹ kg
Reference radius 0.41 km 0.10 km
Degrees the makers send 1 to 10 1 to 10
Degrees the receiving team fits 1 to 5 1 to 3
Density-grid spacing 0.020 km 0.005 km
Frame of the packages the frame and origin of the DART shape model file the frame and origin of the DART shape model file

Where each of these values comes from, and the alternatives: Didymos and Dimorphos values. A run on the full-resolution models takes minutes: the geometry of 3 million facets to degree 10 takes about a minute and 4.5 GB, and a simulation repeats it until the center of mass settles.

Simulation runs#

A simulation runner has four sections:

  1. NAME AND DELIVERY: the run name, the package number n, and the inertia quantities the package contains (any of Ixx … Iyz, libration, or none; sbtk.data.select_moi).
  2. INTERIOR: components and random field (Density distributions), in the axes of the DART shape-model file with positions measured from the center of figure (cof = body.centroid_km), not from the origin of the file, which is 57 m from it for Didymos (Where to place components). The torus lies about the z-axis through cof. align_with_spin_axis names the components whose axis is set along the axis of the largest moment of the whole true model (Didymos: "torus", which forms about the spin axis; Dimorphos: none), with sbtk.interior.align_with_spin_axis.
  3. FRAME OF THE PACKAGES: "shape", as the HLP6 makers agreed: the frame and origin of the DART shape model file as distributed, with the gravity field (degree 1 included) and the moments of inertia about that origin. The alternatives "spin" and "principal" move everything to the center of mass of the true model and rotate it into its spin or principal axes (Frames of a gravity field).
  4. RUN: sbtk.interior.create and sbtk.interior.align_with_spin_axis; sbtk.data.simulate (the true model and its exact values, without uncertainties); sbtk.data.select_moi and, for "shape", sbtk.data.expand_about to the origin of the file (for "spin" or "principal", sbtk.gravity.center_of_mass_frame and sbtk.body.to_frame, sbtk.interior.to_frame, sbtk.data.to_frame, with the shape model moved and rotated: The shape model of a package); then sbtk.io.report_simulation, sbtk.exchange.write_data (a package of exact values: no 1σ columns, no covariance file, Exchange packages) and sbtk.exchange.write_model.

The run folder separates what may be shared from what may not:

Simulation run folder of projects/hera_hlp6
results/hera_hlp6/<date_time>_<name>/
  log.txt                          everything printed, including the true model
  redacted/<team>-DATA<n>-<body>/  the measurement package to share
  unredacted/<team>-MOD<n>-<body>/ the interior-model package, shared after the estimates
  unredacted/                      measurements.*, truth.*, settings.json, figures/

Only the package folder in redacted/ is shared: log.txt and everything in unredacted/ contain the true model.

Maker models#

examples/make_didymos_1.m to make_dimorphos_3.m are six true models made the same way, one script each, into results/didymos_models/ and results/dimorphos_models/, as packages 1 to 6. Didymos and Dimorphos share one numbering because a solution name carries only the number; the T1 demo sets of the simulate scripts are 7 and 8. They send exact values of every degree to 10, normalized and unnormalized, and Ixx, Iyy, Izz, in the frame and about the origin of the DART shape model file (degree 1 and C¯21, S¯21 are not zero). The packages name that file but do not include it.

The interiors of these models are not described on this site, which is public, until the true models are released; projects/hera_hlp6/README.md in the repository lists them. examples/make_didymos_homogeneous.m makes the reference the makers compare, as their cross-validation asks (Didymos and Dimorphos values): Didymos at 2600 kg/m³, every degree to 10 and all six inertia elements, in the same frame and about the same origin, and the potential and acceleration at the 20 agreed points (sbtk.exchange.write_potential; package UCB-DATA0-Didymos-homogeneous). Its degree 1 gives the center of figure. If two makers compute the same homogeneous field from the same shape model file, they work in the same frame with the same conventions. tests/integration/test_maker_scripts.m runs make_didymos_3, make_dimorphos_3 and make_didymos_homogeneous and checks their packages.

Inversion runs#

invert_didymos.m reads the redacted package of the newest simulation of the given name with sbtk.exchange.locate and sbtk.exchange.read_data, exactly as another team receives it. Its coefficients, degree 1 included, and its moments of inertia are about the origin of the shape model file, and the inversion predicts the model's about the same point, with no change of frame (Density estimation). hlp6_uncertainties.m then gives the exact values the receiving team's uncertainties (the Hera radio-science precision, truncating the coefficients to the degree it covers). Its model places the core and the torus at the center of figure of the package's shape model, as a receiving team would, and estimates the torus axis and height (Estimated geometry): estimate_axis = true, estimate_position = [false false true], with a priori 1σ of 1° and 10 m and limits of 10° and 50 m. It writes fit.*, homogeneous.txt, figures and the solution package <team>-SOL_<data team><n>/. invert_received_data.m does the same for a package from another team, or, with the commented lines, for a SHADR-layout gravity file, for which the shape model and the point the coefficients are about must be given.

Comparison runs#

compare_didymos.m loads the newest simulation and inversion of the given names and the body from the simulation's measurement package (so that all three are in the frame of the packages), compares the fit with the true model (sbtk.compare.with_truth) and compares the solution package's density grid with the interior-model package's (sbtk.compare.grids), which is the comparison every team's solution receives.

Example runs#

The delivered interiors (named T1) include a boulder and a random density field that the delivered inversion models do not contain. Weighted by the uncertainties of the end-to-end simulation, the χ2 test rejects the inversion models of both bodies, and the estimated densities are biased accordingly. At this precision an inversion model has to include structure down to the scale of such features to pass the test (Goodness of fit). For Didymos T1, whose torus is aligned with the spin axis of the true model (3.7° from the z-axis of the DART file), the model with the torus about the z-axis and fixed geometry has a reduced χ2 of 157 and R2=0.49. Estimating the torus axis and height lowers χ2 to 49 but R2 to −1.95: the torus moves 50 m, to its limit, and tilts 6.9° to take up the signal of the boulder, which the model lacks (Estimated geometry). The run takes about a minute. For Dimorphos, an ellipsoidal core and the regolith give a reduced χ2 of 47 and R2=0.04.

Projects

Didymos and Dimorphos values#

Every value SBTK uses to model Didymos and Dimorphos, where it comes from and where to find it. Each value is one of:

  • agreed: the value the Hera blind-test group uses;
  • server: from a file on the Hera working-group server (folder paths below are relative to its top folder);
  • published: from a paper or a public data product (references at the end of the page);
  • derived: computed from other values on this page;
  • assumed: an SBTK choice, not a measurement.

The HLP6 makers agreed on the Didymos values on 21 October 2026 [HLP6 cross-validation 2026]: the 1.165 m shape model in its own frame, bulk density 2600 kg/m³, reference radius 410 m, degrees to 10, and the potential and acceleration at 20 given points. There are no agreed Dimorphos values yet.

The values are set in the repository in projects/hera_hlp6/hlp6_didymos.m and projects/hera_hlp6/hlp6_dimorphos.m (shape model, mass or bulk density, reference radius, degree, grid spacing), projects/hera_hlp6/hlp6_uncertainties.m (the receiving team's uncertainties) and the maker scripts examples/make_didymos_1.m to make_dimorphos_3.m.

Shape models#

The shape models are the DART stereophotoclinometry (SPC) models, Didymos version 3 and Dimorphos version 4, from before the DART impact [Daly et al. 2023; Daly et al. 2024]. They are published in two places:

  • PDS: NASA Planetary Data System, Small Bodies Node, bundle pds4-dart_shapemodel-v1.0 [DART shape models 2023]. Each collection holds the global model at four samplings (OBJ files) with the digital terrain maps (FITS):
  • Didymos: https://pds-smallbodies.astro.umd.edu/holdings/pds4-dart_shapemodel-v1.0/data_derived_didymos_model_v003/
  • Dimorphos: https://pds-smallbodies.astro.umd.edu/holdings/pds4-dart_shapemodel-v1.0/data_derived_dimorphos_model_v004/
  • ESA SPICE: the full-resolution models only, as OBJ and digital shape kernel (.bds) files, https://spiftp.esac.esa.int/data/SPICE/HERA/kernels/dsk/. The working-group server has the same two files in Hera_WG/End-to-End Test/Shape/, and the agreed Didymos file in Hera_WG/End-to-End Test/HLP6G BlindTest/inputs/Reference models/Didymos/.

The volume and the volume-equivalent diameter D=(6V/π)1/3 are derived from each file.

PDS has the 1.165 m model as didymos_g_1165mm_spc_obj_0000n00000_v003.obj. MD5 0a585bc46d19f29778d7721970958723. Not in git.

SBTK's blind-test Dimorphos packages (like the agreed Didymos model, the full resolution). PDS has it as dimorphos_g_0243mm_spc_obj_0000n00000_v004.obj. MD5 d8263a016169434e09fd10f8b065f0a1. Not in git.
(not in SBTK yet) dimorphos_g_1940mm_spc_obj_0000n00000_v004.obj 1.94 m published: PDS, Dimorphos collection (3.4 MB). The 1.94 m Dimorphos model the RSE team uses.

Points to know:

  • Use the same file as the other teams. The agreed Didymos file is the 1.165 m model. The 9.3 m file is a separate product, not a subsample of it: its volume is 0.22% smaller, its center of figure is 0.35 m away, and its degree-2 coefficients differ by up to 3×10−4, about the size of the measurement uncertainties. Data made with one file and inverted with another carry that difference as an error. data/shapes/README.md compares all the versions.
  • Packages do not include the file. A package made with one of these files names it (Exchange packages).
  • Dimorphos. The models are from before the DART impact, which may have changed the shape.
  • Frame. Each file has its own body-fixed frame, z along the spin axis. The HLP6 makers keep it ("native reference frame of the shape model, not barycentric"; Frames of a gravity field). The center of figure is 56.765 m from the origin of the agreed Didymos file, at (+15.723, +42.487, −34.204) m, and 0.751 m from that of the Dimorphos file, at (−0.741, −0.117, −0.007) m.

Bulk density#

The bulk density is the background density of a homogeneous model (Density distributions). For Didymos it is agreed, 2600 kg/m³, and sets the mass. For Dimorphos it is derived: 2.700 × 10⁹ kg over the volume of the 0.243 m model, 1534 kg/m³.

Before the agreement SBTK took the mass of the RSE end-to-end test, 5.273 × 10¹¹ kg, which gives 2593 kg/m³ with the 9.3 m file and 2587 kg/m³ with the 1.165 m file.

Potential and acceleration at the cross-validation points#

The makers also give the gravitational potential and acceleration of the homogeneous Didymos at 20 points [HLP6 cross-validation 2026], in m in the frame of the agreed file (projects/hera_hlp6/cross_validation/points.csv):

Points Distance from the origin of the file
1: on the surface at latitude 45°, longitude 45° 332 m
2: near an equilibrium point of the homogeneous body 360 m
3–8, 9–14, 15–20: six points each on spheres of radius 1.2, 1.5 and 2.0 Rref (Fibonacci lattice) 492, 615, 820 m

SBTK computes them exactly from the polyhedron of the shape model (Potential and acceleration at points). The sphere about the origin that encloses Didymos has a radius of 449.7 m, so points 1 and 2 are inside it, where the spherical-harmonic expansion does not converge. At 1.2 Rref the expansion to degree 10 differs from the exact potential by up to 1.5 × 10⁻⁴ of it; a team that evaluates the coefficients there will differ by that much. At point 2 the gravitational acceleration, 2.40 × 10⁻⁴ m/s², points to the center of mass and equals the centrifugal acceleration of the 2.26 h rotation about an axis through it: the point is an equilibrium point, as stated.

Uncertainties of the receiving team#

The makers send exact values. SBTK's inversion runners give them the precision of the RSE end-to-end test (projects/hera_hlp6/hlp6_uncertainties.m), read from the RSE files (server, Hera_WG/End-to-End Test/Radio Science/Gravity/, copies in data/hera_rse/, whose README.md describes them; the files are marked "test product only, not for scientific use"). The blind-test group's precision files are in Hera_WG/End-to-End Test/HLP6G BlindTest/inputs/uncertainties/ (UniBo-PREC1-Gravity_MOIs).

Ixx, Iyy, Izz, 1σ 2.4853 × 10⁹, 2.4852 × 10⁹, 2.4853 × 10⁹ kg km² 1.1081 × 10⁴, 1.1359 × 10⁴, 1.4283 × 10⁴ kg km² RSE_solution_MOIs_Deg2Gravity_Didymos.txt, ..._Dimorphos.txt (labeled kg m², values in kg km²)

Libration ratio, 1σ 0.02 0.02 assumed (placeholder)

The Didymos coefficients and their 1σ are given for Rref = 0.43 km; sbtk.data.use_uncertainties converts the 1σ of degree l to the agreed 0.41 km by the factor (0.43/0.41)l.

The RSE fields are given in principal-axis frames (for the homogeneous body, the axis of the smallest moment is turned 32.2° (Didymos) and 7.8° (Dimorphos) from the shape-model x-axis toward −y, with the axis of the largest moment tilted 3.8° and 0.7° from the shape-model z-axis). Their 1σ table is applied in the axes of the packages without that rotation, which is an approximation (Frames of a gravity field).

The RSE fields are also about the center of mass, while the packages are about the origin of the shape model file. The covariance is therefore moved to that point exactly, K′=TKT𝖳 (sbtk.data.use_uncertainties): moving a field to another point mixes the degrees, so the uncertainty of the center of mass (degree 1) enters the other coefficients. About the origin of the file, C¯20 of Didymos (UCB-DATA1) has 2.3 times the RSE 1σ and some degree-3 coefficients up to 1.8 times; C¯22 of Dimorphos (UCB-DATA4, center of mass 2.5 m from the origin) has 27 times the RSE 1σ, which is only 4×10−6. The inertia elements, about the same point, get the variance the center of mass adds through the parallel-axis theorem: negligible for Didymos, 12 to 19% more 1σ for Dimorphos. A team that applies the RSE 1σ unchanged to coefficients about the file origin weights those coefficients too much. Uncertainties and the expansion point derives these numbers.

Testing with ROB data

Testing with ROB data#

The Royal Observatory of Belgium (ROB), one of the teams that make interiors for the HLP6 blind test, distributed six measurement packages of hidden interiors: three of Didymos (ROB-DATA1 to 3) and three of Dimorphos (ROB-DATA4 to 6). This section reads each of them with the procedure of Reading the gravity coefficients, fits four kinds of solution to the same measurements (models of components, a search of the geometry, sector grids and point masses), compares them on the same terms, and shows where they agree. The hidden interiors are not known to us; everything here comes from the measurements.

The packages#

Each package has

  • shgrav.txt: fully normalized gravity coefficients of degrees 0 to 10 about the origin of the DART shape-model file, in its axes, with ROB's reference radius and GM in the header;
  • moi.txt: the six inertia elements I/(MRref2) about the same origin;
  • for Dimorphos also the gravitational potential and acceleration at one point on the surface, as the GRASS gravimeter on a lander would measure them.

The values are exact (ROB's 1σ columns are 10⁻⁸ to 10⁻⁶, far below what a mission measures). The headers give each package's mass and reference radius:

Package Body Shape model Mass (kg) Bulk density (kg/m³) Rref (km)
ROB-DATA1 Didymos DART v003, 1.165 m 5.30417 × 10¹¹ 2602.5 0.41
ROB-DATA2 Didymos DART v003, 1.165 m 5.30966 × 10¹¹ 2605.2 0.41
ROB-DATA3 Didymos DART v003, 1.165 m 5.29912 × 10¹¹ 2600.0 0.41
ROB-DATA4 Dimorphos DART v004, 0.243 m 2.71071 × 10⁹ 1540.0 0.09
ROB-DATA5 Dimorphos DART v004, 0.243 m 2.70889 × 10⁹ 1539.0 0.09
ROB-DATA6 Dimorphos DART v004, 0.243 m 2.80558 × 10⁹ 1593.9 0.09

Uncertainties#

The packages are weighted with the precision of the Hera radio-science end-to-end simulation, as in the blind test (projects/hera_hlp6/rob_data.m, which calls hlp6_uncertainties.m; Didymos and Dimorphos values):

  • every coefficient's 1σ from the RSE gravity field, with its full covariance moved from the RSE center of mass to the origin of the shape-model file (Uncertainties and the expansion point) and scaled to the package's reference radius;
  • the coefficients truncated to the degrees the RSE field has: 5 for Didymos (35 coefficients) and 3 for Dimorphos (15, of which degree 3 has 1σ of about 10⁻², so that Dimorphos is measured to degree 2);
  • each inertia element's 1σ from the RSE inertia solution, with the variance the center of mass adds about the origin. For Didymos they are about 2.8 × 10⁻² of MR2 and carry no information; for Dimorphos about 5 × 10⁻⁴, and they do.

How to read these pages#

Every package page has the same sections, and every kind of solution is shown the same way.

C − C_CD. Each measured coefficient minus the coefficient of the same shape with constant density (CD), both about the center of figure: what the interior adds to the gravity field. 0 is constant density. The bars are ±1σ of the Hera radio-science solution (Uncertainties). Zonal terms are shown as Jl=−C¯l0; degree 1 is the center-of-mass offset (C¯11,S¯11,C¯10=x,y,z over 3Rref). The figures show degrees 1 to 4 (Dimorphos: 1 to 3, of which degree 3 has a 1σ of about 10⁻², so that Dimorphos is measured to degree 2), each degree on its own scale, and the three moments of inertia.

Reading the geometry. The sign of a coefficient of C − C_CD says where mass was added or taken away, as a mass excess at a point would make it: C¯10,C¯11,S¯11 the side the center of mass moved to; J2 higher, mass moved toward the equator; C¯22>0, toward the ends of the x-axis; C¯21>0, toward +x in the north and −x in the south; J3 higher, toward the south. sbtk.interpret.geometry combines the five coefficients of degree 2 into the axes mass moved toward and away from, and draws each degree as a map. Every component of a model is placed to make some of these; the contribution figure shows which.

The kinds of solution. All are fitted to the same measurements (every coefficient the Hera uncertainties cover and Ixx,Iyy,Izz) and compared the same way:

Kind What it assumes
components a few shapes placed by reading the coefficients: a core, a torus, layers, spheres, polar caps, ellipsoids
search a core, a torus and a layer with their sizes, axis and the core's position searched (Searching the geometry), and compact masses where they pass the likelihood-ratio test
sectors 32 or 64 blocks of latitude, longitude and depth, each with its own density, smoothed (Tikhonov) as much as the measurements allow
point masses a few thousand masses on a grid, smoothed in the same way

χ², reduced χ², p. χ² is the sum over the measurements of ((solution − measured)/σ)², with the correlations of the coefficients taken into account. If the solution were the truth, χ² would be about the number of measurements minus the number of parameters fitted (ν, the degrees of freedom): the reduced χ² = χ²/ν is then about 1, and a value well above 1 means the solution misses something the measurements see. The p-value is the probability that the measurement noise alone gives a χ² this large; p ≥ 0.05 is called consistent: the misfit is no larger than the noise.

Effective parameters. How many independent things the measurements determine in a solution (the trace of the data resolution matrix): 4 for a core with its position, 1 per density, fractions for smoothed sectors and point masses. A solution with more parameters fits more easily, so solutions are ranked by the Akaike information criterion, AIC = χ² + 2 × effective parameters: lower is better, and a parameter must lower χ² by more than 2 to pay for itself.

Mean squared residual to degree 4. The average of ((solution − measured)/σ)² over the coefficients of degrees 1 to 4 alone, without the correlations: 1 is a match within 1σ on average. It is what the comparison figure shows coefficient by coefficient.

The moments of inertia. Degree 2 holds only the differences of the moments of inertia (C¯20, C¯22, and the products of inertia in C¯21,S¯21,S¯22). The moments themselves add their sum, 2∫ρr2dV: how far the mass is from the center, which separates a dense core from a light surface (both change degree 2 alike). The Bennu analysis (Cavale et al.) fitted gravity alone, C¯10 to J4 with equal weights; here the full covariance of the Hera solution weights every coefficient to the degree it is measured, and the moments are added with their own 1σ. For Didymos that 1σ is 2.8 × 10⁻² of MRref2, larger than any change an interior makes, so the moments carry no information; for Dimorphos it is about 5 × 10⁻⁴, and they do.

Exact values. ROB's packages give exact coefficients to degree 10. A solution fitted to the measured degrees is tested on them: the fraction of each degree it reproduces, 1 − |solution − exact|²/|exact|² (1: all of it; 0: no better than constant density; negative: worse).

Method#

For every package (projects/hera_hlp6/analyze_rob.m, then rob_figures.m for the figures and tables of the pages):

  1. Reading (sbtk.interpret.anomaly, sbtk.interpret.geometry): C − C_CD coefficient by coefficient, the center-of-mass offset, the axes of degree 2, each degree as a map.
  2. Models with components chosen from the reading (rob_candidates.m): a core (placed by its χ² profile along the center-of-mass offset, then by Gauss–Newton), layers, tori, ellipsoids, and for some packages polar caps and spheres where the reading put mass. The fits run on the 49,152-facet versions of the shape models with the measurements moved to them (sbtk.data.to_reduced_shape).
  3. The search (sbtk.search.run) of a core, a torus and a layer, and compact masses.
  4. Sector grids and point masses, smoothed as much as the measurements allow (the largest Tikhonov parameter with p ≥ 0.05).
  5. Comparison on the same terms (AIC, the coefficients one by one, ROB's exact values to degree 10), the contributions of each component of the best model, and the best consistent solution of each kind side by side.
  6. For Dimorphos, the GRASS surface point as an independent check.

Across the six packages#

  • Reading the coefficients chose the components that win. In five of the six the best solution by AIC is a model of a few components placed where the reading of C − C_CD put mass: the two equatorial bodies of DATA1 at the ends of the axis degree 2 moves mass toward, the ring of DATA3 from its even degrees, the core of DATA4 and DATA5 on the side of the center-of-mass offset and the axis of degree 2, the light core and dense outside of DATA6 from the moments. Each page's contribution figure shows which coefficients each component makes.
  • Where no component of the candidate set has the right shape, the sector grids win. DATA2's anomaly is tilted and off center at once; cores, tori and layers stay far from it (reduced χ² 13 and more), the sector grids fit it, and the sector grids, the point masses and the search's core all point to the same side.
  • Point masses fit, but at a price, and never win. They are consistent in every package only with many effective parameters (24 to 32 of the 38 Didymos measurements), they leave the moments of DATA5 and DATA6 2–3σ off, and on interiors whose truth is known they explain none of the density at their own resolution (Point masses on the same interiors). Where the anomaly is large and to one side they show it (DATA1 to DATA3: cell by cell they correlate 0.46 to 0.79 with the best solutions of the other kinds); on Dimorphos they keep the mass nearly symmetric about the center (0.12 to 0.47).
  • The kinds agree on where the anomaly is, not on its form. Side by side, the best consistent solution of each kind puts the excess in the same place in DATA1 (the two equatorial ends, the −x end most), DATA2 (below the equator toward the south-west), DATA3 (inside a light equatorial ring) and DATA6 (light inside, dense outside). The sector grids and point masses spread it; the models with components make it compact. On DATA4 and DATA5 the smooth solutions keep the extra mass symmetric about the center where the models with components put one body to one side, and the coefficients cannot tell them apart: on DATA4 the GRASS point decides for the core, on DATA5 ROB's exact values to degree 10 favor the one sphere.
  • The moments matter for Dimorphos only. At the Hera precision the Didymos moments carry no information; for Dimorphos they are as decisive as degree 2 (DATA4, DATA6), and only the models with components reach them.
  • One surface point can decide, or not. On DATA4 the GRASS acceleration picks the model with the core 31 m toward −y (0.2%) over the smooth solutions (10%); on DATA5 the anomaly is too small for one point; on DATA6 it favors the smooth solutions in size and none of the solutions in direction. It tests the material under the lander, which the coefficients see only through degree 2.

Testing with ROB data

ROB-DATA1: Didymos#

In short. Mass is moved from the poles toward the equator and gathered at two opposite ends of the equator, along longitudes −19° and 161°, more at the 161° end. The best solution places a dense body at each end, 235 and 251 m from the center (+1880 and +1130 kg/m³), light polar caps and a light region 155 m below the center; it matches every coefficient to degree 5 within the uncertainties (reduced χ² 0.83, p = 0.70) with 14 parameters. Sector grids and point masses, which assume no shapes, find the same pattern but need 20 to 28 effective parameters for the same measurements. Beyond degree 5, ROB's exact values show that the dense material is more spread out than two spheres.

Read together:

  • Degree 2 moves mass toward an axis in the equator through longitudes −19° and 161° (±2°) and away from the polar axis. Its three principal values (0.51, −0.02, −0.49) make it triaxial: denser at the two ends of an equatorial axis, lighter along the spin axis.
  • Degree 1: the center of mass lies toward longitude −167°, 12° from the 161° end of that axis: that end carries more extra mass than the other.
  • Degrees 3 and 4 put their strongest excess at longitudes −172° and 162°: the same end.

So the model given to the fit was: a light cap at each pole (sectors above 45° and below −45°), a dense sphere at each end of the equatorial axis, started 250 m out along −20° and 160°, and a core of free position and density for the light center.

3. The solutions compared#

  • Every kind matches degrees 1 and 2 within 1–2σ: the center-of-mass offset, J2 and the elongation are what all of them reproduce first.
  • The differences are in degrees 3 and 4. The model with components keeps every coefficient within 1.3σ. The sector grid and the point masses miss J4 by 3σ; the search, whose torus and layer cannot make two equatorial lobes, misses S¯44 by 4σ and C¯31 by 3σ.

Why each component is where it is, and dense or light:

  • The west body (+1880 kg/m³ at 235 m, longitude 167°) and the east body (+1130 kg/m³ at 251 m, longitude −24°) sit at the two ends of the axis degree 2 moves mass toward. Together they make C¯22 and S¯22; being unequal, they move the center of mass toward the west: the west body makes −150σ of C¯11, the east +91σ. The west body reaches the density bound (4500 kg/m³): the extra mass at the 161° end is more than a sphere of 73 m radius can hold.
  • The light north cap (−179 kg/m³) and the light core (−1330 kg/m³, 155 m below the center) take mass away from the spin axis and make J2 higher (the cap −104σ and the core −163σ of C¯20). They also balance each other in C¯10: the cap alone would move the center of mass south, the core alone north.
  • The south cap (+112 ± 65 kg/m³) is barely resolved: below the center the light core and the cap together give a light interior under a normal surface.

moved: the mass above the bulk density M/V (equal to the mass below it), in 41 m cells; excess at, deficit at: where that mass is centered, from the center of figure.

All three put the extra mass at the two ends of the equatorial axis degree 2 points to (−19° and 161°) and take it from along the spin axis, and all three center the excess 34 to 45 m toward −x: the 161° end carries more, as degree 1 said. They differ in how compact the extra mass is and where the missing mass is. The model with components gathers the excess into two spheres and puts the deficit in a light core 155 m below the center and a light north cap; the sector grid spreads the excess over equatorial wedges that reach the center, and the deficit over cones about both poles; the point masses spread the excess over the outer equator and put the deficit in a column along the spin axis. The sector grid and the point masses, which assume no shapes, correlate 0.70 cell by cell; each correlates about 0.5 with the model with components. The measurements fix the two equatorial ends and the lighter spin axis; how compact the dense material is they leave open, and ROB's exact values beyond degree 4 (section 6) say it is more spread out than two spheres.

Testing with ROB data

ROB-DATA2: Didymos#

In short. The extra mass is to one side and below: the center of mass is 2.3 m from the center of figure toward the south-west (latitude −45°, longitude −108°), degree 2 moves mass along an axis tilted 58° from the equator, and degree 3, small in the other Didymos packages, is large. Nothing symmetric about the spin axis makes this: every model of a core, a torus and layers stays far from the measurements (reduced χ² 13 and more). The sector grids and the point masses fit, and agree with each other: denser below the equator toward −x and −y, lighter above it toward +y. The best solution is the 32-sector grid (reduced χ² 1.65 with 22 effective parameters); it reproduces ROB's exact values to degree 5.

All three point to more mass in the southern hemisphere toward the 180° meridian, less in the northern one toward 0°. A core can make the offset, a torus and layers the change of J2, but none of them can be tilted and off-center at once in the way degrees 2 and 3 require.

3. The solutions compared#

  • The sector grid and the point masses keep every coefficient within 3σ (the largest misfits: C¯44 −2.9σ for the sector grid, C¯21 −2.3σ for the point masses).
  • The search and the model with components miss degree 3 by many σ (S¯33 is the largest misfit of both): their components are symmetric about the z-axis (torus, layer) or compact (core), and the tilted structure is neither.

4. The best solution: 32 sectors#

The densest sectors are south of latitude −45° across the 180° meridian (+232 kg/m³ at longitudes −180° to −135°, +163 at 135° to 180°), and between −45° and 0° the same side is denser too (+57 to +78). North of the equator the same side is the lightest (−106 kg/m³ between 0° and 45° latitude, 135° to 180° longitude). Mass moved from north to south on the side of the 180° meridian, as the reading said. No model with components reaches this; the closest is the search, whose dense core (+1440 kg/m³) went to 68 m from the center toward latitude −31°, longitude −135°, the same direction:

7. Details#

Testing with ROB data

ROB-DATA3: Didymos#

In short. The even zonal coefficients change far more than anything else: J2 is 570σ lower and J4 95σ higher than constant density, the signature of a ring about the spin axis. The best solution is a dense core at the center (+1200 kg/m³), a light, thick torus about the z-axis (−425 kg/m³, ring radius 383 m, tube radius 110 m) and a dense thin layer: reduced χ² 1.22 (p = 0.18) with 6 parameters, and it reproduces ROB's exact values to degree 7. The point masses come close but need 30 to 32 of the 38 measurements' degrees of freedom; the sector grids, whose sectors run from the center to the surface, cannot make a ring at all.

3. The solutions compared#

  • The model with components and the search keep J2 and J4, the two largest coefficients by far, within 1σ; their largest misfits are small terms of degrees 2 to 4 (C¯32, C¯43, S¯22, S¯43, 2.0 to 2.4σ).
  • The point masses match every coefficient within 1σ except J4 (3.7σ too high), using nearly all the freedom the measurements have (30 of 38 effective parameters).
  • The sector grids fail: a sector spans the full depth (or half of it) and cannot put a light ring 280 to 490 m from the center under a normal surface.

Why each component is where it is, and dense or light:

  • The light torus (−425 kg/m³; ring radius 383 m, about the body's mean radius; tube radius 110 m) removes mass from the equatorial plane: it makes most of J2 (+478σ of C¯20) and nearly all of J4 (−92σ of C¯40). Its two radii are what make J2 and J4 in the measured proportion.
  • The dense core (+1200 kg/m³, 5 m from the center of figure) concentrates mass at the center: it adds to J2 (+133σ) and makes the small center-of-mass offset.
  • The dense layer (+780 kg/m³, 11 m) takes part of J2 back (−40σ): with the torus taking mass from the outer equator, the surface itself is denser than the background.

All three take mass from the outer part of the equatorial plane, 270 m and more from the spin axis, and put it farther in: their excess and their deficit are both centered within 15 m of the center of figure, as for a structure symmetric about the spin axis. Where farther in differs. The model with components puts the mass in a dense core of 145 m radius at the center, under a dense surface layer; the search makes the whole interior inside its torus denser, under a light crust; the point masses put it toward the poles and, less, at the center. Cell by cell they correlate 0.37 to 0.57. The light equatorial ring is what the measurements fix (J2 and J4); how the mass inside it is arranged they leave open. The sector grids are far from consistent (section 3) and are not shown.

7. Details#

Testing with ROB data

ROB-DATA4: Dimorphos#

In short. Mass is moved from the ends of the long x-axis toward ±y: C¯22 changes sign (50σ) and the moments of inertia say the same (Ixx +13σ, Iyy −10σ). Dimorphos is measured to degree 2 and its three moments, 18 numbers, which several interiors fit. The two best by AIC are both a dense core 31 to 46 m toward −y with a torus and a dense layer (reduced χ² 0.08 and 0.65, 6 to 9 parameters); the sector grids and point masses fit with 4 to 5 effective parameters but not as closely. The GRASS surface point, which no solution was fitted to, decides: the core model predicts the lander's acceleration to 0.2%, the sector grids and point masses miss it by 10 to 11%.

  • Degree 2 moves mass toward an axis through longitudes 85° and −95° (±y), within 9° of the equator, and away from the x-axis. One value stands out (0.61 against −0.22 and −0.39): mass toward both ends of the y-axis.
  • Degree 1: the center of mass toward longitude −95°: more of that mass at the −y end.
  • So the model given to the fit was a core placed by its χ² profile along the center-of-mass offset (it went toward −y), with a torus about the z-axis and a surface layer for J2 and the moments.

3. The solutions compared#

  • The search's core model matches every coefficient and moment within 1σ. The model with components leaves 2.5σ in S¯11 and C¯22 and 1.6σ in J2.
  • The sector grids and the point masses, smoothed as much as the measurements allow, leave about 3σ in J2, C¯22 and S¯11: with 18 numbers, the smoothing that keeps them consistent also keeps them from the largest coefficients.

Why the components are where they are:

  • The dense core toward −y makes most of the change of C¯22 (−50σ in the search's model): mass on the y-axis lowers C¯22. Being on the −y side, it also makes the center-of-mass offset.
  • The torus and the layer add mass in the equator and near the surface: J2 higher and the moments larger. In the search's model they are not resolved (their 1σ exceeds their densities); in the model with components the torus is +419 ± 170 kg/m³ and the layer +1790 ± 800 kg/m³ (a crust about 2 m thick at about 2970 kg/m³ over a background of 1180).
  • The two core models differ in where they put the core: 31 m out at +2530 kg/m³, or 46 m out at +1165 kg/m³. The coefficients do not tell them apart; the surface point does (section 6).

Testing with ROB data

ROB-DATA5: Dimorphos#

In short. The smallest anomaly of the six: degree 2 differs from constant density mainly in C¯22 (+27σ), two moments are 4 to 5σ lower, and the center of mass is not measurably off. A single dense sphere, +293 kg/m³ placed 27 m from the center toward +x, explains all of it with 4 parameters (reduced χ² 0.03), and it reproduces ROB's exact values to degree 10 better than any other solution: the hidden interior is close to one dense body on the +x side. The sector grids and point masses fit with 3 to 8 effective parameters but reproduce little beyond degree 2. At the GRASS surface point every solution is within 2%, as constant density nearly is: the anomaly is too small for one point to choose between them.

8. Details#

Testing with ROB data

ROB-DATA6: Dimorphos#

In short. Mass is pushed outward and toward ±y: the moments of inertia are 30 to 60σ larger than constant density's, J2 is 79σ higher, and C¯22 changes sign (−97σ). The best solution is a light core 54 m toward −x (−950 kg/m³), a dense torus about the spin axis (+820 kg/m³) and a dense crust (+2210 kg/m³): reduced χ² 0.39 with 6 parameters, far ahead of the smoothed solutions by AIC (17 against 33 to 35). It fits degree 2 and the moments, which is all Dimorphos is measured to; beyond, ROB's exact values show structure that none of the solutions has. At the GRASS surface point the smooth solutions predict the size of the acceleration better (0.1% to 1.6% off against 4% for the core model), and every solution, like constant density, is 2.5 to 3.7° off in direction: the material near the lander is not determined by the coefficients.

Degree 2 (chi-square 27540 for 5): second moment of the anomaly triaxial, values 0.55, -0.10, -0.45 of their spread.
  axis toward (largest): lat +0 lon -85 and lat -0 lon 95, +-1 deg
  axis middle: lat +19 lon 5 and lat -19 lon -175, +-4 deg
  axis away from (smallest): lat +71 lon -175 and lat -71 lon 5, +-4 deg
  mass moved toward the axis through lat +0 lon -85 and lat -0 lon 95 and away from the axis through lat +71 lon -175 and lat -71 lon 5.
Rest of degree 2 (without the scaled homogeneous field): triaxial, values 0.50, -0.00, -0.50.
  mass moved toward the axis through lat +1 lon -86 and lat -1 lon 94 and away from the axis through lat +17 lon -176 and lat -17 lon 4.
Each degree on the sphere (strongest excess / strongest deficit; rest after the scaled homogeneous field):
  degree 2 chi2  27540 for  5: excess lat  +0 lon  -84, deficit lat +70 lon -176;  rest: excess lat  +0 lon  -86, deficit lat -18 lon   +4
  • Degree 2 moves mass toward the ±y axis (longitudes −85° and 95°, ±1°) and away from an axis close to the poles (latitude ±71°): toward the equator and toward ±y.
  • The moments, all larger: outward. A light center does both, and a denser outside.
  • Degree 1: the center of mass toward +x: a light body on the −x side, or extra mass on +x.

So the model given to the fit was a core placed by its χ² profile along the offset (it went 54 m toward −x and became light), a torus about the z-axis for the equatorial excess, and a surface layer for the outward shift.

3. The solutions compared#

  • The model with components matches every coefficient and moment within 2σ (its largest misfits C¯11 and C¯22, 1.8σ).
  • The point masses and the sector grids leave the moments 2 to 2.6σ too small: smoothed as much as the measurements allow, they do not push enough mass outward. The search's model misses the offset by 2.9σ in C¯10.

4. The best solution: a light core, a dense torus and a dense crust#

Output
component  type          center - cof (m)   dist m      lat      lon    drho kg/m^3        rho      mass kg  makes most of (sigma)
core       sphere     [  -54    -5     8]       54        8     -175     -953 +- 371        430    -1.07e+08  C22 -93, C20 +16, S22 -11
torus      torus     [    0     0     0] R 71 a 11 tilt 0.0        0        0        0      816 +-  66       2199     1.45e+08  C20 -68, C22 -4, S22 +1
regolith   layer            0 to 2 m deep      NaN      NaN      NaN     2214 +- 345       3597     3.35e+08  C20 -27, C22 +2, S22 -0
background 1383 kg/m^3 (bulk 1594); makes most of: the component's share of each coefficient in units of its 1-sigma

Why each component is where it is, and dense or light:

  • The light core (−950 ± 370 kg/m³, 54 m toward −x, 430 kg/m³ in all) makes nearly all of the change of C¯22 (−93σ): mass missing on the x-axis is the same, in degree 2, as mass added along y. Being on the −x side, it moves the center of mass toward +x.
  • The dense torus (+816 ± 66 kg/m³) puts mass in the equatorial plane: J2 higher (−68σ in C¯20).
  • The dense crust (+2210 ± 350 kg/m³, about 2 m thick: 3600 kg/m³) adds to J2 (−27σ) and, with the torus, carries the larger moments: mass outward.

5. The solutions side by side#

Output
solution (AIC rank)                                         moved (% M)          excess at (m)         deficit at (m)
1. core, placed; torus; layer                                      5.90              [6 -1 -1]             [-14 -1 2]
3. point masses (2674, sensitivity weighting)                     10.78               [2 -0 0]               [-1 0 0]
4. search: core, torus (radii, axis), layer; 0 masses              6.67              [7 -0 10]            [-13 -1 -4]
6. sectors 2 x 4 x 8                                               9.12               [13 3 0]               [2 2 -1]

correlation of the cells of each pair:
           1     3     4     6
     1  1.00  0.12  0.62  0.23
     3  0.12  1.00  0.22  0.47
     4  0.62  0.22  1.00  0.37
     6  0.23  0.47  0.37  1.00

moved: the mass above the bulk density M/V (equal to the mass below it), in 8 m cells; excess at, deficit at: where that mass is centered, from the center of figure.

All four make the interior lighter and the outer part denser, and move more mass than in any other package (5.9% to 10.8% of M): what the larger moments say. The model with components and the search's model are alike (correlation 0.62): a light core toward −x (their deficit centered 13 and 14 m toward −x), a dense ring in the equatorial plane around it and a dense crust. The point masses and the sector grid (correlation 0.47 with each other, 0.12 to 0.37 with the models with components) keep the light part at the center of figure, the point masses as a narrow column along the spin axis, the sector grid as its inner sectors, and make the outer part denser toward ±y, which C¯22 asks for. Light inside and dense outside is common to all; that the light part is off center toward −x, as the 3σ center-of-mass offset suggests, comes from the models with components only.

6. Independent check: the GRASS surface point#

Output
surface point [85.4 7.5 12.0] m; every model consistent with the coefficients and inertia, and the best of each kind
                                                                  U (m^2/s^2)    |a| (m/s^2)   |a| vs %  angle deg
given                                                            2.329658e-03   3.176463e-05      0.000      0.000
homogeneous                                                      2.303306e-03   3.119500e-05     -1.793      2.638
1. point masses (2674, sensitivity weighting)                    2.303906e-03   3.126095e-05     -1.586      2.584
2. core, placed; torus; layer                                    2.369193e-03   3.306649e-05      4.098      3.002
3. point masses (2674, equal weighting)                          2.315576e-03   3.178047e-05      0.050      2.526
4. sectors 2 x 4 x 8                                             2.326433e-03   3.205818e-05      0.924      2.644
5. search: core, torus (radii, axis), layer; 0 masses            2.380418e-03   3.300662e-05      3.910      3.727
6. core, placed; torus (height, axis); layer                     2.380386e-03   3.390141e-05      6.727      2.665

The surface point is 86 m toward +x. Constant density predicts 1.8% too little acceleration there and 2.6° off in direction. The smoothed solutions predict the size best (point masses with equal weighting +0.05%, sector grid +0.9%); the models with a light core and a dense crust give +3.9% to +6.7%: their crust is too dense near this point. Every solution stays 2.5° to 3.7° off in direction, as constant density is (2.6°): the coefficients and the moments do not constrain the material near the lander, and on DATA6 the surface point does not confirm the best model by AIC.

Every solution reproduces degree 2 of ROB's exact values (99–100%) and none reproduces degree 3 (negative fractions): the true interior has structure at those scales that a model fitted to degree 2 and the moments cannot know. With better measurements the model would have to be extended; at the Hera precision it is truncated at degree 2.

8. Details#

Reference

API reference

The supported interface of SBTK: every function in the namespace packages below, generated from the help text and arguments block of its source file. Functions are called by their full name, sbtk.<package>.<function>. Arguments have no default values except where the Default column states one (three functions). Structures passed between functions are described in Data structures; error identifiers in Error identifiers. Helper functions in sbtk.internal are not part of the supported interface and are listed separately in Internal functions.

sbtk.shape.reduce#

A shape model with fewer facets, checked to stay closed, outward and star-shaped.

Syntax

MATLAB
small = sbtk.shape.reduce(shape, n_facets)

Arguments

NameSizeClassUnitDefaultDescription

Outputs

Description

Uses MATLAB's reducepatch. Gravity coefficients to degree 4 or so need far fewer facets than a high-resolution shape model has; check what the reduction changes by comparing sbtk.shape.properties (volume, centroid) and the homogeneous-body coefficients of both (tools/make_reduced_shapes.m does both). Errors if the reduced surface is not closed, not ordered outward, or not star-shaped about its centroid. Save it with sbtk.shape.write_obj.

MATLAB, from the help text
