sbtk.shape.reduce_spc#

Every step-th grid point of an SPC shape model: the same surface, sampled step times coarser.

Syntax

MATLAB
small = sbtk.shape.reduce_spc(shape, step)

Arguments

NameSizeClassUnitDefaultDescription
shape1 × 1structrequiredan SPC (stereophotoclinometry) shape model in its grid order, as in the DART g_<sampling>_spc_obj_<body>_... OBJ files: 6 cube faces of (q+1) x (q+1) vertices each, the first index fastest, 12 q^2 triangles Fields: shape.
stepscalardoublerequireda divisor of q, e.g. 8 Validation: mustBeInteger, mustBePositive.

Outputs

NameDescription
small12 (q/step)^2 facets and 6 (q/step)^2 + 2 vertices: the grid points (i, j) with i and j multiples of step, triangulated like the original (diagonal from (i, j) to (i+1, j+1)), the copies along the cube edges merged. A cell whose triangles would face the body's center (a steep slope seen almost edge on, e.g. 1 of 24,576 cells of Dimorphos v004 at step 8) is split along its other diagonal; no point moves. Fields: shape.

Description

The grid is radial (one surface point per direction from the body's center), so the result stays star-shaped about the center, unlike a general mesh reduction (sbtk.shape.reduce). Each cube face's triangles are ordered outward.

Example

MATLAB, from the help text
big   = sbtk.shape.load("g_00243mm_spc_obj_dimo_0000n00000_v004.obj", "km");   % q = 512
small = sbtk.shape.reduce_spc(big, 8);                                         % q = 64, 49,152 facets
sbtk.shape.write_obj(small, "g_00243mm_spc_obj_dimo_0000n00000_v004_every8.obj");

Related functions

sbtk.body.to_frame#

A body with its shape model in another frame: x' = (x - origin_km) * axes.

Syntax

MATLAB
body = sbtk.body.to_frame(body, origin_km, axes, shape_name)

Arguments

NameSizeClassUnitDefaultDescription
body1 × 1structrequiredfrom sbtk.body.create or sbtk.body.from_mass Fields: body.
origin_km1 × 3doublekmrequiredorigin of the new frame in the current frame [km]; [0 0 0] keeps the origin Validation: mustBeFinite.
axes3 × 3doublerequired3 x 3 rotation, columns: the new axes as unit vectors in the current frame, e.g. cf.axes of sbtk.gravity.center_of_mass_frame; eye(3) keeps the axes Validation: mustBeFinite.
shape_name1 × 1stringrequiredname of the transformed shape model; an exchange package writes it as <data set>_<shape_name>.obj

Outputs

NameDescription
bodyfrom sbtk.body.create or sbtk.body.from_mass Fields: body.

Description

The vertices become (v - origin_km)*axes; the mass, reference radius and name of the body are kept, and the center of figure moves with the shape. shape.source keeps the name of the original file (not its path, which a package must not carry), and shape.frame_origin_km and shape.frame_axes give the frame relative to that file, combined over successive changes of frame: vertices = (file vertices - frame_origin_km)*frame_axes. An exchange package states them in conventions.txt. Use the same origin_km and axes for the measurements (sbtk.data.to_frame) and the interior or true model (sbtk.interior.to_frame).

Example

MATLAB fragment from the help text. Uses variables defined by earlier calls: truth, body.

sbtk.interior.align_with_spin_axis#

Set the axis of components along the axis of the largest moment of the whole model.

Syntax

MATLAB
[interior, axis_dir, iterations] = sbtk.interior.align_with_spin_axis(body, interior, names, tol_deg, max_iter)

Arguments

NameSizeClassUnitDefaultDescription
body1 × 1structrequiredthe body Fields: body.
interior1 × 1structrequiredfrom sbtk.interior.create Fields: interior.
names1 × anystringrequiredthe components to align (string array; tori, ellipsoids or sectors), e.g. "torus"; strings(1, 0) for none
tol_degscalardoubledegrequiredconvergence: the axis moves by at most this angle in the last iteration [deg] Validation: mustBePositive.
max_iterscalardoublerequiredlargest number of iterations (sbtk:iteration:notConverged beyond it) Validation: mustBeInteger, mustBePositive.

Outputs

NameDescription
interiorfrom sbtk.interior.create Fields: interior.
axis_dir1 x 3 axis of the largest moment of the aligned interior, in the frame of the shape model (pointing to +z's side)
iterationsnumber of simulations made

Description

A body in principal-axis rotation spins about its axis of the largest moment, so a component that formed about the spin axis, such as an equatorial torus, lies about that axis. The axis depends on every component, the aligned ones included, so the alignment is a fixed-point iteration (sbtk.internal.fixed_point): simulate to degree 2, take the axis of the largest moment (sbtk.gravity.center_of_mass_frame), turn the named components to it (sbtk.interior.set_axis), repeat. Each iteration is one simulation; the axis usually settles to 0.01 deg in 2 to 4.

Example

MATLAB fragment from the help text. Uses variables defined by earlier calls: body, core.
t = sbtk.interior.torus("torus", 0.370, 0.055, 0, -500);
t.center_km = body.centroid_km;
interior = sbtk.interior.create([core, t], sbtk.interior.no_random_field());
[interior, axis_dir] = sbtk.interior.align_with_spin_axis(body, interior, "torus", 0.01, 20);
fprintf('axis %.2f deg from the shape-model z-axis\n', acosd(axis_dir(3)));

sbtk.interior.sphere_grid#

Small spheres on a cubic grid filling the body (mass concentrations, a model without assumed structure).

Syntax

MATLAB
components = sbtk.interior.sphere_grid(body, spacing_km, radius_km)

Arguments

NameSizeClassUnitDefaultDescription
body1 × 1structrequiredfrom sbtk.body.create Fields: body.
spacing_kmscalardoublekmrequiredgrid spacing [km]; the grid is centered on the center of figure Validation: mustBePositive.
radius_kmscalardoublekmrequiredradius of each sphere [km]; a sphere entirely inside the body is an exact point mass of its volume times its relative density Validation: mustBePositive.

Outputs

NameDescription
componentsThe spheres, one per grid point inside the body (component array). Fields: component.

Description

One sphere per grid point whose sphere lies inside the body (with a margin of one radius), named 'm<k>', drho_kgm3 = 0. With radius_km well below spacing_km the spheres are point masses on the grid, the classic mass-concentration (mascon) model: a density anomaly drho in sphere k carries the mass drho*4/3*pi*r^3, which the grid cell around it (spacing^3) represents. Thousands of them need regularization (sbtk.invert.choose_regularization), and the data determine only a few combinations of them: read the estimate as where the anomaly is concentrated, not as a density map.

Example

MATLAB fragment from the help text. Uses variables defined by earlier calls: body, obs, an.
grid = sbtk.interior.sphere_grid(body, 0.040, 0.005);           % Didymos: about 3,000 points
sg   = sbtk.interpret.signatures(sbtk.interpret.anomaly(obs, body, 5), body, grid, an.labels);

sbtk.interior.to_frame#

An interior or a true model in another frame: x' = (x - origin_km) * axes.

Syntax

MATLAB
model = sbtk.interior.to_frame(model, origin_km, axes)

Arguments

NameSizeClassUnitDefaultDescription
model1 × 1structrequiredan interior (sbtk.interior.create) or a true model (truth from sbtk.data.simulate)
origin_km1 × 3doublekmrequiredorigin of the new frame in the current frame [km]; [0 0 0] keeps the origin Validation: mustBeFinite.
axes3 × 3doublerequired3 x 3 rotation, columns: the new axes as unit vectors in the current frame, e.g. cf.axes of sbtk.gravity.center_of_mass_frame; eye(3) keeps the axes Validation: mustBeFinite.

Outputs

NameDescription
modelan interior (sbtk.interior.create) or a true model (truth from sbtk.data.simulate)

Description

Every position is transformed as x' = (x - origin_km)*axes and every direction as d' = d*axes: the centers of spheres, ellipsoids and tori, the axes of ellipsoids, tori and sectors (c.axes), the random field, and for a true model origin_km and com_km. Its coefficients are rotated (exact, sbtk.internal.sh_rotation) and its inertia elements become axes'*I*axes; both stay about the same point. The density at every point of the body is unchanged, so the model, the body from sbtk.body.to_frame and the measurements from sbtk.data.to_frame (same origin_km and axes) describe the same body in the new frame: simulating, gridding, plotting and comparing there gives the transformed results. An inversion result cannot be transformed: transform the measurements and the body and invert in the new frame.

Example

MATLAB fragment from the help text. Uses variables defined by earlier calls: body, interior.
[exact, truth] = sbtk.data.simulate(body, interior, 4, "T1");
spin  = sbtk.gravity.center_of_mass_frame(truth, body, "spin");   % origin: center of mass; z: largest moment
truth_s = sbtk.interior.to_frame(truth, spin.com_km, spin.axes);
body_s  = sbtk.body.to_frame(body, spin.com_km, spin.axes, "didymos_com_spin_axes");
grid = sbtk.exchange.density_grid(body_s, truth_s, 0.020);         % the grid in the new frame

sbtk.gravity.center_of_mass_frame#

A gravity field about its center of mass, in the shape-model, spin or principal axes.

Syntax

MATLAB
cf = sbtk.gravity.center_of_mass_frame(set, body, axes)

Arguments

NameSizeClassUnitDefaultDescription
set1 × 1structrequiredthe field: a measurement set (sbtk.data.simulate, sbtk.exchange.read_data, sbtk.exchange.read_shadr, ...), a true model (truth from sbtk.data.simulate) or an inversion result (fit from sbtk.invert.run: the field of the fitted model)
body1 × 1structrequiredthe body: the shape model for a fitted model, the reference radius for a true model or a fitted model Fields: body.
axes1 × 1stringrequired"shape": the axes of the shape-model frame; "spin": z along the axis of the largest moment of the field (the spin axis of a body in principal-axis rotation), x the shape-model x-axis projected onto the plane normal to it, y = z x x: the frame of body-fixed radio-science fields such as the OSIRIS-REx field of Bennu, with C21 = S21 = 0 and S22 not 0; "principal": the principal axes of inertia of the field (x the axis of the smallest moment, z of the largest, each pointing to the positive side of the shape-model axis nearest to it, right-handed), with C21 = S21 = S22 = 0 Validation: mustBeMember(axes, ["shape", "spin", "principal"]).

Outputs

NameDescription
cfThe field about its center of mass in the chosen axes, with its principal axes and moments. Fields: cf.

Description

cf.labels1 x n names of the coefficients, 'C10' ... (degree 1 to cf.degree)
cf.coef1 x n fully normalized coefficients about the center of mass: degree 1 is 0; in spin axes C21 = S21 = 0, in principal axes C21 = S21 = S22 = 0
cf.sigma1 x n 1-sigma (NaN without uncertainties); degree 1: of the center of mass
cf.covn x n covariance (NaN without uncertainties)
cf.com_kmthe center of mass in the shape-model frame [km]
cf.axes3 x 3, columns: the axes of cf.coef as unit vectors in the shape-model axes (eye(3) for "shape"); sbtk.body.to_frame, sbtk.data.to_frame and sbtk.interior.to_frame take cf.com_km and cf.axes to express everything in the frame with the center of mass as origin and these axes
cf.principal3 x 3, columns: the principal axes (smallest, middle, largest moment) in the shape-model axes
cf.moments1 x 3 principal moments minus their mean, A <= B <= C, as I / (M R_ref^2) (the degree-2 field fixes the moments up to their trace)

cf.R_ref_km, cf.degree

Moving the expansion point to the center of mass makes degree 1 vanish: about a point O, C10, C11, S11 = (z, x, y of the center of mass - O)/(sqrt(3) R_ref). The translation of solid harmonics mixes lower degrees into higher ones (degree 2 into 3, ...), so all coefficients change; it is exact (sbtk.internal.sh_translation). Rotating the axes mixes the 2l+1 coefficients within each degree and leaves every degree's power unchanged; in the principal axes the degree-2 inertia tensor is diagonal, so C21 = S21 = S22 = 0 and C20 = (A + B - 2C)/(2 M R^2), C22 = (B - A)/(4 M R^2) (unnormalized). The rotation is exact too (sbtk.internal.sh_rotation). In the spin axes only the tilt of the axis of the largest moment is removed: C21 = S21 = 0, and the angle of the axis of the smallest moment from x is (1/2) atan2(S22, C22).

The center of mass: a true model's com_km; a fitted model's own center of mass (computed from its densities); for a measurement set, origin_km plus the offset its degree-1 coefficients give. A measurement set with coef_about 'origin' whose degree-1 coefficients put the center of mass more than 3 sigma from origin_km (more than 1 mm for exact values), e.g. a SHADR field about the shape-model origin, is moved to that center of mass; otherwise it is taken as about its center of mass already (its degree-1 values are then noise about zero). A set without degree-1 coefficients (e.g. sbtk.io.read_jpl_gravity) is taken as about its center of mass, origin_km; its degree-1 sigma is NaN. Moving a set and the principal axes need every coefficient of degree >= 2 up to the set's degree; a set that lacks some can be used only with axes "shape" and only if it is about its center of mass (missing coefficients are NaN).

The covariance is propagated through the translation and the rotation as linear maps; the uncertainty of the center of mass and of the principal axes themselves, which the data also determine, is not added.

Example

MATLAB fragment from the help text. Uses variables defined by earlier calls: body, interior.
[exact, truth] = sbtk.data.simulate(body, interior, 4, "T1");
cs = sbtk.gravity.center_of_mass_frame(truth, body, "shape");       % degree 1 = 0
cz = sbtk.gravity.center_of_mass_frame(truth, body, "spin");        % and C21 = S21 = 0

sbtk.gravity.component_integrals#

Integrals over one component per unit density, clipped to the body.

Syntax

MATLAB
I = sbtk.gravity.component_integrals(geo, c)

Arguments

NameSizeClassUnitDefaultDescription
geo1 × 1structrequiredGeometry from sbtk.gravity.geometry: the expansion origin and degree of the integrals. Fields: geo.
c1 × 1structrequiredOne component. Fields: component.

Outputs

NameDescription
IIntegrals of the part of the component inside the body, per unit density. Fields: integrals.

Description

I.U1 x (L+1)^2 int (r/R)^l Ybar_lm dV (packed as geo.pk) [km^3]
I.Vvolume [km^3]
I.m1first moment [km^4]
I.Qsecond moments [xx yy zz xy xz yz] [km^5]

all about geo.origin_km and limited to the body.

A sphere entirely inside the body is an exact point mass. Every other component is integrated ray by ray: each interval of a sub-ray inside the component, between scaled facets s_a and s_b, adds its exact cone-scaling integrals (see sbtk.gravity.geometry). Layers and sectors give the interval directly; for spheres, ellipsoids and tori the crossings of each ray with their surface are the real roots of a quadratic (sphere, ellipsoid) or quartic (torus) in the distance along the ray, so a ray may cross a component any number of times and the integrals change smoothly with the component's geometry.

Example

MATLAB fragment from the help text. Uses variables defined by earlier calls: body.
geo = sbtk.gravity.geometry(body, [0 0 0], 4);
I = sbtk.gravity.component_integrals(geo, sbtk.interior.sphere("core", [0 0 0], 0.170, 0));
fprintf('volume inside the body %.4f km^3\n', I.V);

sbtk.gravity.field_at#

Gravitational potential and acceleration of a model of the body at given points.

Syntax

MATLAB
f = sbtk.gravity.field_at(body, model, points_km, grid_km)

Arguments

NameSizeClassUnitDefaultDescription
body1 × 1structrequiredfrom sbtk.body.create Fields: body.
model1 × 1structrequireda true model (sbtk.data.simulate) or a fit (sbtk.invert.run): rho_bg_kgm3, components, random_field
points_kmany × 3doublekmrequiredn x 3 points in the frame of the shape model [km]: outside, on or inside the body Validation: mustBeFinite.
grid_kmscalardoublekmrequiredcell edge [km] of the grid that carries the departures from the background density (components, random field); not used for a homogeneous model Validation: mustBePositive.

Outputs

NameDescription
fPotential U_km2_s2 (n x 1) and acceleration acc_km_s2 (n x 3) at the points, and method, how they were computed.

Description

The background density fills the shape model, and its field is exact (sbtk.gravity.polyhedron). A sphere entirely inside the body is a point mass outside it and a uniform ball inside it, also exact (a grid of point masses, sbtk.interior.sphere_grid, as well as a core). The other departures from the background (components that reach the surface, layers, tori, sectors, a random field) are taken at the cell centers of the density grid of the model (sbtk.exchange.density_grid), each cell a uniform cube (sbtk.internal.prism_field): the cubes follow the boundaries of these components and of the body only to within a cell, so a finer grid gives a more accurate field near them.

f.U_km2_s2n x 1 potential [km^2/s^2], positive: U = G integral rho / |r - r'| dV
f.acc_km_s2n x 3 acceleration [km/s^2], the gradient of U (the rotation of the body is not included)
f.methodthe method, for the file header: "Werner and Scheeres 1997", and the cubes for a model that is not homogeneous

Example

MATLAB fragment from the help text. Uses variables defined by earlier calls: body.
[~, truth] = sbtk.data.simulate(body, sbtk.interior.create(sbtk.interior.no_components()), 4, "homogeneous");
f = sbtk.gravity.field_at(body, truth, [0.5 0 0; 0 0.6 0], 0.020);

sbtk.gravity.geometry#

Facet-cone geometry of a body about an expansion origin (the integration workspace).

Syntax

MATLAB
geo = sbtk.gravity.geometry(body, origin_km, degree)

Arguments

NameSizeClassUnitDefaultDescription
body1 × 1structrequiredfrom sbtk.body.create Fields: body.
origin_km1 × 3doublekmrequiredexpansion origin in shape-model coordinates [km] (1x3). Gravity coefficients, first moments and inertia are all about this point; layers and sectors are measured along rays from it. Validation: mustBeFinite.
degreescalardoublerequiredhighest spherical-harmonic degree (0 when only volumes, inertia or densities are needed: much faster) Validation: mustBeInteger, mustBeNonnegative.

Outputs

NameDescription
geoThe facet-cone geometry and integrals. Fields: geo.

Description

The body is the union of tetrahedral cones with apex at the origin and a surface facet as base. For every cone geo stores, per unit density,

Tspherical-harmonic integrals int (r/R)^l Ybar_lm dV [km^3] (nf x (L+1)^2)
Vvolume [km^3], m1 first moment [km^4],
Qsecond moments [xx yy zz xy xz yz] [km^5]

(T from the polyhedral kernel sbtk.internal.ComputePolyhedralCSBar_mex). Shrinking a cone about its apex by s multiplies r^l dV by s^(l+3), so the portion of a cone between the scaled facets s_a and s_b contributes exactly T (s_b^(l+3) - s_a^(l+3)), V (s_b^3 - s_a^3), m1 (s_b^4 - s_a^4), Q (s_b^5 - s_a^5). Interior components are described by such radial intervals along 9 sub-rays of every cone (sbtk.gravity.component_integrals).

geo fields (km units throughout)

  body, origin_km, degree, R_ref_km, pk (coefficient packing, sbtk.internal.sh_packing)
  nf, K                 number of facets, sub-rays per facet (9)
  faces, verts          mesh with vertices relative to origin_km
  D, E, F, det6, EF, FD, DE    facet corners, 6 x cone volumes, edge cross products
  T, V, m1, Q           per-cone integrals (above)
  U_body, V_body, m1_body, Q_body   whole-body sums
  ray_t, ray_dir        sub-ray surface distances [km] and unit directions (nf*K rows)

Didymos (49,152 facets): about 1 s at degree 4.

Every facet should face away from the origin (the shape star-shaped about it). Facets that face it are accepted when their cones hold less than 1e-6 of the volume: small overhangs of a high-resolution model, such as the 0.243 m Dimorphos model seen from a point a few meters from its center. Their cones count with their sign (negative), which is exact for the body and leaves an error of the order of their volume in layers and sectors. Otherwise sbtk:gravity:notStarShaped.

Example

MATLAB fragment from the help text. Uses variables defined by earlier calls: body.
geo = sbtk.gravity.geometry(body, body.centroid_km, 4);
fprintf('%d facets, volume %.4f km^3\n', geo.nf, geo.V_body);

sbtk.gravity.polyhedron#

Potential and acceleration of a homogeneous polyhedron, exact (Werner & Scheeres 1997).

Syntax

MATLAB
[U, acc] = sbtk.gravity.polyhedron(shape, density_kgm3, points_km)

Arguments

NameSizeClassUnitDefaultDescription
shape1 × 1structrequiredfrom sbtk.shape.load (a closed mesh, triangles ordered so that their normals point outward) Fields: shape.
density_kgm3scalardoublekg/m³requireduniform density [kg/m^3] Validation: mustBeFinite.
points_kmany × 3doublekmrequiredn x 3 points in the frame of the shape model [km]: outside, on or inside the body Validation: mustBeFinite.

Outputs

NameDescription
Un x 1 gravitational potential [km^2/s^2], positive: U = G integral rho / |r - r'| dV
accn x 3 gravitational acceleration [km/s^2], the gradient of U (no rotation)

Description

The closed form of Werner and Scheeres (1997, Celestial Mechanics and Dynamical Astronomy 65, 313-344), with r_e and r_f the vectors from the point to an edge and to a face, n_f the outward normal of the face and n_fe that of its edge in the plane of the face:

acc = -G rho sum_f sum_(e of f) n_f (n_fe . r_e) L_e + G rho sum_f n_f (r_f . n_f) w_f

where L_e = ln((a + b + e)/(a + b - e)) for an edge of length e whose ends are at distances a and b, and w_f is the signed solid angle of the face seen from the point (the sum of w_f is 4 pi inside the body and 0 outside). Each edge enters once for each of its two faces, which is the edge dyad of the paper. The expressions hold on the surface too. On an edge or a vertex L_e is infinite, but both factors in front of it are zero there and the terms go to zero (as d^2 ln d with the distance d from the edge), so they are taken as zero. About 1 s per point for 3 million facets.

Example

MATLAB, from the help text
shape = sbtk.shape.bundled("didymos_highres");
[U, acc] = sbtk.gravity.polyhedron(shape, 2600, [0.5 0 0]);        % 500 m along x
fprintf('U %.6e km^2/s^2, |acc| %.6e km/s^2\n', U, norm(acc));

sbtk.data.add_center_of_mass#

Add degree-1 coefficients that place the center of mass at a given point.

Syntax

MATLAB
obs = sbtk.data.add_center_of_mass(obs, com_km, sigma_km)

Arguments

NameSizeClassUnitDefaultDescription
obs1 × 1structrequiredThe measurement set, without degree-1 coefficients. Fields: obs.
com_km1 × 3doublekmrequiredcenter of mass in shape-model coordinates [km]; obs.origin_km when the coefficients are expanded about the center of mass (degree 1 = 0) Validation: mustBeFinite.
sigma_kmscalardoublekmrequired1-sigma uncertainty of each component of the center of mass [km] Validation: mustBePositive.

Outputs

NameDescription
obsThe measurement set with C10, C11 and S11 added and coef_about set to 'center_of_mass'. Fields: obs.

Description

With fully normalized coefficients, C10 = dz/(sqrt(3) R), C11 = dx/(sqrt(3) R), S11 = dy/(sqrt(3) R), with [dx dy dz] = com_km - obs.origin_km. In an inversion these terms constrain the first moment of the density, which sphere positions (estimate_position) can satisfy. Errors if the data already have degree-1 terms.

obs = sbtk.data.add_center_of_mass(obs, [0 0 0], 0.001);

sbtk.data.add_libration#

Add a measured libration ratio (B - A)/C.

Syntax

MATLAB
obs = sbtk.data.add_libration(obs, ratio, ratio_sigma, Izz_norm)

Arguments

NameSizeClassUnitDefaultDescription
obs1 × 1structrequiredThe measurement set; it must contain C22 and S22. Fields: obs.
ratioscalardoublerequiredmeasured (B - A)/C: A <= B are the principal moments of inertia about the axes in the xy-plane (the long and intermediate axes of a body spinning about z) and C = Izz. This is what the libration of a synchronously rotating body depends on (amplitude 2e/(3 ratio - 1) for forced libration in an orbit of eccentricity e). Validation: mustBeFinite.
ratio_sigmascalardoublerequiredits 1-sigma Validation: mustBePositive.
Izz_normscalardoubleM R_ref²requiredIzz / (M R_ref^2) used to scale the uncertainty (a homogeneous-body value is accurate enough) Validation: mustBePositive.

Outputs

NameDescription
obsThe measurement set with the libration row added. Fields: obs.

Description

The principal axes need not be the shape-model axes: their direction in the xy-plane comes from the measured C22 and S22 of obs (which must have them), and the measurement is stored as the linear row

    cos(2a) (Iyy - Ixx) + sin(2a) 2 Ixy - ratio Izz = 0 +- ratio_sigma Izz_norm,

(B - A) written with the principal-axis angle a (sbtk.internal.libration_weights). Together with C22 and S22, which give B - A, the ratio measures C to a relative precision of about ratio_sigma/ratio.

sbtk.data.expand_about#

Measurements with the gravity field and the inertia about another point.

Syntax

MATLAB
obs = sbtk.data.expand_about(obs, point_km)

Arguments

NameSizeClassUnitDefaultDescription
obs1 × 1structrequireda measurement set whose coefficients are about obs.origin_km (coef_about = 'origin', as those of sbtk.data.simulate), with every coefficient of degree 1 to obs.degree and with moment-of-inertia element rows only (select them with sbtk.data.select_moi: the libration ratio is defined about the center of mass) Fields: obs.
point_km1 × 3doublekmrequiredthe new expansion point in the frame of the shape model [km]; [0 0 0] is the origin of the shape model file Validation: mustBeFinite.

Outputs

NameDescription
obsa measurement set whose coefficients are about obs.origin_km (coef_about = 'origin', as those of sbtk.data.simulate), with every coefficient of degree 1 to obs.degree and with moment-of-inertia element rows only (select them with sbtk.data.select_moi: the libration ratio is defined about the center of mass) Fields: obs.

Description

The coefficients are expanded about point_km exactly (sbtk.internal.sh_translation), with their covariance; degree 1 then gives the center of mass relative to point_km. The inertia elements are moved to point_km by the parallel-axis theorem, from the center of mass that degree 1 gives: I(P) = I(C) + M (|b|^2 delta_ij - b_i b_j), b = P - C. A package written from a set about [0 0 0] gives the gravity field, degree 1 included, and the moments of inertia about the origin of the shape model file (sbtk.exchange.write_data).

Example

MATLAB fragment from the help text. Uses variables defined by earlier calls: body, interior.
[exact, truth] = sbtk.data.simulate(body, interior, 6, "T1");
raw = sbtk.data.expand_about(sbtk.data.select_moi(exact, ["Ixx" "Iyy" "Izz"]), [0 0 0]);

sbtk.data.libration_ratio_from_amplitude#

(B - A)/C from the forced libration of a synchronous satellite.

Syntax

MATLAB
[ratio, ratio_sigma] = sbtk.data.libration_ratio_from_amplitude(amplitude_deg, amplitude_sigma_deg, e, e_sigma)

Arguments

NameSizeClassUnitDefaultDescription
amplitude_degscalardoubledegrequiredsigned amplitude G of the forced libration gamma = G sin(M) [deg]: gamma is the angle of the long axis from the direction to the primary, M the mean anomaly. G < 0 (the long axis lags behind the primary direction while the satellite moves fastest) for (B - A)/C < 1/3, which covers elongations up to about 1.4 : 1; G > 0 above that. Validation: mustBeNonzero.
amplitude_sigma_degscalardoubledegrequired1-sigma of G [deg] Validation: mustBeNonnegative.
escalardoublerequiredorbital eccentricity and its 1-sigma Validation: mustBeInRange(e, 0, 1, 'exclude-upper').
e_sigmascalardoublerequiredorbital eccentricity and its 1-sigma Validation: mustBeNonnegative.

Outputs

NameDescription
ratio(B - A)/C (principal moments, see sbtk.data.add_libration) and its 1-sigma, from first-order error propagation
ratio_sigma(B - A)/C (principal moments, see sbtk.data.add_libration) and its 1-sigma, from first-order error propagation

Description

Planar forced libration in a Keplerian orbit about a point-mass primary, to first order in e: gamma'' + 3 n^2 ratio gamma = 2 e n^2 sin(M), so G = 2e/(3 ratio - 1) and ratio = (1 + 2e/G)/3. Free libration, the primary's oblateness and the mutual dynamics of a binary are not included. The sensitivity grows near ratio = 1/3, where the free libration period equals the orbital period: an elongated body gives a large amplitude and a precise ratio, a nearly axisymmetric one a small amplitude that depends little on the ratio.

Example

MATLAB fragment from the help text. Uses variables defined by earlier calls: obs.
% amplitude -12 +- 0.2 deg, e = 0.027 +- 0.001: (B - A)/C = 0.247 +- 0.0035 (1.4%)
[k, sk] = sbtk.data.libration_ratio_from_amplitude(-12, 0.2, 0.027, 0.001);
obs = sbtk.data.add_libration(obs, k, sk, 0.39);
% a nearly axisymmetric body: -4.0 +- 0.2 deg gives 0.075 +- 0.016 (21%)

Related functions

Mentioned in the help text

sbtk.data.set_uncertainties#

Give measurements a 1-sigma uncertainty per degree and per inertia quantity.

Syntax

MATLAB
obs = sbtk.data.set_uncertainties(obs, unc)

Arguments

NameSizeClassUnitDefaultDescription
obs1 × 1structrequiredmeasurements, e.g. the exact values from sbtk.data.simulate, which have none Fields: obs.
unc1 × 1structrequiredfrom sbtk.data.uncertainties Fields: unc.

Outputs

NameDescription
obsmeasurements, e.g. the exact values from sbtk.data.simulate, which have none Fields: obs.

Description

Every gravity coefficient of degree l gets the 1-sigma unc.coef_sigma_by_degree(l), and the coefficient covariance becomes diagonal. Every inertia element (Ixx, Iyy, Izz, Ixy, Ixz, Iyz) gets unc.moi_sigma. The libration row gets unc.libration_sigma times the Izz / (M R_ref^2) of the Izz row (set the uncertainties before sbtk.data.select_moi removes that row). Rows with other labels (sbtk.data.add_moi_row) keep their sigma. The values themselves do not change; sbtk.data.add_noise then draws noise from these uncertainties.

For other uncertainties: sbtk.data.use_uncertainties (those of another data set), sbtk.data.set_covariance (a full coefficient covariance), sbtk.data.set_moi_sigma (inertia rows by label).

Example

MATLAB fragment from the help text. Uses variables defined by earlier calls: body, interior.

obs = sbtk.data.add_noise(sbtk.data.set_uncertainties(exact, unc), 1);

sbtk.data.simulate#

True model of an interior and its exact gravity coefficients and moments of inertia.

Syntax

MATLAB
[exact, truth, geo] = sbtk.data.simulate(body, interior, degree, name)

Arguments

NameSizeClassUnitDefaultDescription
body1 × 1structrequiredfrom sbtk.body.create (shape, total mass, reference radius) Fields: body.
interior1 × 1structrequiredfrom sbtk.interior.create (components + random field) Fields: interior.
degreescalardoublerequiredmaximum degree of the gravity coefficients Validation: mustBeInteger, mustBePositive.
name1 × 1stringrequiredname of the data set, e.g. "didymos_T1"

Outputs

NameDescription
exactthe exact values as a measurement set (docs/data_formats.md), without uncertainties (coef_cov and every inertia sigma are NaN); for Didymos to degree 4: coef_labels 24 x 1 {'C10';'C11';'S11';'C20';...}, coef 24 x 1, moi 7 rows (Ixx Iyy Izz Ixy Ixz Iyz, I/(M R_ref^2); libration: (B - A)/C with principal moments, see sbtk.data.add_libration), origin_km the center of mass the coefficients are about [km] Fields: obs.
truththe true model (rho_bg_kgm3, components, random_field, origin_km, exact values) Fields: truth.
geogeometry about the center of mass (for plots and comparisons) Fields: geo.

Description

The gravity field and inertia are expanded about the center of mass. Layers and sectors are defined along rays from the expansion origin, so the interior, and with it the center of mass, depend on the origin: the geometry is rebuilt about the center of mass until it moves by less than 1 mm (sbtk.internal.fixed_point, at most 50 times; sbtk:iteration:notConverged otherwise). No measurement uncertainties are involved: the values are exact.

To make measurements of the true model, give the exact values uncertainties (sbtk.data.set_uncertainties: one 1-sigma per degree and per inertia quantity; sbtk.data.use_uncertainties: those of another data set; sbtk.data.set_covariance, sbtk.data.set_moi_sigma) and draw noise from them (sbtk.data.add_noise).

Errors when the density is negative anywhere.

Example

MATLAB, from the help text
body = sbtk.body.from_mass("Didymos", sbtk.shape.bundled("didymos"), 5.273e11, 0.43);
interior = sbtk.interior.create(sbtk.interior.sphere("core", [0 0 0], 0.170, +450));
[exact, truth] = sbtk.data.simulate(body, interior, 4, "T1");          % the true model
unc = sbtk.data.uncertainties([sbtk.units.offset_to_degree1(0.002, 0.43), 1e-4, 2e-4, 4e-4], 2e-3, 0.02);
obs = sbtk.data.add_noise(sbtk.data.set_uncertainties(exact, unc), 1);  % measurements of it

sbtk.data.to_frame#

A measurement set in another frame: x' = (x - origin_km) * axes.

Syntax

MATLAB
obs = sbtk.data.to_frame(obs, origin_km, axes)

Arguments

NameSizeClassUnitDefaultDescription
obs1 × 1structrequireda measurement set; to change the axes it must have all six inertia elements without uncertainties, as the exact values of sbtk.data.simulate have (or no inertia rows): a measurement is made in the frame it is reported in, so transform the exact values, then give uncertainties, select and add noise Fields: obs.
origin_km1 × 3doublekmrequiredorigin of the new frame in the current frame [km]; [0 0 0] keeps the origin Validation: mustBeFinite.
axes3 × 3doublerequired3 x 3 rotation, columns: the new axes as unit vectors in the current frame, e.g. cf.axes of sbtk.gravity.center_of_mass_frame; eye(3) keeps the axes Validation: mustBeFinite.

Outputs

NameDescription
obsa measurement set; to change the axes it must have all six inertia elements without uncertainties, as the exact values of sbtk.data.simulate have (or no inertia rows): a measurement is made in the frame it is reported in, so transform the exact values, then give uncertainties, select and add noise Fields: obs.

Description

origin_km becomes (origin_km - o)*axes and com_minus_cof_km becomes com_minus_cof_km*axes. The coefficients stay about the same point and are rotated degree by degree, with their covariance (exact, sbtk.internal.sh_rotation); every degree present must be complete. The inertia elements Ixx ... Iyz are recomputed as the elements in the new axes (axes'*I*axes); the libration row and libration_ratio use the new z-axis (C = Izz) and the principal axes in the new xy-plane; any other row keeps its meaning (its weights are transformed). A translation alone (axes = eye(3)) applies to any set. Use the same origin_km and axes for the body (sbtk.body.to_frame) and the interior or true model (sbtk.interior.to_frame).

Example

MATLAB fragment from the help text. Uses variables defined by earlier calls: truth, body, exact, unc.
spin    = sbtk.gravity.center_of_mass_frame(truth, body, "spin");
exact_s = sbtk.data.to_frame(exact, spin.com_km, spin.axes);      % C21 = S21 = 0
obs_s   = sbtk.data.add_noise(sbtk.data.set_uncertainties(exact_s, unc), 1);

sbtk.data.to_reduced_shape#

Measurements for a coarser version of the same shape model, for faster fits.

Syntax

MATLAB
[obs, reduced] = sbtk.data.to_reduced_shape(obs, body, shape)

Arguments

NameSizeClassUnitDefaultDescription
obs1 × 1structrequiredmeasurements of a body with the shape model of body (e.g. 3 million facets) Fields: obs.

Outputs

NameDescription

reducedthe coarser body (same mass and reference radius)

Description

The interior's part of the measurements depends on the shape only through the edge of the body, which the two models put within a few meters of each other, so fits on the coarse body give nearly the same densities as on the full one; the homogeneous part follows the facets and is replaced exactly. For the HLP6 Didymos model (1.165 m sampling, every 8th point) the replaced part is up to 1.5 sigma of the Hera radio-science precision at degree 2: without it, a fit on the coarse model would be biased. Check final results on the full model.

sbtk.data.use_uncertainties#

Give measurements the coefficient uncertainties of another data set (e.g. a precision file).

Syntax

MATLAB
obs = sbtk.data.use_uncertainties(obs, ref)

Arguments

NameSizeClassUnitDefaultDescription
obs1 × 1structrequiredmeasurements whose uncertainties are replaced (usually exact values from sbtk.data.simulate, before sbtk.data.add_noise) Fields: obs.
ref1 × 1structrequiredmeasurements holding the uncertainties to use, e.g. a precision file read with sbtk.exchange.read_shadr or sbtk.exchange.read_data Fields: ref.

Outputs

NameDescription
obsmeasurements whose uncertainties are replaced (usually exact values from sbtk.data.simulate, before sbtk.data.add_noise) Fields: obs.

Description

Every coefficient of obs that ref also has takes ref's variances and covariances; the others (e.g. degree 1 if ref has none) keep theirs and become uncorrelated with them (exact values from sbtk.data.simulate have none: give them with sbtk.data.set_uncertainties first). If ref is about another point than obs (ref.origin_km, e.g. a radio-science field about the center of mass for data about the origin of a shape model file), its covariance is first moved to obs.origin_km exactly, K' = T K T' (sbtk.internal.sh_translation): moving a field to another point mixes the degrees, so the uncertainty of degree 1 (the center of mass) enters the others; ref then needs every coefficient of degree 1 to its degree. If the reference radii differ, ref's covariance is converted to obs.R_ref_km: a coefficient of degree l scales by (R_ref / R_obs)^l. Moment-of-inertia uncertainties are not changed (sbtk.data.set_moi_sigma sets them).

Example

MATLAB fragment from the help text. Uses variables defined by earlier calls: body, interior.
shape = sbtk.shape.load("didymos_g_9309mm_spc_obj_0000n00000_v003.obj", "km");
prec  = sbtk.exchange.read_shadr("Didymos_gravity_fromRS.tab", "Didymos", shape, [0 0 0], 4);
[exact, truth] = sbtk.data.simulate(body, interior, 4, "didymos_T1");
exact = sbtk.data.use_uncertainties(exact, prec);      % every coefficient, degree 1 included
exact = sbtk.data.select_moi(exact, {});               % gravity only in this example
obs = sbtk.data.add_noise(exact, 1);

sbtk.invert.choose_regularization#

Tikhonov regularization parameter by the discrepancy principle.

Syntax

MATLAB
lambda = sbtk.invert.choose_regularization(prob)
prob.opts.regularization = lambda;  fit = sbtk.invert.run(prob);

Arguments

NameSizeClassUnitDefaultDescription
prob1 × 1structrequiredPrepared inversion; prob.opts.regularization is not used. Fields: prob.

Outputs

NameDescription
lambdaTikhonov parameter chosen by the discrepancy principle.

Description

The regularization term lambda * sum((drho_c / rho_mean)^2) damps the relative densities. Models with many components (a sector grid) or weak data need it to keep noise from producing large alternating densities. This returns the largest lambda for which chi^2 <= max(n, chi^2_min + sqrt(2n)), n measurements, chi^2_min the unregularized value: chi^2 may rise by about one standard deviation of its distribution. Bisection on log10(lambda) over [-2, 8] (9 solves, about 0.2 s with prob reused).

Example

MATLAB fragment from the help text. Uses variables defined by earlier calls: body, obs.
sectors = sbtk.interior.sector_grid([0 0.5 1], [-90 0 90], [-180 0 180]);
prob = sbtk.invert.setup(body, sectors, obs, sbtk.invert.options(background="bulk"));
prob.opts.regularization = sbtk.invert.choose_regularization(prob);
fit = sbtk.invert.run(prob);

sbtk.invert.predict#

A fitted model's values of every measurement of a set, including those it was not fitted to.

Syntax

MATLAB
pred = sbtk.invert.predict(fit, body, obs)

Arguments

NameSizeClassUnitDefaultDescription
fit1 × 1structrequiredfrom sbtk.invert.run, fitted to some of the coefficients of obs (for example after sbtk.data.select_coefficients) or to all of them Fields: fit.
body1 × 1structrequiredthe body of the fit Fields: body.
obs1 × 1structrequiredthe measurements with every coefficient to predict (and the inertia rows the fit used, fit.moi_labels) Fields: obs.

Outputs

NameDescription
predThe fitted model's values of every measurement of obs. Fields: pred.

Description

The fitted model (its components with their fitted geometry, background and relative densities) is set up for obs (sbtk.invert.setup) and evaluated: the same predictions as the fit for the measurements it was fitted to, and predictions for the others. For measurements about the center of mass (coef_about 'center_of_mass') the coefficients of degree >= 2 and the inertia are predicted about the model's own center of mass, as the fit does. The model must be about the same point as the fit: obs must give the same measured center of mass (the same degree-1 coefficients), so that layers and sectors are measured from the same point; otherwise sbtk:invert:predictOrigin. Comparing the predictions of coefficients left out of a fit with their measurements tests the model on data it was not fitted to.

pred.labels, pred.measured, pred.predicted, pred.sigma every measurement of obs

                (coefficients, then the inertia rows of the fit), its prediction, 1-sigma
pred.normalized_residual(predicted - measured)/sigma
pred.chi2, pred.n_obschi-square of every row (full covariance) and their number
pred.fittedlogical, one per row: the rows the fit was fitted to
pred.chi2_fitted, pred.n_fittedchi-square and number of those rows (with their covariance)
pred.chi2_other, pred.n_otherthe same for the other rows
pred.fit_labelsthe rows the fit was fitted to

pred.data_name, pred.body

Example

MATLAB fragment from the help text. Uses variables defined by earlier calls: obs, body, components.

fit  = sbtk.invert.solve(body, components, part, sbtk.invert.options(moi_labels={}));
pred = sbtk.invert.predict(fit, body, obs);
fprintf('fitted: chi2/n = %.2f; other coefficients: chi2/n = %.2f\n', ...
        pred.chi2_fitted/pred.n_fitted, pred.chi2_other/pred.n_other);

sbtk.invert.recenter#

Move one component so that the fitted model's center of mass matches the measured one.

Syntax

MATLAB
[prob, step_km] = sbtk.invert.recenter(prob, fit, name)

Arguments

NameSizeClassUnitDefaultDescription
prob1 × 1structrequiredfrom sbtk.invert.setup, with degree-1 coefficients among the measurements Fields: prob.
fit1 × 1structrequiredsbtk.invert.run(prob) Fields: fit.
name1 × 1stringrequiredthe component to move: a sphere, ellipsoid or torus

Outputs

NameDescription
probfrom sbtk.invert.setup, with degree-1 coefficients among the measurements Fields: prob.
step_km1 x 3 the move [km]

Description

Degree 1 is the first moment of the density: moving a component of relative density drho and volume V_c by s moves the model's center of mass by drho V_c s / M. The component is moved by

    s = M (measured center of mass - model center of mass) / (drho V_c),

which makes the model's degree 1 equal to the measured one at the fitted densities (for a sphere inside the body exactly, otherwise to first order), and its integrals and design-matrix column are updated (no new geometry). A sphere is kept inside the body. Fitting the densities again and repeating until the step is small solves the degree-1 equations for the position while the densities fit every measurement: a fixed-point iteration. Gauss-Newton on the position (estimate_position, sbtk.invert.run) fits the position to every measurement at once instead; this step is a starting point for it or a check on it.

Example

MATLAB fragment from the help text. Uses variables defined by earlier calls: body, components, obs, opts.
prob = sbtk.invert.setup(body, components, obs, opts);
for k = 1:10
    fit = sbtk.invert.run(prob);
    [prob, s] = sbtk.invert.recenter(prob, fit, "core");
    if norm(s) < 1e-4, break, end                        % 0.1 m
end
fit = sbtk.invert.run(prob);

Related functions

Mentioned in the help text
sbtk.invert.run, sbtk.invert.setup
Calls

Description

obs must have the same coefficient labels, moment-of-inertia rows (weights), origin, degree and mass as the data prob was set up with; only the values and uncertainties may differ (e.g. another noise seed). sbtk.invert.run#

Estimate the densities for a prepared inversion (bounded, mass-constrained least squares).

Syntax

MATLAB
fit = sbtk.invert.run(prob)          % prob from sbtk.invert.setup

Arguments

NameSizeClassUnitDefaultDescription
prob1 × 1structrequiredPrepared inversion from sbtk.invert.setup (or sbtk.invert.replace_data). Fields: prob.

Outputs

NameDescription
fitInversion result. Fields: fit.

Description

Unknowns: the background density, the relative density of each component, and the geometry asked for: the center of spheres, ellipsoids and tori with estimate_position (all coordinates, or those of a mask [x y z]) and the axis of ellipsoids and tori with estimate_axis = true. The total mass is an equality constraint and every component's density is bounded to [0, opts.rho_max_kgm3]. Measurements are whitened by the Cholesky factor of their covariance and the columns scaled to unit norm; the problem is solved with lsqlin (active set, or interior point if the active set does not converge). The geometry is refined by Gauss-Newton (at most opts.max_iter steps) with a trust region (opts.step_km for center coordinates, opts.step_deg for axis tilts): a step that does not lower the objective is undone and the trust region halved; it has converged when the objective changes by less than 1e-10 relative or a step changes every parameter by less than opts.geometry_tol of its step limit. Optional a priori constraints keep the geometry near its start (opts.position_sigma_km, opts.axis_sigma_deg), hard limits bound how far it may go (opts.max_shift_km, opts.max_tilt_deg), and spheres are kept inside the body. The parameters are listed by sbtk.internal.geometry_parameters. Optional Tikhonov regularization (opts.regularization) penalizes the relative densities. The covariance is the linearized one with the mass constraint eliminated (inequality bounds are not included; see fit.at_bound).

fit (a model: rho_bg_kgm3, components, random_field, origin_km, plus)

rho_bg_kgm3, rho_bg_sigma_kgm3background density and its 1-sigma [kg/m^3]
componentsthe components with the estimated relative densities drho_kgm3
drho_sigma_kgm31-sigma of each relative density
rho_kgm3, rho_sigma_kgm3density of each component (background + relative) and its 1-sigma
center_sigma_kmn x 3 1-sigma of the center coordinates (NaN unless estimated)
axis_sigma_degn x 3 1-sigma of the rotations about the component's first, second and third axes [deg]: the tilts of its axis and, for an ellipsoid, its turn about it (NaN unless estimated)
at_bounddensity at 0 or rho_max
resolved|relative density| > its 1-sigma
determinedfalse if the measurements (with any prior or regularization) do not determine all free parameters; cov is then a pseudo-inverse and the solution is not unique
chi2, n_obs, dofchi-square, number of measurements, degrees of freedom (n_obs minus the effective number of parameters, trace of the data resolution matrix)
chi2_reduced, p_value chi2/dof and P(chi2 >= observed) for a correct model
consistentp_value >= 0.05 (model consistent with the measurements)
labels, measured, predicted, sigma, normalized_residual
every measurement, its predicted value, (predicted - measured)/sigma
names, cov, corrparameters, their covariance and correlation
iterations, regularization, moi_labels, background, body, data_name
coef_about'origin' or 'center_of_mass' (from the measurements)
com_shift_kmthe point the predictions are about minus origin_km: for 'center_of_mass' data the model's center of mass (coefficients of degree >= 2 and inertia); for 'origin' data the point the data are about (every coefficient and the inertia), origin_km being their measured center of mass
frame_iterationsGauss-Newton steps on the model's center of mass (0 for 'origin')
frame_offset_kmchange of that center in the last step (below 1e-6 km when converged)

When obs.coef_about is 'center_of_mass' (packages read with sbtk.exchange.read_data, fields from sbtk.data.add_center_of_mass), the predicted coefficients of degree >= 2 and inertia are moved to the fitted model's own center of mass (exact translation), and the fit repeated until that center moves less than 1 mm. The model itself stays fixed: origin_km is the measured center of mass, from which layers and sectors are measured.

Example

fit  = sbtk.invert.run(prob);
sbtk.invert.summary(fit)

sbtk.invert.scan_position#

Fit the densities with one component placed at each of a list of centers: chi-square as a function of its position.

Syntax

MATLAB
sc = sbtk.invert.scan_position(prob, name, centers_km)

Arguments

NameSizeClassUnitDefaultDescription
prob1 × 1structrequiredfrom sbtk.invert.setup Fields: prob.
name1 × 1stringrequiredthe component to place: a sphere, ellipsoid or torus
centers_kmany × 3doublekmrequiredk x 3 centers to try [km], e.g. points along the measured center-of-mass offset from the center of figure, or a grid Validation: mustBeFinite.

Outputs

NameDescription
scChi-square and densities at each center. Fields: sc.

Description

For each center the component is moved there (its integrals and design-matrix column recomputed, no new geometry) and sbtk.invert.run fits the densities (and any geometry the other components estimate). The chi-square profile shows where the data put the component and whether more than one position fits: degree 1 fixes only the first moment, drho V_c times the offset, so a dense core on one side and a light one on the other give the same degree 1, and other components can make both fit. Start Gauss-Newton (estimate_position) from the lowest point, or compare the minima.

sc.centers_kmk x 3
sc.chi21 x k
sc.chi2_reduced, sc.p_value1 x k
sc.drho_kgm3k x n relative density of every component at each center
sc.rho_bg_kgm31 x k background density
sc.bestindex of the lowest chi-square
sc.fitthe fit at sc.best

sc.name, sc.names (the components)

an  = sbtk.interpret.anomaly(obs, body, 5);
u   = an.com_offset_km/norm(an.com_offset_km);              % direction of the center-of-mass offset
t   = (-0.08:0.005:0.08)';                                   % km along it

plot(1e3*t, sc.chi2)

sbtk.invert.setup#

Prepare an inversion: geometry and the design-matrix column of every component, computed once.

Syntax

MATLAB
prob = sbtk.invert.setup(body, components, obs, opts)

Arguments

NameSizeClassUnitDefaultDescription
body1 × 1structrequiredfrom sbtk.body.create (shape; the mass used is obs.mass_kg) Fields: body.
components1 × anystructrequiredthe model's components (sbtk.interior constructors). Their geometry is fixed except for the center of spheres, ellipsoids and tori with estimate_position (true, or a mask [x y z]) and the axis of ellipsoids and tori with estimate_axis = true (sbtk.invert.run). Their drho_kgm3 is estimated (the value given is not used), except for components with estimate_density = false, whose value is kept. Fields: component.
obs1 × 1structrequiredthe measurements (sbtk.data.simulate, sbtk.io.load_measurements, ...) Fields: obs.
opts1 × 1structrequiredfrom sbtk.invert.options Fields: opts.

Outputs

NameDescription
probeverything sbtk.invert.run needs. Further runs with other options (prob.opts.regularization = ...), sbtk.invert.homogeneous and sbtk.invert.replace_data reuse it (Didymos, three components: setup 0.7 s, each run about 0.2 s; tools/benchmark.m). Fields: prob.

Description

Layers and sectors are measured along rays from the measured center of mass, as in sbtk.data.simulate: for data about the center of mass it is obs.origin_km, and for data about a fixed point (coef_about 'origin', e.g. a package about the origin of its shape model file) it is the center of mass their degree-1 coefficients give, unless that is within 3 sigma of the point (the 1-sigma of the measured center of mass along the offset): the data then do not tell the point from the center of mass, and the point is kept. The geometry is built about it (prob.geo.origin_km, the fit's origin_km), and the predictions are moved exactly to the point the data are about (prob.shift_km, sbtk.internal.observe).

fit  = sbtk.invert.run(prob);                      % about 0.2 s
prob.opts.regularization = 5;                      % settings that do not select measurements
fit5 = sbtk.invert.run(prob);                      % can change between runs

sbtk.compare.evaluate#

Compare a fit with the true model, using a prepared reference (see sbtk.compare.reference).

Syntax

MATLAB
cmp = sbtk.compare.evaluate(ref, fit)

Arguments

NameSizeClassUnitDefaultDescription
ref1 × 1structrequiredPrepared reference from sbtk.compare.reference. Fields: ref.
fit1 × 1structrequiredInversion result with the same components and origin as the reference. Fields: fit.

Outputs

NameDescription
cmpComparison with the true model. Fields: cmp.

Description

fit must use the same components (same geometry) as ref. Returns the fields described in sbtk.compare.with_truth.

Example

MATLAB fragment from the help text. Uses variables defined by earlier calls: body, truth, components, prob, exact.
% many fits of the same components against one true model
ref = sbtk.compare.reference(body, truth, components, prob.geo.origin_km);   % once, about 0.5 s
for k = 1:100
    fit = sbtk.invert.run(sbtk.invert.replace_data(prob, sbtk.data.add_noise(exact, k)));
    cmp = sbtk.compare.evaluate(ref, fit);                                  % milliseconds
    R2(k) = cmp.R2;
end

sbtk.compare.reference#

The true model sampled once for comparisons with fits that use a given set of components.

Syntax

MATLAB
ref = sbtk.compare.reference(body, truth, components, origin_km)

Arguments

NameSizeClassUnitDefaultDescription
body1 × 1structrequiredThe body. Fields: body.
truth1 × 1structrequiredTrue model from sbtk.data.simulate. Fields: truth.
components1 × anystructrequiredthe components of the fits to be compared (their geometry; densities are not used) Fields: component.
origin_km1 × 3doublekmrequiredthe point their layers and sectors are measured from: the fits' origin_km (the true model's origin for data in its frame, the measured center of mass for data about the center of mass) Validation: mustBeFinite.

Outputs

NameDescription
refThe prepared reference. Fields: ref.

Description

Evaluates the true density at points filling the body (24 radial shells per facet cone, weighted by volume, in the true model's frame), the membership of every point in every component, and R2_max for these components. A model with more than 50,000 facets is sampled in the cones of 50,000 of them, chosen at random with a fixed seed (the same on every run, whatever the order of the facets in the file): about 1.2 million points, as for the 49,152-facet Didymos model, instead of 75 million for the 3,145,728-facet one, with R2 within 0.002 of the value from 9.4 million points. sbtk.compare.evaluate(ref, fit) then compares any such fit in milliseconds.

Example

MATLAB fragment from the help text. Uses variables defined by earlier calls: body, truth, components, prob.
ref = sbtk.compare.reference(body, truth, components, prob.geo.origin_km);
cmp = sbtk.compare.evaluate(ref, sbtk.invert.run(prob));
% (see sbtk.compare.evaluate for a loop over noise realizations)

sbtk.compare.with_truth#

Compare an estimated density with the true density (synthetic tests).

Syntax

MATLAB
cmp = sbtk.compare.with_truth(body, truth, fit)

Arguments

NameSizeClassUnitDefaultDescription
body1 × 1structrequiredThe body. Fields: body.
truth1 × 1structrequiredthe true model, from sbtk.data.simulate Fields: truth.
fit1 × 1structrequiredthe estimate, from sbtk.invert.run Fields: fit.

Outputs

NameDescription
cmpComparison with the true model. Fields: cmp.

Description

Both densities are evaluated at points filling the body (24 radial shells per facet cone, 1.18 million for Didymos, each weighted by its volume); the true model's layers and sectors are measured from truth.origin_km, the fit's from fit.origin_km. About 0.5 s for Didymos.

cmp.R2coefficient of determination of the estimated density: R2 = 1 - sum w (rho_est - rho_true)^2 / sum w (rho_true - mean)^2, the fraction of the variance of the true density (about its volume-weighted mean) that the estimate explains. 1 = exact; 0 = no better than a homogeneous body; < 0 = worse than that.
cmp.R2_maxthe largest R2 attainable with the same components (weighted least-squares fit of the true density by the background and the components): the limit set by the choice of components
cmp.rms_kgm3volume-weighted RMS density error [kg/m^3]
cmp.std_true_kgm3volume-weighted standard deviation of the true density [kg/m^3]
cmp.componentscomponents with the same name in both: name, estimate_kgm3, sigma_kgm3, true_kgm3 (densities), deviation_sigma (|estimate - true| / sigma)
cmp.chi2_reduced, cmp.p_valuecopied from the fit

For many fits with the same components against one true model, call sbtk.compare.reference once and sbtk.compare.evaluate for each fit.

Example

MATLAB fragment from the help text. Uses variables defined by earlier calls: body, truth, fit.
cmp = sbtk.compare.with_truth(body, truth, fit);
sbtk.compare.summary(cmp)
sbtk.plot.comparison(cmp);

sbtk.exchange.density_grid#

Density of a model at the centers of a cubic grid inside the body.

Syntax

MATLAB
grid = sbtk.exchange.density_grid(body, model, spacing_km)

Arguments

NameSizeClassUnitDefaultDescription
body1 × 1structrequiredfrom sbtk.body.create Fields: body.
model1 × 1structrequireda true model (sbtk.data.simulate) or a fit (sbtk.invert.run)
spacing_kmscalardoublekmrequiredcell edge [km] Validation: mustBePositive.

Outputs

NameDescription
gridThe density grid. Fields: grid.

Description

Cell centers lie at integer multiples of spacing_km along each axis of the shape-model frame, so grids with the same spacing coincide whoever makes them; cells whose center is inside the shape model are kept (tested along rays from the center of figure, so every model of a body has the same cells). The density is the model's density at the cell center (random field included).

grid.spacing_km, grid.x_km (n x 3), grid.density_kgm3 (n x 1), grid.density_sigma_kgm3 (n x 1, zero here; sbtk.exchange.write_solution fills it from the fit's covariance), grid.member (n x ncomp: the cell center is inside component c)

Example

MATLAB fragment from the help text. Uses variables defined by earlier calls: body, truth.
grid = sbtk.exchange.density_grid(body, truth, 0.020);                % 20 m cells
scatter3(grid.x_km(:,1), grid.x_km(:,2), grid.x_km(:,3), 4, grid.density_kgm3, 'filled');

sbtk.exchange.read_data#

Measurements and body from a measurement package (sbtk.exchange.write_data format).

Syntax

MATLAB
[obs, body] = sbtk.exchange.read_data(folder)

Arguments

NameSizeClassUnitDefaultDescription
folder1 × 1stringrequiredthe package folder (README.txt, gravity_field.txt, gravity_covariance.txt, center_of_mass.txt, moments_of_inertia.txt, conventions.txt, shape model). The shape model file the package names is read from the package, or from data/shapes/ when the package does not include it (sbtk.exchange.write_data) Validation: mustBeFolder.

Outputs

NameDescription
obsthe measurements, ready for sbtk.invert, in one of two forms: - a package about the origin of its shape model file (gravity_field.txt lists degree 1): the coefficients of degree 1..L as given, about obs.origin_km = [0 0 0] (coef_about = 'origin'), and the moments of inertia about the same origin; - a package about the center of mass: coefficients of degree 2..L with their full covariance, expanded about the measured center of mass (obs.origin_km, coef_about = 'center_of_mass'), plus degree-1 coefficients 0 +- sigma that carry the uncertainty of the center of mass, and the moment-of-inertia rows Fields: obs.
bodyfrom the package's shape model (lengths in km), mass = GM / G and the package's reference radius Fields: body.

Description

A package of exact values (no 1-sigma columns, no gravity_covariance.txt) gives a set with NaN uncertainties: give it uncertainties (e.g. sbtk.data.use_uncertainties with the precision file of the test) before sbtk.invert.

The libration ratio (B - A)/C becomes the row (B - A) - ratio*Izz = 0 with sigma ratio_sigma * Izz, where Izz is the measured Izz if the package has one, otherwise the Izz of the homogeneous body.

Example

MATLAB fragment from the help text. Uses variables defined by earlier calls: components.
[obs, body] = sbtk.exchange.read_data("UCB-DATA1-Didymos");
fit = sbtk.invert.solve(body, components, obs, sbtk.invert.options());

Write a measurement package to send to other teams (nothing about the interior).

MATLAB
folder = sbtk.exchange.write_data(parent, data_set, body, obs, prepared_by)

Arguments

NameSizeClassUnitDefaultDescription

grid_kmscalardoublekmrequiredcell edge [km] for the departures from the background density (sbtk.gravity.field_at; not used for a homogeneous model) Validation: mustBePositive.

Outputs

NameDescription
filePath of the potential_acceleration.txt file that was written.

Description

Writes potential_acceleration.txt, one row per point, in SI units as the HLP6 makers' cross-validation asks: the position [m], the potential U [m^2/s^2] (positive, U = G integral rho / |r - r'| dV) and the acceleration, the gradient of U [m/s^2], without the rotation of the body. The header names the method (sbtk.gravity.field_at). The file is added to the list of files in README.txt.

Example

pkg = sbtk.exchange.write_data(fullfile(out.folder, "redacted"), data_set, body, exact, prepared_by);
sbtk.exchange.write_potential(pkg, body, truth, points_km, 0.020);

sbtk.io.read_jpl_gravity#

Measurements from a JPL SSD gravity-field file (normalized coefficients + covariance).

Syntax

MATLAB
obs = sbtk.io.read_jpl_gravity(file, body, name, origin_km, degree)

Arguments

NameSizeClassUnitDefaultDescription
file1 × 1stringrequiredJPL SSD gravity file in MATLAB-assignment form (REF_RADIUS, NORMALIZED, NAMES = {...}, VALS = [...], COV = [...]), e.g. the OSIRIS-REx Bennu field Validation: mustBeFile.
body1 × 1structrequiredfrom sbtk.body.create; body.R_ref_km must equal the file's REF_RADIUS Fields: body.
name1 × 1stringrequiredname of the data set
origin_km1 × 3doublekmrequiredpoint the field is expanded about, in shape-model coordinates [km] (the center of mass of the gravity solution) Validation: mustBeFinite.
degreescalardoublerequiredhighest degree to keep (2 .. the file's DEGREE) Validation: mustBeInteger, mustBeGreaterThanOrEqual(degree, 2).

Outputs

NameDescription
obsThe measurement set: coefficients of degree 2 … degree with their covariance, coef_about = 'origin'. Fields: obs.

Description

The file is parsed as text (not executed). Zonal terms J_l are converted to C_l0 = -J_l (with the matching sign changes in the covariance); C_lm, S_lm are kept. The covariance of the kept coefficients is the full submatrix of the file's covariance (GM row and column removed). The mass is GM / G. Degree-1 terms are absent in such files (the expansion is about the center of mass); add them with sbtk.data.add_center_of_mass.

Example

MATLAB, from the help text
body = sbtk.body.create("Bennu", sbtk.shape.bundled("bennu"), 1190, 0.290);
file = fullfile(sbtk.root, "data", "gravity", "bennu_osirisrex_jpl_2019.txt");
obs  = sbtk.io.read_jpl_gravity(file, body, "bennu_jpl2019", [0 0 0], 4);
obs  = sbtk.data.add_center_of_mass(obs, [0 0 0], 0.001);

Related functions

Mentioned in the help text
sbtk.body.create, sbtk.data.add_center_of_mass, sbtk.root, sbtk.shape.bundled
Calls

Description

Keywords (see sbtk.io.write_measurements and docs/data_formats.md):

Other keywords are ignored. This is the entry point for data from other teams: convert their files to this format, or build the measurements from arrays with sbtk.data.from_coefficients.

One keyword per line, values separated by spaces, '#' lines are comments, so every block can be pasted into a spreadsheet or another code. sbtk.plot.anomaly#

The measured anomaly coefficient by coefficient, with the anomalies of models and how well they match it.

Syntax

MATLAB
fig = sbtk.plot.anomaly(an, models, names)

Arguments

NameSizeClassUnitDefaultDescription
an1 × 1structrequiredthe measurements' anomaly (sbtk.interpret.anomaly of a measurement set) Fields: an.
models1 × anycellrequiredcell array of model anomalies (sbtk.interpret.anomaly of a fit or a true model, same degree), or {} for the measurements alone
namesrequiredone name per model Validation: mustBeText.

Outputs

NameDescription
figHandle of the new figure.

Description

Top: each coefficient's anomaly (field minus homogeneous body, about the center of figure) divided by its 1-sigma, so that every degree can be read on one axis: black, the measurements with their +-1 sigma; colors, the models. A model fitted to some of the coefficients (a fit, an.fitted_labels) has filled markers on those and open markers on the others, which it predicts. Bottom: (model - measurement)/sigma; the gray band is +-1, the dashed lines +-3. Both axes are symmetric logarithmic, sign(v) log10(1 + |v|): linear near 0, logarithmic beyond a few sigma. Zonal coefficients are shown as J_l = -C_l0 (the sign of their anomaly flips with them); degree 1 is the center-of-mass offset (C11, S11, C10 = x, y, z / (sqrt(3) R_ref)). Vertical lines separate the degrees.

Example

MATLAB fragment from the help text. Uses variables defined by earlier calls: obs, body, fit.
an  = sbtk.interpret.anomaly(obs, body, 5);
fig = sbtk.plot.anomaly(an, {sbtk.interpret.anomaly(fit, body, 5)}, "core + torus");

Related functions

Mentioned in the help text

sbtk.plot.anomaly_map#

Each degree of the anomaly as a map: where mass is added and where it is taken away.

Syntax

MATLAB
fig = sbtk.plot.anomaly_map(ge)

Arguments

NameSizeClassUnitDefaultDescription
ge1 × 1structrequiredfrom sbtk.interpret.geometry Fields: ge.

Outputs

NameDescription
figHandle of the new figure.

Description

One row per degree from 2: left, the anomaly C - C_CD of that degree as a pattern on the sphere (latitude and longitude from the center of figure, in the axes of the shape model); right, its rest after the scaled homogeneous field. Red where a mass added near the surface in that direction would make the pattern, blue where a mass taken away would; each panel on its own color scale symmetric about 0. + marks the strongest excess, x the strongest deficit; the star is the direction of the center-of-mass offset (degree 1). The same direction of excess at every degree points to one compact mass; extremes along the equator and at the poles in the even degrees to a belt, a ring or polar caps.

sbtk.plot.coefficient_comparison#

The measured anomaly C - C_CD coefficient by coefficient with +-1 sigma, the solutions' anomalies, and their residuals.

Syntax

Arguments

NameSizeClassUnitDefaultDescription

models1 × anycellrequired1 x k cell of the solutions' anomalies (sbtk.interpret.anomaly of a fit or of the model of a point-mass solution), or {} for the measurements alone
moiany × 3doublerequiredk x 3 each solution's (predicted - measured)/sigma of the inertia rows of an (an.moi_labels), e.g. from the fit's normalized residuals; zeros(0, 3) without solutions or without inertia rows

max_degreescalardoublerequiredthe highest degree shown Validation: mustBeInteger, mustBePositive.

Outputs

NameDescription

Description

One column per degree (its width proportional to its number of coefficients) and one for the moments of inertia, if the measurements have them. Top: the measured coefficient minus that of the constant-density body, with +-1 sigma, in the units of the coefficients (zonal terms as J_l = -C_l0, degree 1 as C10, C11, S11); each solution's difference from the constant-density body as a marker; 0 is the constant-density body. Each degree has its own linear scale, its power of ten in its title. Bottom (with solutions): (solution - measurement)/sigma, the band +-1, the dashed lines +-3; values beyond +-6 drawn at the edge as triangles. sbtk.plot.coefficient_residuals#

Map of normalized residuals: one row per fit, one column per measurement, fitted ones outlined.

Syntax

MATLAB
fig = sbtk.plot.coefficient_residuals(preds, names)

Arguments

NameSizeClassUnitDefaultDescription
preds1 × anycellrequiredcell array of sbtk.invert.predict results for the same measurements (fits to different subsets of them, or with different models)
namesrequiredone name per row Validation: mustBeText.

Outputs

NameDescription
figHandle of the new figure.

Description

Each cell is (predicted - measured)/sigma of one measurement for one fit, colored on a symmetric logarithmic scale, sign(v) log10(1 + |v|), saturated at 100 (blue: predicted too small, red: too large; nearly white within 1 sigma). The measurements a fit was fitted to are outlined, so one row shows how well a fit matches its own coefficients (outlined cells) and how well it predicts the others. Right: chi-square per measurement of the fitted rows and of the others (with their covariance). Zonal coefficients are labeled J_l; their residual is that of C_l0 (the same size, opposite sign of J_l).

    fit = sbtk.invert.solve(body, components, sbtk.data.select_coefficients(obs, sets{k}), opts);
    preds{k} = sbtk.invert.predict(fit, body, obs);
end
fig = sbtk.plot.coefficient_residuals(preds, ["degree 1 + J2", "+ J3"]);

sbtk.plot.contributions#

How much of each coefficient's anomaly each component of a model makes.

Syntax

MATLAB
fig = sbtk.plot.contributions(an, fit, body, max_degree)

Arguments

NameSizeClassUnitDefaultDescription
an1 × 1structrequiredthe measurements' anomaly (sbtk.interpret.anomaly of a measurement set) Fields: an.
fit1 × 1structrequireda fitted model with a few components (sbtk.invert.run) Fields: fit.
body1 × 1structrequiredthe body Fields: body.
max_degreescalardoublerequiredthe highest degree shown Validation: mustBeInteger, mustBePositive.

Outputs

NameDescription
figHandle of the new figure.

Description

The anomaly of a model, its coefficients minus those of the constant-density body, is the sum over its components of their relative density times their signature (sbtk.interpret.signatures: the coefficients of the component with the mass it moves taken evenly from the rest of the body). For every coefficient of degrees 1 to max_degree a bar is split into these parts, positive ones stacked up and negative ones down; the black dot with its bar is the measured anomaly +-1 sigma, the white diamond the model's sum. Which component makes a coefficient, and with which sign, is the reason it sits where it does: a dense core off the center of figure makes degree 1 and lowers J2, a light torus about the z-axis raises J2 and changes J4, and so on. Zonal terms are shown as J_l = -C_l0.

Example

MATLAB fragment from the help text. Uses variables defined by earlier calls: obs, body, fit.
fig = sbtk.plot.contributions(sbtk.interpret.anomaly(obs, body, 4), fit, body, 4);

sbtk.plot.difference_from_homogeneous#

Gravity coefficients minus those of the homogeneous body, coefficient by coefficient.

Syntax

MATLAB
[fig, differences] = sbtk.plot.difference_from_homogeneous(body, sets, names, scale, frame)

Arguments

NameSizeClassUnitDefaultDescription
body1 × 1structrequiredthe body: its shape model gives the homogeneous body (density M/V everywhere) Fields: body.
sets1 × anycellrequiredcell array of coefficient sets, each one of a measurement set exact values (sbtk.data.simulate), measurements (sbtk.data.add_noise), a package (sbtk.exchange.read_data), ... a true model truth from sbtk.data.simulate an inversion result fit from sbtk.invert.run: the field of the fitted model
namesrequiredone legend entry per set, e.g. ["true model" "estimate"] Validation: mustBeText.
scale1 × 1stringrequired"linear": the signed difference, with +-3 sigma bars for sets that have uncertainties (measurement sets with coef_cov); "log": the absolute difference, with 3 sigma drawn as a separate line Validation: mustBeMember(scale, ["linear", "log"]).
frame1 × 1stringrequiredthe axes both fields are expressed in (sbtk.gravity.center_of_mass_frame): "shape": the axes of the shape-model frame; "spin": z along the axis of the largest moment of the set, x the shape-model x-axis projected onto the plane normal to it, as in body-fixed radio-science fields (the OSIRIS-REx field of Bennu). The set has C21 = S21 = 0, so the homogeneous body's C21, S21 show how far its axis of the largest moment is tilted from the set's; "principal": the principal axes of inertia of the set (x the axis of the smallest moment, z of the largest). The set has C21 = S21 = S22 = 0, so the homogeneous body's C21, S21, S22 show how its principal axes are tilted and turned. Validation: mustBeMember(frame, ["shape", "spin", "principal"]).

Outputs

NameDescription
figthe figure
differencesstruct array, one per set: name, labels (as plotted: C10, C11, S11, J2, ...), difference, sigma (1-sigma; NaN where the set has none), axes_deg ([tilt turn]: angle between the axes of the largest moment of the set and of the homogeneous body, and angle about that axis between their axes of the smallest moment, deg)

Description

Both fields are about their own center of mass, as radio-science fields are:

  degrees >= 2   the set about its center of mass minus the homogeneous body about its
                 center of mass (the center of figure)
  degree 1       the set's center of mass minus the center of figure, as C11, S11, C10 =
                 (x, y, z)/(sqrt(3) R_ref) in the axes of the plot: about its own center of
                 mass each field's degree 1 is zero, so this shows where the interior moves
                 the center of mass instead

sbtk.gravity.center_of_mass_frame moves each set to its center of mass and into the axes (it states how the center of mass of each kind of set is found); the homogeneous field is rotated into the same axes. Differences are fully normalized, in SBTK order; zonal coefficients are shown as J_l = -C_l0, so their difference has the opposite sign of the C_l0 difference. The reference radius is the set's (body.R_ref_km for truth and fit). One geometry is built per set (about 1 s for 49,152 facets at degree 4, about a minute for 3 million facets).

The plot shows how far the gravity field of an interior departs from that of a uniform density, and, against 3 sigma, which departures measurements resolve. The three frames show the same information: the spin and principal axes move the difference in orientation of the principal axes into the homogeneous body's degree-2 terms.

Example

MATLAB fragment from the help text. Uses variables defined by earlier calls: body, interior, unc, components.
[exact, truth] = sbtk.data.simulate(body, interior, 4, "T1");
sbtk.plot.difference_from_homogeneous(body, {truth}, "true model", "linear", "principal");
obs = sbtk.data.add_noise(sbtk.data.set_uncertainties(exact, unc), 1);
fit = sbtk.invert.solve(body, components, obs);
sbtk.plot.difference_from_homogeneous(body, {obs, fit}, ["measured" "estimate"], "log", "shape");

Related functions

Mentioned in the help text
sbtk.data.add_noise, sbtk.data.set_uncertainties, sbtk.data.simulate, sbtk.exchange.read_data, sbtk.gravity.center_of_mass_frame, sbtk.invert.run, sbtk.invert.solve
Calls
sbtk.gravity.center_of_mass_frame, sbtk.gravity.forward, sbtk.gravity.geometry, sbtk.interior.create, sbtk.interior.no_components

Each measurement with its +-1 sigma interval against the constant-density (homogeneous) value.

Syntax

MATLAB

For every gravity coefficient (about the center of figure) and every inertia row: (measured - homogeneous)/sigma with its +-1 sigma interval. The homogeneous body, the same shape model with the bulk density everywhere, is the line at 0: an interval that does not reach it is a measurement that differs from constant density at 1 sigma. Gray: within 1 sigma of constant density; amber: 1 to 3 sigma; red: more than 3 sigma. The axis is symmetric logarithmic, sign(v) log10(1 + |v|). Zonal coefficients are shown as J_l = -C_l0; degree 1 is the center-of-mass offset from the center of figure. The title counts the measurements in each class.

Example

MATLAB fragment from the help text. Uses variables defined by earlier calls: obs, body.
fig = sbtk.plot.significance(sbtk.interpret.anomaly(obs, body, 5));

Related functions

sbtk.plot.solution_cuts#

Several solutions side by side on the same cuts and color scale, and their density in the same cells.

Syntax

MATLAB
[fig, cs] = sbtk.plot.solution_cuts(body, models, names, spacing_km)

Arguments

NameSizeClassUnitDefaultDescription
body1 × 1structrequiredthe body Fields: body.
models1 × anycellrequired1 x k cell of solutions: fits (sbtk.invert.run), point-mass models (pm.model of sbtk.interpret.point_masses), true models
namesrequiredone name per solution Validation: mustBeText.
spacing_kmscalardoublekmrequiredthe cell size [km]; cells on the grid of sbtk.interior.sphere_grid Validation: mustBePositive.

Outputs

NameDescription
figHandle of the new figure.
csEach solution's density minus the bulk density in the same cells, the cells' volumes inside the body, and the correlation of each pair of solutions.

Description

One row per solution, the planes z = 0 (left) and y = 0 (right) through the center of figure: its density minus the bulk density M/V (red: denser, blue: lighter), on one color scale for all, at the median of the solutions' ranges (the strongest saturate). Components and sectors are drawn with their own boundaries. A sphere smaller than half a cell inside the body (a point mass of a grid) has no shape at this resolution: its mass is spread over the cell of its center, so point masses show as cells.

To compare the solutions in numbers, each is also averaged over the same cubic cells (the small spheres in the cell of their center, everything else sampled at 27 points per cell inside the body):

cs.centers_kmK x 3 cell centers
cs.volume_m3K x 1 the volume of each cell inside the body
cs.anomaly_kgm3K x k each solution's cell density minus the bulk density
cs.correlationk x k correlation of the cells of each pair of solutions

Example

MATLAB fragment from the help text. Uses variables defined by earlier calls: body, fit1, fit2, pm.
fig = sbtk.plot.solution_cuts(body, {fit1, fit2, pm.model}, ["core", "sectors", "point masses"], 0.040);

Reference

Data structures

SBTK passes MATLAB structures between its functions. Each structure has a fixed set of fields, listed below; the field names carry their units (see Units). Sizes refer to the Didymos examples (49,152 facets, degree 4) unless stated: n is the number of measurements, nc the number of components, nf the number of facets, L the highest degree.

A model is any structure with the fields rho_bg_kgm3, components, random_field and origin_km: a true model (truth) or an inversion result (fit). Functions that evaluate, plot or compare densities accept either.

component: Interior component#

Created by sbtk.interior.sphere, sbtk.interior.ellipsoid, sbtk.interior.torus, sbtk.interior.layer, sbtk.interior.sector, sbtk.interior.sector_grid.

One region of uniform relative density. Every component has every field, so components of different types can be concatenated into one structure array ([c1, c2]); fields that a type does not use are zero. The geometry definitions are in Density distributions.

name#textName; unique within a model.

ring_radius_km#scalarkmTorus: radius of the circle at the center of the tube.
tube_radius_km#scalarkmTorus: radius of the tube.
